en: Oṃ (Included within the Divine Scriptures of the Illustrious Pāñcarātra) Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā
The First Chapter: The Method of the Introduction of the Treatise.
Auspiciousness: Salutations to Śrī Vāsudeva, whose nature is truth and knowledge.
To the one who bestows grace upon his own devotees and grants liberation as the sole fruit;
[here begins] the sages' question regarding the means to liberation.
The sages:

The Vedas have been heard by you previously, as well as the various Dharmaśāstras; yet, O ascetic, we do not perceive the means to liberation within them. Therefore, teach us that great, auspicious scripture which brings about the supreme good.
"Thus we shall cross over the suffering of saṃsāra by the path of knowledge. This was Vasiṣṭha’s reply. Vasiṣṭha: [continued].

The glorification of the Pāñcarātra Āgama and its introduction: Devotion to the Lord alone is the cause of liberation for devotees; the scripture that teaches such devotion is known as the Pāñcarātra Āgama. 4.

O best of sages, listen to that supreme secret tradition called the Pāñcarātra, which was formerly spoken by Viṣṇu to Brahmā for the purpose of dispelling the quality of rajas, and which enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra.
The entire *Pāñcarātra-āgama* was heard by Brahmā from Keśava over the course of five nights, amounting to one and a half crores [of verses].
By means of this scriptural tradition (*āgama-śāstra*), the construction of sacred images, temples, and so forth is prescribed.
Having fashioned [an image] and installed it, a person who constantly worships it attains the eternal state,
free from rebirth.
(Pañcarātrāgama 8)
The sages,
for the purpose of hearing the traditional teaching, asked the sage:
"O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, you who are proficient in all the scriptures."
"Reveal the procedure for that Pāñcarātra scripture for us who desire the state of liberation and seek refuge.
This is Vasiṣṭha’s reply.
Vasiṣṭha said:
O all you sages, listen to this Ekāyana Veda, which is named after its single goal; it is the definition of the words and meanings of the Śrī Pañcarātra Āgama, including its designations. 10.
It is recited under such names as Pāñcarātra, Mūlaveda, Sātvata-tantra, and Bhagavac-chāstra; indeed,
there is no other path for the attainment of liberation than this.
Therefore, the wise declare it to be the "Single Path" (ekāyana),
because it is the traditional scripture (āgama) that explains right conduct and prescribes the means for attaining the destination of the soul.
Because it explains the reality of the self, it is counted as an *āgama*. This great system is the root of the great tree of the Vedas; thus, it is the Root Veda (*mūlaveda*).

O twice-born ones, those yogins who have become the *Ṛg* and other *skandhas* are the branches of that [Veda]. For the Veda, which is the root of the world and is essentially Vāsudeva, its status as the "Root Veda" is established by virtue of being its primary expositor. (14–15)
Because it was spoken by Hari, whose nature is purity (*sattva*), this *tantra* is called *Sātvata*;
it extends the vast range of meanings based on the essence of reality. (16)
Because it provides protection, it is called a *tantra*;
indeed, the *Pañcarātra* is the root cause of all scriptures. Among all castes, the Brahmin is supreme; among all stages of life, the ascetic is supreme.
Just as Gaṅgā is among rivers and Acyuta is among deities, so too is the Pāñcarātra praised among all the scriptures. 18.
Thus, among all the sacred texts, the Pāñcarātra is extolled.
The Pāñcarātra is a great, divine scripture that elucidates the Vedas;
it should be mastered especially as it was sung by the Blessed One himself.
One should worship the Supreme Person directly, or appropriately through images and other such forms.
O Blessed One,
the sages [inquired] regarding the method of worshipping Him; thus begins the inquiry of the sages.
Who indeed is the person [Puruṣa] when so described? What is the injunction regarding his worship?
O best of the twice-born, tell me in detail the characteristics of the image (pradimālakṣaṇa). O blessed sage, tell me, what is it like?
(21) This is the speech of Vasiṣṭha.
Vasiṣṭha [relates] the introduction of the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā by the Lord Puruṣottama himself in former times.
The divine Pāñcarātra Āgama was spoken by me to my father, the Self-born;
it was obtained by me from the ocean like nectar—
this is the praise of the Saṃhitā.

From the plowing [of the ground] up to the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), and from the consecration up to the festival (utsava); indeed, O Puruṣottama, the Puruṣottama-saṃhitā declares that the festival begins with the commencement [of the rites] and ends with the expiation (prāyaścitta). 23–24.
The purpose of this treatise is liberation, which is difficult to attain by nature;
the subject matter is the supreme propitiation of the Blessed One; and the relationship is perceived by the wise as that between the goal to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment. 25.
This Tantra has its root in the Śruti and is an authoritative source, like the Kalpasūtras.
There is no scripture higher than the Veda, and no deity higher than Keśava.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, worship the Lord of Gods according to this very injunction alone. (26-27)
O sages, listen to the name of that Tantra, O sages!
"How many divisions are there of the tantras, and what are their names?
O best of Brahmins, I wish to hear this, for my curiosity is great. (28)
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Vasiṣṭha, I have learned from this tantra that there are one hundred and eight recitations of the name of the Tantra."
Listen with full concentration to their names as well:
the Mārkaṇḍeya, the Pārṣada, the Nāradīya Saṃhitā, the Viśvāmitra, the Vainateya, and the Garuḍa Saṃhitā. (29–30)
The *Kāśyapa*, the one called *Paiṅgala*, the *Vāsiṣṭha* named *Puṣkara*,
the one called *Sattva*, and the one called *Manaka* constitute the *Viṣṇusiddhāntasaṃhitā*.
The *Pādma* is to be known as the *Padmodbhava*, as well as the *Vihageṃdra* and the *Vāruṇa*.
Nalakūbara, Māgneya, Vāmana, and likewise Śaunaka; Pāvika, Pārama, Aiśvarya, and thereafter Pārāśarya;
Viṣvaksena (and Khageṃdra), Khageśa, and likewise Vīramāṅgalika. 32–33.
The Śrīviṣṇutilaka, the Lakṣmītilaka-saṃhitā,
the Daśottara, the Śāṇḍilya, the Mārīca-saṃhitā, the Maudgala, the Romaśa, the Vāmadeva, and the Subodhaka. 34.
Meru, Gaṅgā, Satyokta, Aindra, Paramapuruṣa (35), Nārasiṃha, Hayagrīva, Dūrvāsa, Kṛṣṇasaṃhitā,
Puṣṭitantra, Mahātantra, and Puruṣottamasaṃhitā (36).
The Brahmāṇḍa, Cāpikoma, Īśvara, Matsyasaṃhitā,
Bhāradvāja, Yājñavalkya, Gajeṃdra, Manusmṛti, Śrīpuṣkara, Mahālakṣmī, Kuśala, Ānanda, and Pāvana. 37.
Then [he taught] the question of Pañcapraśnaśrī, Prahlāda Sātvata,
Kapiñjala as spoken by Brahmā, Agastya, and likewise Jaimini; as well as the Viṣṇuvaibhavika, the Saura, the Saumya, and the Hārīti.

The Kātyāyanasaṃhitā, the Vālmīkisaṃhitā, the Hairaṇyasaṃhitā, the Kāpilasaṃhitā, as well as the Jābālisaṃhitā, the Vāyavīyasaṃhitā, the Vāruṇasaṃhitā, the Āṅgirasasaṃhitā, the Nārāyaṇasaṃhitā known as the Vyāsasaṃhitā, and the Brahmanāradasaṃhitā. (40)
The Dattātreyasaṃhitā, Kaṇvasaṃhitā, Gārgyasaṃhitā, Kalirāghavasaṃhitā, Prācetasasaṃhitā, Pauṣkarasaṃhitā, Madhusūdanasaṃhitā, Mathusaṃgrahasaṃhitā,
the dialogue between Mitra and Śukra, and the one called Umāmāheśvara. 41–42.
The *Bodhāyana*, the *Ananta*, the *Vārāha*, the *Nanandana*,
as well as the *Pulastya* and *Pulaha*, constitute the *Saṃhitā* of Vāsudeva (43).
The *Saṃkarṣaṇa*, the *Bhṛgu*, and the *Gāndharva-gaṇa-saṃhitā* [also belong to it].
Thus, the one hundred and eightfold higher knowledge (uttara-vijñāna) from Nārada; that which is not mentioned here should be taken from elsewhere—
for what is not mentioned in one place should be taken from another among the various Saṃhitās.
"The sacrificer, with great diligence, should first choose an Ācārya"—
thus [ends] the chapter titled "The Rule for the Descent of the Scripture" in the *Puruṣottama-saṃhitā*, within the *Śrī-pāñcarātra-mahopaniṣad*.
The First Chapter. Oṃ.
In the Śrīmat Pāñcarātra Divyāgama, within the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā.
The Second Chapter:
The Characteristics of the Preceptor and Others, and the Procedure for Examining the Ground.
The Sages.
The Sage’s Question for the Sake of Hearing the Characteristics of the Preceptor and Others:
"O Lord of Sages, you have stated that 'one should choose a preceptor';
what kind of person is the sacrificer, and what are the characteristics of the preceptor? (1)
"Tell us the characteristics of both the teacher and the sacrificer.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha replied: "The characteristics of the teacher..."
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra born in the natural order (anuloma),
provided he is endowed with faith and devotion, wealthy, devoted to dharma, and possessed of a serene mind, such a patron (yajamāna) may, out of reverence, perform a sacrifice for the gods.
First, one should choose an Ācārya, for spiritual accomplishments depend upon him;
he should be a knower of the Pañcarātra, tranquil, one who has exerted effort in the Siddhāntas, born of the lineage of the Lord, pure, free from greed, and devoid of pride. 4.
The most excellent of great devotees, firm in his vow of having only one wife, observed that auspicious vow of monogamy. He was a Brāhmaṇa endowed with truthfulness, possessed of virtuous conduct,
complete in all his limbs, beautiful, young, and a knower of the Vedas.

One who knows the true meaning of all scriptures, who maintains the sacred fire, who is pure, who understands the origin, maintenance, and dissolution [of the world], and who is a proponent of Brahman. (7) [Additional readings]
To one who is endowed with faith and devotion, who has surrendered to the Guru and been initiated,
who is dedicated to the service of others, who has exerted effort in the knowledge of Yoga,
who is peaceful, self-controlled, renowned, and adorned with all excellent qualities;

The sequence for the selection of the preceptor (ācārya) is as follows: one who is far from evil, whose self is serene, who is devoted to the eight-syllable mantra, who knows the essential principles of the rite of installation (pratiṣṭhā), and who is intent upon the practice of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana).
Then, the patron, at the time of the ritual, should seek out a teacher endowed with such characteristics; at the commencement of the rite, he should present a cow, land, gold,
and a coconut to the teacher.
Regarding the examination of the site:

for the successful completion of the temple, the preceptor and the patron should perform the examination of the ground and other preliminary rites according to the path prescribed by the scriptures. (10)
Regarding the description of the classification of earth and the determination of suitable and unsuitable ground:
there are four types, namely Supadmā, Bhadrakā, Pūrṇā, and Dhūmrā;
O best of the twice-born, the first three are to be accepted, while the last is to be rejected.
That place which is strewn with *kuśa* and *darbha* grass, always provided with water, and where deer possessing the characteristics of beautiful lotuses reside, is celebrated as "Supadmā. 12.
The auspicious characteristic is that it bears fruit; it is like a sacrificial tree endowed with creepers and shrubs,
full— this is the characteristic.
She is seen as Bhadrakā and is proclaimed to be Pūrṇā; Dhūmrā possesses auspicious marks and,
accompanied by water, rests upon the peak of the mountain.
Abounding in crows, hawks, and vultures, hard, and crowded with wolves;
joined with saline soil—this is proclaimed as "Dhūmra" (smoky). One should avoid such smoky ground and cause [the ritual] to be performed on auspicious ground and the like. 14–15.
The procedure for digging:
one should dig the ground to the depth of a knee; having removed the earth, one should fill it back in—this is the most excellent ground.
Where the soil contains an abundance of dust, that ground is considered the best (16).

The middling and the inferior [grounds] are determined by plowing and sowing; through the process of sowing, one ascertains whether the ground is fit or unfit for cultivation. Even when the soil is level, it may be considered middling or, if deficient, regarded as inferior.
Having examined it thoroughly in many ways, one should gradually draw furrows with ploughs.
One should sow sesame and mung beans, barley, wild rice,
and mustard seeds, or else all kinds of grains suitable for sacrifice on every side.
They ascend for three nights; this is called the highest ground.
One should diligently avoid that ground which has not yet sprouted. At the time when the crops are ready to bear fruit, one should ensure the satisfaction of the cattle.
Then the best of preceptors should worship the world-protectors;
he should offer a bali-oblation at night with parched grain, fruits, and cakes, and he should worship Kumuda and the other [deities] with red perfumes and flowers. 20–21.
Then, having worshipped the earth and likewise having worshipped the Goddess Earth (Bhūdevī), one should perform the Vāstupūjā;
thereafter, having performed the Śāntihoma, one should observe a vigil at night. 22.

Then, when the dawn has become clear and pure, having fulfilled his duties, he should perform the *puṇyāha* rite; thereafter, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas. Then, the digging [of the pit] is performed again.
Thereafter, one should have that field excavated on all sides until reaching the water; having worshipped Varuṇa in that water, one should cause the stone pegs (śaṅku) to be set.
This is the procedure for the installation of the pegs (śaṅkusthāpanavidhi).
Having fashioned that gnomon (śaṅku) in three parts— with four [units] at the base and eight square faces in its middle— its tip should be shaped like a lotus.
Then, one should worship the gnomon endowed with such characteristics.
Having wound it with a protective thread (*rakṣāsūtra*), one should place jewels and other items into the pit (verse 26).
Having consecrated the tortoise-diagram (*kūrmayantra*) and the great Sudarśana diagram, one should place a stone pillar (*śilāśaṅku*) upon it and fix it in place (verse 27).
The procedure for filling:
in the first [layer] one fills with sand; likewise, in the second with gravel;
in the third with *dhātrī* fruit; and in the fourth with *jaṃbuka* fruit. 28.
In the fifth [section] there is the *kapittha* fruit, and in the sixth the coconut;
in the seventh, however, the *bilva* fruit—this is the extent up to the stone slab (29).
Having filled it, one should then fill the eighth part with mud.
One should make it square and level, and strike it with the elephant-foot [mallet]. Having thus established the stake, one should begin to move it;
one should cause the height of the temple to be constructed in accordance with one's wealth.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Examining the Ground and the Characteristics of the Preceptor and Others," in the *Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the *Śrī Pañcarātra*.
Oṃ.
In the divine scripture of the glorious Pañcarātra, in the Śrīpuruṣottama-saṃhitā,
this is the third chapter.
The Procedure for Explaining the Fruits of Building a Temple;
the Question of the Sages regarding the Hearing of the Fruits of Building a Temple.
"O Sage, tell me of the merit of one who, having constructed a temple and installed a deity there with devotion, performs worship for that [deity].
This is the speech addressed to Vasiṣṭha, concerning the proclamation of the fruits of constructing a temple.
Vasiṣṭha shall describe the fruits and other benefits for one desiring to construct a temple for Vāsudeva and others— a divine abode that removes the sins of a thousand births. 2.
Even those who rejoice in a house being built for Kṛṣṇa by the builders in their minds— having the sins of a hundred births destroyed—
they too are liberated from evils and attain the supreme goal.
A man who, having caused a temple of Hari to be built, quickly leads ten million ancestors of his lineage to the world of Viṣṇu;
indeed, his ancestors dwell in the world of Viṣṇu, beautifully adorned, once they have seen it.
Released from the sufferings of hell, they go to the abode of the Creator, the temple of Viṣṇu, which destroys the flood of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin;
that fruit which is not obtained through sacrifices is obtained by building a temple.

By constructing a temple for the gods, one obtains the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas). Whatever merit is gained from [offering] one's own body to the gods or from [dying] in battle, that fruit and so forth is certainly attained even by one who acts with deceit, provided they have offered flowers and performed worship. 7–8.
One who maintains one house attains heaven; one who maintains two houses reaches the world of Brahmā;
one who maintains five houses reaches the world of Śambhu; by maintaining six houses, one finds stability with Hara; but one who maintains sixteen houses shall attain both devotion and liberation.
Having caused the temple of Hari to be made as inferior, middling, or superior,
one attains heaven, the world of Viṣṇu, and liberation respectively;
by building a superior abode for Viṣṇu, one obtains that which even a wealthy man might seek.
Even a man possessing great wealth obtains that same merit by merely constructing a small temple for the Lord;
having acquired wealth and built even a modest abode for Hari,
he attains a most excellent and superior merit.
Even with a hundred thousand, a thousand, a hundred, or even half of that, one reaches the abode of Hari; there the Lord whose banner bears Garuḍa dwells.
Those who playfully throw dust into the temple of Hari [attain the same].

The ancestors who have gone to the higher worlds perform [meritorious acts] for Vāsudeva at a sacred ford (tīrtha), a holy sanctuary (āyatana), a field of the Siddhas, or likewise in a hermitage (āśrama).
By constructing a sanctuary for Viṣṇu, one obtains three times the fruit as previously described.
Regarding the specific fruits of sweeping and other services in the temple:
those who smear the Vaishnava abode with lime-wash and with arrangements of bandhūka flowers go to the city of the Blessed Lord.
A person who, having lifted up one who has fallen or is falling— and who has already fallen for the sake of another— attains twice the fruit of reaching the abode of Hari. Furthermore,
he who is the rescuer of the fallen and the protector of the fallen [attains that same reward].

O Viṣṇu, the man who performs the installation of Your temple here becomes a partaker of the world of Viṣṇu; he who builds even a single brick for the abode of Hari is honored in the world of Viṣṇu along with his entire lineage. 19.19

He alone is meritorious and worthy of worship both in this world and the next—20—who causes a temple to be built for Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva; he alone is truly born with merit performed, and his lineage is indeed protected. 21.
One who builds a house for Viṣṇu, Rudra, the Sun, the Goddess, or others does not possess fame;
O fool, what is the use of vast hoards of wealth to one who merely guards them? He who does not have a temple built for Kṛṣṇa with wealth acquired through hardship [is truly lost].
The wealth of one who does not provide for his ancestors, Brahmins, and the gods is not to be enjoyed;
nor is it for the enjoyment of kinsmen. Thus, the acquisition of that wealth is useless, for as certain as death is for men, so too is the loss of wealth.
The deluded man clings there to life and wealth; he does not give according to his means for the sake of charity or for the enjoyment of embodied beings.
Nor is it for fame, nor for the sake of dharma; thus, his ownership possesses no excellence whatsoever.

Therefore, having acquired wealth— whether by chance or through human effort— one should duly give it to the foremost of the twice-born and cause monuments of fame to be made; for since [the merit] from monuments is superior to that from gifts, one should do so.

Therefore, at that time, the wise man, having established the temples and other dwellings of Viṣṇu and the others, should have the abode of Hari established by the most excellent of men who are devoted to Him;
thus the three worlds, including all things moving and stationary, would be rendered difficult to overcome [by enemies].
The past, the present, and the future; the gross, the subtle, and likewise the other;
everything from Brahma down to a blade of grass—all this has its origin in Viṣṇu, the God of gods, the all-pervading Great Soul. 29–30.
O Blessed One, having invested [the image] with the thread, one is not born again on earth; the fruit obtained from making the cord for Viṣṇu is the same as that for the gods.
(31) This is the description of the fruit resulting from the fashioning of the image.
The merit gained from constructing a temple for Śiva, Brahmā, the Sun, Vighneśa, Caṇḍī, Lakṣmī, and others is great; however, it is even greater when making an image.
There is no end to the fruit obtained through the rite of consecrating an image.

The merit from a temple made of wood is greater than one made of clay; that of a stone temple is greater than one made of bricks; and the fruit of a golden temple is even greater still. By the mere commencement of such a temple, the sins committed throughout seven lifetimes are destroyed.

One who causes a temple of the Lord to be built shall become a denizen of heaven and never goes to hell; he leads himself to the realm of Acyuta. Viṣṇu consists of the seven worlds; for him who constructs a house for Him, [those worlds become his].
He delivers the worlds from destruction and attains the imperishable state.
For as many years as the arrangement of the brick-pile remains standing, for that many thousands of years does its maker abide in heaven. (36–37)
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Constructing the Mālā," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, within the glorious Śrī Pāñcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Oṃ.
The fourth chapter in the Śrī Puruṣottama-saṃhitā, within the divine scripture (divyāgama) of the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
The method for laying the foundation bricks above the characteristic marks of the foundation;
the procedure for the construction of the foundation— by Vasiṣṭha.
O best of sages, listen to the measurements for temples:
stone is considered the best material, wood is middling, and brick is remembered as the lowest. One should construct the abode of the Lord using one of these materials alone.
O best of sages, I shall describe the determination of the fruits according to the colors of the *prasthas*, as well as the specific colors of those *prasthas*:
the red color brings good fortune, while the yellow color portends great fear.
Smoke-colored [abhraka] has the form of disease, while the white variety brings death;
the white-colored [variety] brings merit, and the blue increases longevity.
The ruby (māṇikya) destroys death, and abhraka bestows liberation.

O Brahmin, the Cintāmaṇi stone brings about the welfare and auspiciousness of the maker; this is the rule for determining the Linga by the foot. This determination of these four colors bestows the fourfold fortune. 5.

The male is the sound of the palm-clap (*tālanāda*), the neuter is the sound of the flute (*veṇunāda*), and the most beloved is the sound of the bell (*ghaṇṭānāda*); these are the determinations of gender. [This concludes] the description of the appropriate sounds for the *dinādis* and so forth, excluding those belonging to the Brahmins and other such classes.
The sequence for the temples is declared as follows: the resonance of bells for the images (bimba), the sound of flutes for the pedestals (pīṭha), and rhythmic beats (tāla) for the stone structures.
White is the color of the twice-born (brāhmaṇa) caste, and red is the color of the kṣatriya caste.
This yellow color belongs to the Vaiśya; others are of the Śūdra color. Having collected the well-spoken mantras for the stone, the wise one should worship the artisan.
This is the rule for the measurement of inches and so forth.
The middle of the middle finger is equal to half the circumference of the thumb;
the measure of three barley grains is the standard for one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
That which is joined with twelve finger-breadths is designated as a *tāla*. 9–10.
By this *tāla*, the womb-chamber (*garbhālaya*) is said to be twice as long as it is wide; the length and breadth of the womb-chamber should be made with eighteen cubits (*hasta*). 11.
The middle [size] is ten *hasta*s, and the lowest is five *hasta*s; he fashioned the pedestal consisting of five parts, such as the sandals and so forth.
It may be five *hasta*s, four *hasta*s, or two *hasta*s, according to one's desire.

The staff (daṇḍa) is half of that, and its height is said to be one-quarter less than that. Once that base (adhiṣṭhāna) has been constructed, one should avoid placing a pillar within it; [the height] should be increased sequentially by one, two, three, or four cubits. 13–14.

The great nose (mahānāsā) of the temple has a height equal to the śāla; the pillar (sāla) joined with the pedestal (upapīṭha) is declared to be the staff (daṇḍa). One should diligently construct a pavilion (maṇṭapa) that is half the size of that [temple] structure.
Or it may be level with the top of the neck, as if measured by a counterpart;
the height of those pillars is known to be equal to the interval between them.
This is declared to be the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha); in front of it, there should be a half-maṇḍapa. 16–17.

One should cause a half-maṇḍapa to be constructed measuring five cubits or four cubits; in the absence of sufficient wealth, the half-maṇḍapa should then have its exit from the two sides of the temple. 18.

They may be at the front or at the back, or on the side path; they should be raised equally or more, according to one's desire. They should be twice as wide [as the door], and for both [sides] together, it should be double.
The staircase should be specified as having exits at both the inner and outer ends. Six rows of steps should be made, six finger-breadths in height;
and one should install Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa as the door-keepers on either side of the entrance.
O best of the twice-born, one should construct a dance pavilion in front of that [main pavilion] for the purpose of dancing; it should be provided with thirty-six pillars or even sixteen pillars. 22.

An ardhamaṇṭapa (half-canopy) made of pearls, raised to one, two, three, four, or five cubits according to one's desire and equal or superior [in size], is prescribed with an interval; its exit is from the sides and below. 23.

Stairways should be constructed on both sides as well; they should be as wide as the [main] width, and both [the width and height] should be doubled. One should make the stairways one cubit (hasta) thick. 24–25.

Alternatively, one may construct a chariot-frame, or even a lion or a serpent, as an inner screen in the middle of the dance pavilion (26). Or else, there may be a door, a lattice, or even a wall-enclosure; never otherwise.
There will be the destruction of the lineage, ruin, or disease resulting from the construction of a wall [without a gap].
Alternatively, if the intermediate space is half, a quarter, or even a third of the pavilion's width, it should be equal to that for the sake of the interval. 27–28.
One should reduce that width on both sides of the interval;
one should also reduce it by one cubit, one tāla, or half of that on both sides.
It may be joined with paired pillars, or likewise, it may have a binding (bandha).
One may construct it in the shape of a plough, or it may be without either [of those shapes]. It should be square or rectangular, with four doors facing the four directions;
one should provide it with double windows and a solid wall construction.
One who is learned in the treatises on architecture should design Garuḍas on the inner and outer sides of the intermediate enclosure, as well as in the corner areas;
above that, one should fashion a single hand-pedestal (hastabandha) at the front.
There are pavilions on all the walls, and pavilions all around;
the most excellent pavilion shall measure twenty-two dhanus.
A pavilion measuring eighteen *dhanus* shall be considered medium;
a pavilion of twelve *dhanus* is declared to be inferior.
This refers to the assembly hall pavilion (*āsthānī-maṇḍapa*).
Or the assembly hall (maṇṭapa) may be seven cubits as previously stated;
it is considered excellent if ten cubits, middling if eight cubits,
and inferior if six cubits, while the sacrificial ground (kṣetra) shall measure three cubits.
On the back of the south and north [sides], walls should be constructed;
there, one should arrange a staircase provided with eight pillars. One should construct a long hall below and likewise cause a pavilion (maṇḍapa) to be made.
All the pavilions (maṇṭapa) should face the east and be situated within all the enclosures (āvaraṇa).
One should construct all the assembly pavilions (āsthānamaṇṭapa) facing every direction, as well as the Soma-thread (somasūtra).
A Śūdra should establish the characteristic mark of the *somasūtra* on the pedestal;
a Vaiśya should fashion a crocodile-seat (*makarāsana*) upon the stone of the foot-pedestal, and he should make it in the shape of an elephant's face upon the dove-pedestal (*kapotavedī*). 39–40.

O twice-born ones, a Kṣatriya should have the shape of a lion's head on his forehead-band, and a Brāhmaṇa should have it like a cow's face on his double-forehead-band. This concludes the description of the differences in results based on the different types of doors for the sanctum sanctorum.
In this manner, the door for that inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) is prescribed;
a door facing east is said to bestow auspiciousness, one on the south increases prosperity, one on the west brings victory, and one on the north shall grant wealth. 42.
The height shall be nine tālas and the width five;
palaces (vimānas) are distinguished by the differences in their floors (talas) and foundations (adhiṣṭhānas).
This is the characteristic of a temple (prāsāda).
The temple (prāsāda) is divided into five types: Nāgara, Drāviḍa, Vṛtta, Vṛttāyata, and Vesara; these are thus proclaimed. First, the Nāgara...
Having the form of a nose facing all directions and provided with a gabled hall (kūṭaśālā), it is square at the beginning and circular-elongated at the front;
that is declared to be the Nāgala style, and now the Drāviḍa style is described. 45–46.
One should fashion the Drāviḍa style as a square from the base (pāda) up to the pinnacle (sthūpi); alternatively, one may make it hexagonal—this is said to be the Drāviḍa style. 47

The *vesara* style, from the base up to the top of the dome, may be circular or oval; it is called *vesara*, as previously stated, and is used in temples according to the sequence [of its application]. 48.

A Vesara temple is defined as one equipped with gabled halls (kūṭaśālā), provided with projections on all sides and at the cardinal points, and having a width extending from the neck upwards. It is characterized by openings on every side. 49. Sarvato-nirgama.
From the base (pāda) up to the pinnacle (stūpyanta), it is octagonal or twelve-sided;
that which is devoid of a peaked hall (kūṭa-śālā) is known as having exits on all sides. This is the rule for the bricks at the summit (mūrdha-iṣṭakā-vidhi).

O Brahmin, listen now as I describe the procedure for the crown-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā). One should cause an Āgama-maṇḍapa to be constructed in front of the temple; in its center, one should construct an altar measuring one, two, or three cubits.
Adorned with all ornaments and beautified by archways (toraṇas),
four bricks for the foundation were prepared during the first part of the night;
they should be free from the defects of stone, well-baked, made of clay, and white in color.
Having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise strewn it around with kuśa grass,
and having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, one should sprinkle it with water from a kuśa-grass vessel.
Then, the knower of mantras should bind the protective amulet (kautuka) there with the root mantra (mūlamantra).
Having provided a cloth for each [deity], one should place it before them. Afterwards, one should set down the jars together with cloths and lids;
having arranged five pitchers, one should install the central jar.
The most excellent practitioner should place the jars, filled with scented water and adorned with *kuśa* grass and the tender shoots of mango, while reciting the root mantra.
[These are] Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.
Śaṅkhukarṇa, Sarpanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita—58—the best of preceptors should worship these eight pitchers placed all around:
Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, and Hayaśīrṣaka. 59.
One should worship Jāmadagnya-Rāma, Vāmana, and Vāsudeva; thus the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) are declared, and one should worship them in sequence within the pitchers.
The wise man, equipped with all ornaments, should accomplish [the rite] together with the *kūrca* grass.
Then the preceptor should begin the fire sacrifice (homa) at the side of the altar;
likewise, he should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) in the eight directions and in the center,
while those reciting the Vedas in their entirety chant the Śākuna [Sūtra].

One should offer oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and milk to the *Ṛgveda* in the eastern quarter, to the *Yajurveda* in the south, to the *Sāmaveda* in the west, and likewise to the *Atharvaveda* in the north. (63)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks and clarified butter separately,
and having taken the residual drops (saṃpāta) and other portions, he should then perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having passed the remainder of the night, and having performed his bath and daily rites, [he should proceed].
Then, as before, one should worship the jars with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
thereafter, the preceptor, being free from darkness, should kindle incense and lamps and perform the worship. He should then offer the bali-oblation according to the rules and in the proper sequence.
The preceptor, together with the carpenters and accompanied by the patron,
should perform the circumambulation of the temple while preceded by the chanting of the Vedas; accompanied by the sound of the Vedas,
he should then place all those [wooden beams] upon the upper surface of the celestial chariot (vimāna).
There, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be made;
facing east, composed and having placed the bricks upon the head, he should meditate on the Lord Nārāyaṇa and mutter the *praṇava* within the lotus of his heart. 69.
Having offered all the bricks according to the sequence starting from the east,
the patron, having prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground before the preceptor once more,
should then honor him with garments, wealth, grain, cattle, land, and gold.
One should offer five-fold ornaments and likewise satisfy male and female servants; one should also gratify the carpenters with garments, food, wealth, and grain.
(72) This is the procedure for the pinnacle and the central pin.
O lotus-faced one, I shall now describe the finial-pinnacle (stūpikākīla) using honey;
it may be made of metal or even of wood, for such is desired as the finial-pinnacle. It should be equal to the neck of the temple (vimāna-kaṇṭha), or perhaps twice that length.
For one who desires non-rebirth, the pillar for the pinnacle (sthūpikā) should be in pairs;
for others, it should not be in pairs, as the insertion of the pillar for the pinnacle is small.
When the evening has arrived, one should prepare a pit for the pinnacle. 74–75.
One should have an excellent pit made, either circular or square;
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) regarding the pit and deposit nine gems within it.
Then, having cast [the materials] into the pit, one facing west should place the *sthūpī* with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).

The preceptor should cause the *sthūpī* (finial), adorned with the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) and ornaments, to be installed. Immediately thereafter, one should make the peg of the *sthūpikā* firm with lime, and then perform the installation of the *śikhā-kumbha* (the crest-pot).
One should place the crest-pot (śikhā-kuṃbha) made of gold, silver, or copper,
or else of brass or even clay, at an auspicious moment;
one should place the discus of Viṣṇu upon the top of the crest-pot.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Temple and the Rules for the Bricks of the Image," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Oṃ. In the Śrī Pāñcarātra Divyāgama, within the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā,
this is the fifth chapter.
Brahmā spoke on the procedure for selecting stone and the characteristics of an image.
For the sake of hearing [the truth],
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, please explain to me in great detail the characteristics of the images, for I desire to hear them according to their true nature. 1.

The Blessed Lord said: Regarding the reply of the Blessed Lord, which describes the occasion for the creation of the image: "First, the practitioner, being well-composed, should have an image fashioned."
Having projected the life-force into that beautiful form endowed with auspicious marks belonging to the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, and having worshipped it, one does not suffer;
for the mind finds no delight in the Lord of gods when he is formless.
This is the specific method for propitiating the deity through the physical form;
therefore, a wise person, first examining the characteristics of one possessing form and constantly contemplating it, shall attain stability of mind. 4.
When the mind is steady there, one attains the destruction of the afflictions in this very life;
and the person whose afflictions are destroyed reaches supreme nirvāṇa.
Therefore, when the image has been fashioned, it leads to detachment as its root.
Therefore, one should indeed perform worship for the sake of supporting one's wealth.
The varieties of materials for images are:
gems, metals, stone, clay, wood, and crystal.

O twice-born one, excellent materials are suitable for the making of an image. First, I shall describe the collection of stone— the specification of the places where stone is found— in whatever mountains it is seen.
Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, Himavat, Nīlaparvata, Mandara, Mālyavān, Trikūṭa, Malaya,
Gandhamādana, and Meru— these ten are the most excellent of all.
Among these, an image should be accepted; if those are unavailable, listen regarding stone.
Stone found on the ground should be accepted; if that is unavailable, listen regarding stone from Citrakūṭa, known as Raivata, the great mountain.
10. On the mountain named Citrakūṭa and on the great mountain named Raivata.
At Siṃhācala, Citrakūṭa, and likewise at Veṅkaṭādri;
similarly, it should be taken from Śveta-giri. If that is unavailable, hear now the description of stones found on the earth.
I shall now describe the characteristics of those stones that are said to be found on the earth.
The four types of stones mentioned are the Vāruṇī, the Māhendrī, the Āgneyī, and the Vāyavī; their characteristics are now being stated.
That Vāruṇī which is filled with flowering groves and surrounded by reservoirs of water is to be known as the manifest Vāruṇī; the stone situated there bestows all desires. 14.
That [direction] in which Māheṃdrī is situated to the north, where there is a field of rice to the south, and milk-trees to the west— that is proclaimed as Māheṃdrī. 15.
The south-eastern quarter belongs to Agni; there dwell the Pālāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, and Kāśmīra trees, as well as the Tinduka, Cakora, Kapota, Gṛdhra, and Vāyasa birds. 16.
Where clouds and cranes are constantly seen, that should be known as the Āgneyī Sākṣitī; there, the stones grant all desires. [17] Vāyavī...
Where very little water is seen upon digging within the ground,
and which is strewn with *pilu*, *śleṣmātaka*, *snuhī*, and *vibhītaka* trees; where it is devoid of grass and water, and filled with heaps of gravel— 18.
Where jackals are seen, there likewise are mirages;
the wind is to be known as the witness, while the stone there is devoid [of moisture],
and the ground is barren.

On a riverbank, at the edge of a well, on putrid ground, or among quadrupeds; on an anthill, on a site for ancestral rites, in water mixed with salt, on impure ground, or in places frequented by Śabaras, Caṇḍālas, and others.

In a place heated by the rays of the sun or other sources near a temple, all stones that are free from flaws should be taken for the purpose of making the pedestal; these are the locations from which they should be taken. 22.
Locations for selection.
In an auspicious region that is a field of merit, densely covered with *brahma* trees,
endowed with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass and water, frequented by black deer, and filled with lotuses and water-lilies amidst fields of rice; 23.
In a region endowed with *hintāla*, betel nut, *punnāga*, and coconut trees, and frequented by ascetics, stones should always be taken;
having thus understood what is to be avoided and having carefully examined both merits and defects. (24–25)

Having understood the distinctions of regions, the distinctions of lands, and likewise the distinctions of lingas, as well as the transgression incurred in the collection of stones to be rejected, one should select an auspicious stone endowed with these characteristics. 26.
If one, deluded by greed, should himself fashion or cause to be fashioned images devoid of the proper characteristics of stone, there shall be a corresponding result for that maker.
(27) Regarding stone, there are distinctions of caste such as Brāhmaṇa and others, as well as their specific characteristics.
O Brahmin, there are four kinds of stones according to the distinction of castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇa:
the stone of a Brāhmaṇa is white, that of a Kṣatriya is pale-red, that of a Vaiśya is yellow, and that of a Śūdra is black; these are the primary stones as they have been described.
A Brāhmaṇa’s stone is three *śrasti*s; likewise that of a Kṣatriya is three. Two are to be known for a Vaiśya, and one is proclaimed for a Śūdra.
This is the regulation of time regarding the collection of stones, as well as the procedure for collecting the stone.
O twice-born one, the collection of stones is recommended in all months;
provided with favorable omens such as those of birds and other signs,
accompanied by a chariot-maker and groups of master builders.
Having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce the words of auspiciousness (*svastivācana*), he should depart;
from that time forward, he should daily perform the rites beginning with the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) and the installation of the water-pot (*kumbhasthāpana*). 32.
In a place where stones have been cleared away, one should cause a large water-shed (prapā) to be constructed;
there, the wise preceptor, observing celibacy and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), together with the patron, should perform the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa). 33.
There, the wise preceptor, together with the patron...
There, the practitioner should place the water-pot with the root mantra (34).
Then, he should invoke the omnipresent deity using the image-mantra;
having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, he should display the discus-mudrā (35).
Having displayed the mahāmudrā and prostrated with the añjali-mudrā,
one should draw a maṇḍala upon the stone and joyfully worship Viṣṇu therein. Whichever form one desires to create, one should worship it with its specific mantra.
Having worshipped the deities of the directions, one should cast the oblation for the cruel spirits (*bhūta*).
The offering of the *bali* consists of minced meat,
powdered turmeric, parched rice grains, curd, and barley meal.
That which is called "bhūta" is said to be cruel; with that, one should offer the *bhūtabali*.
One should perform the *homa* offering in each of the four directions, either in a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or even upon a ritual mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
One should offer fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, flowers, fruit, clarified butter, and sprouts,
each separately one hundred and eight times with the root mantra; and likewise, one should offer oblations of *caru* with the *Nṛsūkta* in each of the four sacrificial pits separately.
There, in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should offer oblations to the serpents, the forest deities, the attendants (pārṣadas), the Nanda mountains, the mountain ridges,
the cascades, the oceans, as well as the trees, herbs, and great forest lords (vanaspatis). 41.

Then, with mantras containing the names of their respective deities followed by "svāhā," he should offer oblations for those born from a womb, those born from eggs, those born from sweat, and likewise those born from sprouts;
thereafter, he should likewise offer oblations with the Vyāhṛtis, beginning with the word "svāhā. 42–43.

The wise one, having performed the entire rite— including the sleeping upon the dream-object and the dream-entry mantra— separately one hundred and eight times each, ending with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti). 44.
Having observed the fast upon a bed of *darbha* grass, at dawn, with his senses subdued and remaining well-composed, the preceptor should utter this mantra:
"Oṃ, salutations to Viṣṇu, the source of all worlds, the all-pervading Lord. (45)
Having recited this mantra one hundred and eight times for Viśva, the omniformed Lord of Dreams, the wise man should sleep. Then,
having slept, if he should see a mountain blazing intensely in his dream—

If, in such a place, there should be a dream of a beautiful image featuring a highly elevated peak adorned with golden trees, endowed with fruits and flowers, and surrounded by mountain-born trees; 48. If, in such a state, the dream-image should be auspicious.

In the morning, one should take the stone and perform a rite for peace to ward off misfortune (49). At an auspicious moment, the most excellent of preceptors should inspect the stone in a place where yakṣas, piśācas, nāgas, and other beings constantly reside (50).
"May all these depart; may Hari always be present.
Having said this, one should place the *siddhārtha* grains, perfected by that mantra, there.
With that same mantra, one should offer the *bali* oblation to the spirits in every direction.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should touch the stone with the *Puruṣasūkta* (verse 52).
Having offered the water of honor (*arghya*) with the root mantra, one should mutter it one hundred and eight times. [Then follow] the laying of the lines (*sūtrapāta*) and other rites.
O Lotus-born one, one should drop the cord according to the proportions of the image;
then, standing there by the instruction of the chariot-maker, one should establish the stone,
for the difference in the result depends on the division of the neck.
The measurement from south to north as well as from east to west is thus established.
(54) With the neck facing north, the southern neck bestows victory; with the neck facing east, it brings prosperity; and with the neck facing west, it always brings success to the performer. (55)
The northern neck should be a bestower of nourishment (*pūṣṭi*), while the corner-neck should be avoided;
the stone of the base portion should always be situated above.
If the upper part is cut off from below, there is misfortune for the eyes and the fangs.

One should bathe the prepared stone with water from the great pitcher (mahākuṃbha). After performing the bathing with the great pitcher and so forth, and having given gold, cows, land, and sesame seeds, one should perform the propitiatory fire-oblation (śāntihoma).

Where sparks are seen like those from a fire as [the stone] is being split, where the sound is that of an irreproachable stone, and where the resonance is like that of a bronze bell—one should avoid such stones marked by these signs. 58. One should avoid stones with these characteristics.
If, upon striking the base with bronze at the middle part of the vessel,
a sound like that of bronze arises and the *liṅga* is clearly discerned through the resonance, that stone is proclaimed to be a "man" (*puruṣa*).
When that sound is slightly deficient and its resonance is cut off, it is called *sāra*. However, that which is devoid of resonance is declared to be *napuṃsaka* (neuter).
Regarding the applications of female, male, and neuter stones: a stone containing a *garbha* (inclusion) must be rejected; [the following is] the examination for *garbha*.
An image in the masculine gender is prescribed [for the deity], while a footstool is for the feminine gender.

However, the placement of gems (ratnanyāsa) is declared for a stone of the neuter gender; stones that are pregnant (garbhavatī) are to be avoided, as the [deities] are situated within the womb. 61–62.

Therefore, one should examine the fetus by means of cutting or piercing; or else, having ground buffalo butter, powdered ram horn, and the powder of *kuraviṃda* together with cow’s milk, one should drink it. (63)
One should smear all over the stone; from that, the manifestation of the embryo occurs.
Where circular patterns (maṇḍalas) are seen, there one should deposit the embryo.
In a circle resembling the color of madder (māñjiṣṭha), a frog appears. 64–65.
In a yellow mandala there is a lizard; in a black one, a black snake;
in a tawny one, a mouse is said to be present; and in a dark-blue one, a chameleon. In a stone the color of jaggery, there is a house-lizard.
In a cloud resembling water or a sword, one should recognize a scorpion; in one resembling sand or a lotus, a spider; in a blue or pale-colored one, a moth;
and in a honey-colored orb, the wise man should indicate a firefly.
The results of the various wombs are as follows: from the womb of a frog comes the lordship of a kingdom; from that of a cow comes health; from that of a lizard, there will be fear of evil;
one dies by poison from the womb of a snake; and from the womb of a mouse, one is childless. 69.
If it falls on a lizard, there will be a short lifespan; on a stone, one is struck by Saturn;
on an earthworm, there is loss of wealth; in water, there is destruction of the fetus (70);
on sand, there is a loss of water; and likewise, on a scorpion, there is quarrel.
If it is a grasshopper, there will be the destruction of the kingdom; if it is a firefly, there is the ruin of the family.
Therefore, one should always examine the fetus with great effort and constant vigilance; for in the collection of stones by a pregnant woman, there is sin.

If, out of delusion, a stone containing an embryo is fashioned into an image, then the king who is the lord of that region, as well as the maker and the one who heats it, shall all become paralyzed; therefore, one should examine the interior of the stone.
Regarding the construction of images of Śrī and others, there is a specific rule for the selection of stone:
for the making of goddesses such as Lakṣmī (Ramā), a female stone is best;
a male stone should serve as the footstool; and for a neuter [image], the placement of gems is prescribed. 74.
The wise one, having invoked Śrī, the mother of the three worlds, into the middle of the jar within the manifestation of the Goddess’s image by means of the root mantra (mūlamantra),
should perform the fire oblation (homa) and other rites as before, accompanied by the Śrīsūkta.
If the goddess is fashioned from a stone that is not female by a negligent person possessed of greed, he meets with destruction;
so too does the collection of stones for her retinue.
In that very place, one should collect auspicious stones for the retinue (77). One should perform the collection of those stones with the respective mantras in due order;
the preceptor should give the fee for the master according to the extent of his means (78).

Having taken that stone with effort and having placed it upon carts and other vehicles, the architects and carvers, following the tradition of the craftsmen, should carry it to the temple and fashion the image according to the scriptures, endowed with the characteristics prescribed therein.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Collection of Stones," in the *Puruṣottama-saṃhitā*, a great Upaniṣad of the venerable *Pañcarātra*.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ.
In the Śrī Pāñcarātra Śāstra, in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā,
this is the sixth chapter.
The procedure for collecting wood;
images made of jewels are faultless, and all those born of jewels bestow the fruits of all desires.

Where there is a crystal image, it increases good fortune; an iron image [brings] various types of wealth; a golden image brings the fruit of gold, silver, and copper—these three are called "iron" (loha). 1.
The golden radiance is not merely that; it shall bring about all prosperity.
Wealth, fame, power, and wisdom shine as its fruit.
The silver image is the fruit.
An auspicious image made of copper bestows wealth and sons;
one made of wood should be known as bringing prosperity; and one made of clay grants all desires. (3) [The fruit of] the copper image...
The collection of wood is recommended during the eight months beginning with Kārtika;
for objects made of wood, clay, and so forth, the results are auspicious when the lunar fortnight, asterism, and yoga are favorable on a propitious day. 4.
Aloe-wood, deodar, the rājavṛkṣa, and sandalwood;
this is the time for collecting wood.
Also the bilva, mango, nameru, neem, and khadira.
The śirīṣa, the panasa, the vakula, the kuṭaja, and the arjuna; likewise,
those born from suitable trees,
as well as the śiṃśupā, the kadamba, the śirīṣa, and the campaka.
Kāśmarya, madhuka, sāla, śamī, punnāga,
and red sandalwood— these are prescribed for the purpose of making an image.
An image should never be made from materials other than these.
I shall not describe those trees that are to be abandoned and avoided; listen to them:
trees that are dried up by themselves, those broken by themselves, and those whose bark is stripped away.
Those that are curved, scorched by the sun, or possessed of hollows and wounds;
those situated on quadrupeds, and those that grow on *putraka* trees; those not located in temples, nor those originating from anthills. 9–10.

The trees that had reached their end, the trees standing in cremation grounds, those which were the nesting places of birds, those that were withered, and those trees that were leafless, unprotected, scorched by fire, or ruined by lightning; 11.
[And] the elephants, defenseless and struck by fire, or afflicted by thunderbolts.
Those trees on the great highway that are frequented by cattle and provide shade,
as well as those devoid of one, two, or three branches, which are constantly resorted to by outcasts such as Caṇḍālas and those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), [are not to be used]. 12–13.
One should avoid those that have withered foliage, those standing on a path, those surrounded by other trees,
those situated near a well, those near a pond, and those that have been sold.
There is sin in the collection of such trees.
One should fashion images using trees that have been avoided; otherwise, both the maker and the one who commissioned them, along with their lineages, shall perish through negligence.
[This should be done] in a pure, level, and secluded place, free from hair, charcoal, and bones.

For the purpose of collecting wood, one should first smear the ground all around below that site—which should be pleasant, free of thorns, and sloping toward the northeast—with substances such as perfumes. 16.
Then, having smeared the earth beneath it on all sides...
Having purified it thoroughly with the Gāyatrī mantra and sprinkled it all around with water,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in a place where timber is gathered, to the east;
an expert in the ritual system (tantra) should prepare that site just as one does for the gathering of stones.
The best of instructors should offer twigs and sprouts from the *anoka* tree into the fire in the southeast direction as before;
then the instructor should wash the root of the tree with the *praṇava*.
The one most skilled in mantras should cover it with a cloth made of darbha grass (20).
Having sprinkled the axe at the foot of the tree, he should cause it to be placed there;
the knower of mantras should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the Astra-mantra (21).
Having performed [the oblations] with the *avyāhṛti* mantras, he should thereafter worship the tree with palms joined in reverence; being full of affection, he should utter this mantra:
"By virtue of my former deeds, you have assumed the form of an immobile being. (22)
I choose for the sake of the Viṣṇu-image that which brings all prosperity to you. Depart from this state of being stationary and assume a divine, unsurpassed form;
enjoy abundant pleasures through the grace of Vāsudeva. 23–24.
"I do not cut you down because you are a tree, but rather I release you from birth;
having reached this auspicious divine abode for the sake of pacifying the sorrow of being a tree, you shall attain divinity there, free from burning and cutting. (25)
"By offering water and flowers, as well as oblations accompanied by incense,
people will worship you, and thereby they shall attain peace.
Having thus performed the ritual attendance with the mantra, one should wrap [the image] with a protective thread.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), the Guru should cause the fire to rise up. In the morning, the preceptor, having bathed and being pure at an auspicious moment,
should worship the excellent tree with incense, flowers, and other offerings facing the east.
Then, facing eastward, pure and acting out of affection,
the chariot-maker, with the permission of his preceptor, should cut down that tree with an axe;
[this is] the examination of the fruits and non-fruits in the forest of trees.
If it falls toward the east or the north, it brings prosperity to the performer. A fall toward the southwest, southeast, or south is not auspicious;
likewise, a fall toward the northwest or west is not auspicious.

Having first cut those branches that stand outside in the eight directions on all sides, the knower of mantras should thereafter [cut] the tree; this is the examination of the interior (garbhaparīkṣā). 32.
Just as there are embryos within a stone, so too are they within trees;
one should sprinkle them with water from the pitcher while meditating on Hari situated therein.
(33) One should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor as before, O Lotus-seated One.
One should have the temple and the tree constructed by a carpenter according to the rules;
the image should be of a form that inspires devotion, adorned with all its limbs—thus has been correctly declared the supreme method for the selection of wood. (34–35)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Collecting Wood," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā of the glorious Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
In the venerable *Puruṣottama-saṃhitā* within the illustrious *Pañcarātra*.
The seventh chapter: The procedure for collecting clay for the image.
The Blessed One said:
The distinction between the baked and unbaked clay image:
O lotus-faced one, I shall describe the clay image exactly as it is;
the clay image is said to be of two kinds, according to the sequence of the baked and the unbaked. 1.
An unbaked image is praised as bestowing the fruits of all desires;
clay should be collected from suitable locations such as sacred fields, riverbanks, forests, mountains, or lakes.
One should take clay that is complete and free from all defects, collected from a low-lying area on a road, and avoided from places such as shrines (caityas) and cremation grounds.
[This applies to] the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
O Lotus-born One, it is traditionally held that for a Brāhmaṇa the clay should be white and soft, for a Kṣatriya it is remembered as reddish,
for a Vaiśya it should be known as yellow, and for a Śūdra it is black.
This is the rule following the collection of the clay.
Having uprooted all the bark from the trees— khadira, udumbara, aśvattha, nyagrodha, and arjuna— one should place them in water for a month; then,
one should mix the clay with that water infused for a month and press it.
One should employ a potter who is young, skilled, tranquil, and free from disease for all tasks prescribed in the scriptures;
one should have the potter perform everything according to the procedure taught by the wheelwright.

Having placed that in new vessels and covered them carefully, one should set the vessel in the shade so that it is not touched by wind or other elements. [One should take] three parts of *dhātrī* fruit and six parts of *harītakī*.
One should prepare this powder consisting of three parts of *dhātrī*.
[It should be used] in a sacred field, on a riverbank, on a mountain, on a sandbank, in a lake, on a waterfall, at a confluence, in a dry place, or likewise on a sacrificial altar or fertile soil.
Twenty-one types of earth are recommended: from a field of rice, from a place dug by the gods (a natural spring), from the horns of a bull or an elephant,
from a boar’s track, from a black anthill, from the dwelling of a crab,
and likewise from a lotus pond or a large oblong pool.
One should mix these with portions of raw clay and then press it firmly. Furthermore, one should mix that [clay] again with the powders of Triphalā in the previously mentioned proportions,
along with river-clay, smooth stones, and powdered iron, each constituting a quarter-part of the clay.
One should grind these— sandalwood, saffron, black [resin], *śrīveṣṭa*,
yellow sandalwood, *guggulu*, turmeric,
orpiment, realgar, and *tamālapattra*— into a powder.
With twenty-one parts of fine powder and an equal amount of sand,
one should mix them with those powders of metals and gems and knead them; then,
one should add one part of the juice of *kapiddha* to that mixture.

Having prepared this clay by mixing it with honey, oil, ghee, milk, curd, and buttermilk in equal proportions, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and place it in new vessels. 17.
Having covered them with a new cloth, the best of preceptors should place the earthen vessels in the midst of grain and worship them with the root mantra. (18) [The Procedure for the Homa]
Then the Guru should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) either in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
he should offer clarified butter into the fire one hundred and eight times with the root mantra (mūla).
Thereafter, he should offer the sacrificial porridge (caru) one by one with the Puruṣasūkta.
One should sprinkle that clay situated in the vessels with [the water] called *saṃpāta*;
the expert in the ritual manual (*tantra*) should perform everything up to the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).
Having let it remain for a month, one should then have an image fashioned from it.
This collection concerning clay has been fully declared; now hear the characteristics of the image according to its various divisions, such as those made of gems, metals, stone, wood, and clay. 22.
Thus, in the *Śrī Pañcarātra Mahopaniṣad*, within the *Puruṣottama Saṃhitā*.
The Seventh Chapter: The Taking of the Clay for the Image.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
The eighth chapter of the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā in the Śrī Pañcarātra,
concerning the rules for the characteristics of the fixed image (dhruvabera) and other forms.
The sages said:
"O Blessed One, O tiger among sages, these additional readings bestow the fruits of the goals sought by those who take refuge in them."

Please describe the procedure for fashioning the image and the emanation-form according to the authority of the scriptures; how many types of images are there for the worship of the Enemy of Madhu, and tell me their characteristics in detail and according to the rules.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"I shall now explain the characteristics of stone idols, as well as the characteristics of [other] physical forms."

One should determine the measurement of the door according to the measurement of the *ālaya* (sanctum); one should cause the threefold [structure] on the ground to be made according to the measurement of the patron (*yajamāna*), and the measurement of the image according to the measurement of the inner sanctum (*garbhālaya*).
The length of the womb-chamber (garbhālaya) is calculated by dividing it into nine parts;
according to the available materials and in accordance with the door,
one should construct the primary image (mūlavigraha) with a size ranging from one to nine [parts].

O twice-born one, the measurement of the door of the womb-chamber is one-quarter less than the [main] door; alternatively, it may be half of that door's measurement or half of that again—thus the measurement of the door is fourfold. 4.

One should fashion it equal to the sacrificer according to the sacrificer's own measurement; or up to the eyes, or as desired by the patron; or up to the eyes according to the rule, or including the chin, or including the mouth, or up to the breasts, or ending at the heart. 5.

This sevenfold measurement is to be known; those who understand the will of the sacrificer should have an auspicious house constructed according to the architectural scriptures (*śilpa-nāgama-śāstra*). The measurements beginning with finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) constitute the *mānāṅgula*.
Next, I shall explain the measurement of a finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
Eight minute particles (*aṇu-reṇu*) are declared to constitute one mustard seed (*sarṣapa*);
eight mustard seeds are prescribed to constitute one sesame seed (*tila*).
Eight sesame seeds are said to be one barleycorn (*yava*), and eight barleycorns are one horizontal finger-breadth (*tiryag-aṅgula*).
(This is declared to be the *mānāṅgula*); thus the *mānāṅgula* has been declared. Now hear this *mātrāṅgula*.
This is the *mātrāṅgula*.
The measure of a finger-breadth (mātrāṅgula) is the horizontal distance from the middle joint of the middle finger to its tip;
furthermore, there are two kinds of finger-breadths: the body-measured finger-breadth (dehalabdha-aṅgula) and the [standard] finger-breadth.
Of these, the body-measured finger-breadth is—
It is elevated for the purpose of a thumb-ring and for the purpose of the base;
this is declared in all scriptures as being of two kinds, according to the application of measurement in finger-breadths and so forth.
The Ālaya and other items are fashioned according to the measure of a *mānāṅgula*;

the preceptor should prepare all the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), the *kūrca* grass-bundle, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the fuel (*idhma*), and the fire-vessels according to the measure of a *mātrāṅgula*. 11–12.

One should fashion all the deities using exactly the finger-measures obtained from one's own body; [alternatively], according to the dimensions of the temple and likewise according to the dimensions of the door. This is the procedure for the construction of the image, depending on the size of the temple and likewise on the size of the door. 13. The Procedure for the Manufacture of the Image.

Then, according to the will of the patron, one should fashion the image in three ways; its bodily dimensions shall be measured by the *deha-aṅgula* derived from the left hand of that [patron's] reflection. 14.

From the feet up to the hair on the head, nine *tālas* are calculated at twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) each, totaling one hundred and eight; this is the definitive measurement for all physical forms.
The divisions of the body, the location of the *liṅga*, and the purpose of the body—downward and upward, these are equal.
The upper body consists of four parts; the distance from the navel to the *liṅga* is one part.
One part [should extend] from the heart to the end of the chest;
one part is prescribed from the heart up to the chin; and one part should be extended from there upward to the end of the hair on the head. 17–18.
The rule for the measurement of the parts is as follows:
the two ears are four finger-breadths [in width]; the nose is four finger-breadths; the eyes are equal to the nose; and the mouth is equal to the eyes. (19)
The neck is four finger-breadths [in width], and the penis is four finger-breadths;
for the sake of the penis, the scrotum is ten finger-breadths from the middle of the breast. Between the lower body and the knees, it is said that the hands reach as far as the knees. 20.
The middle of the forearm should be equal to the navel, and the wrist should be equal to that;
the wise one should fashion the palm of the hand, including the nails, to be half the measure of that [forearm]. 21. This is the characteristic of the hand.

The middle finger should be raised to a measurement of three fingers; one should fashion it with three joints, even and endowed with all auspicious characteristics. The index and ring fingers are prescribed to be one *māṣa* less.

The little finger should be two māṣas, and the thumb is said to be three māṣas; the wise man should fashion [the image] according to the proportions of the icon. (24) This is the characteristic of the feet.
Listen to the rule for the measurement of the feet in terms of finger-breadths (*aṅgula*):
the middle finger of the foot is traditionally held to be three *aṅgulas* in measure;
from that, the best of artisans should fashion the fingers of the hands.
The characteristic of the parts is that the location of the ears is prescribed in the middle of the head;
one should fashion the hips and the forehead so that they are as high as the back of a tortoise.

One should fashion the ears, eyes, nostrils, knees, ankles, hips, and arms; the scrotum, chin, lips, wrists, the pair of eyebrows, the two armpits, and the pair of breasts, making them symmetrical according to the prescribed rule. (27–28)

In the *sthānaka* posture, one should assume a standing pose; for the *pratimā*, the abdomen is slightly protruding, the hands are raised level with the shoulders, and the tips of the eyes reach the hairline. 29.

One should fashion the ornamented seat without deliberating over its dimensions; according to the measurement of the face, the seat should likewise be elevated. The crown, extending from the nose to the end of the lips, should be twice that measure.

One should act according to the available means and construct a pit and a stūpa (31). This is the rule for the measurement of the deity; next, I shall describe the measurement of the Goddess, up to the end of the nose of the image.
The [image] reaching up to the lips is declared to be middling, while that reaching up to the chin is the lowest.
Seated with four arms, or likewise standing with two arms, O twice-born one, she should be placed on both sides of the Lord, standing in every image.

On the left [side] is the left hand of Śrī hanging down, and likewise on the right side is the right lotus of Śrī; on the left is a lotus, and on the right is a hanging hand—such is the characteristic of the two goddesses, Śrī and Bhū. 34.

The characteristic of all Viṣṇu images is that there are two *śrīs* on the sides. Others should be installed in the temple; [according to additional readings: Vīra-lakṣmī is four-armed, and Rājya-lakṣmī is four-armed.
Vīralakṣmī is depicted with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, holding an upward-pointing lotus, and seated upon a lotus throne;
her face resembles the full moon, and all her limbs are beautiful and auspicious.

One should have Rājyalakṣmī fashioned as seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with all ornaments, remembered in every respect as having hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a lotus in her right and left [hands]. 36.
One should bestow the glory of heroism upon all the incarnations, and one should bestow the glory of sovereignty [upon them].

(37) [Thus, O twice-born ones, one characteristic of the permanent image has been told. In this way, the characteristic of the permanent image (*dhruvabera*) is approved by all; [now follow] the measurements for the portable image (*kautukabera*) and other true images.

The *kautuka* is for the sake of the permanent image (*dhruvabera*), as is the *kautuka* for the festival; the bathing is for the sake of the festival, while the offering of oblations (*bali*) is for the sake of the ceremonial bath. The *sālagrāma* is for the sake of the *dīrgha*; such is the definition of the six types of images.
One should perform the rites in sequence from the *dhruva* [offering] up to the *snāna* (ablution), just as in the case of Dhruva;
[according to additional readings,
this ritual procedure for the *arcā* (idol) is prescribed for all incarnations].
The form of Sudarśana is described as having six arms in the center of a hexagonal wheel;
[he holds] a lotus, the king of weapons (the discus), and a mace in his right hands. 40.
One should hold the conch, the mace, and the Śārṅga bow with the two left arms.
It is considered to be whirling, accompanied by six spokes on a hexagonal wheel. These are the characteristics of the forms of the gatekeepers.
And at every door, one should fashion two forms of door-keepers. At all the locations of the doors, there are two images as door-keepers.
In the left [hand] is a discus and likewise a conch, while in the right hand is a mace;
with feet either apart or together, such is the form on the right side of the door.

In the left [hand] he holds a conch and likewise a discus; in his left hand he carries a mace, while the other [left hand] is in the boon-granting gesture—such are the characteristics of his left form. 44. [Additional readings]
The conch, discus, mace, and lotus are the universal characteristics [of the deity];
the measurements of the door-frames,
the measurement of the door itself, its purpose, the purpose of that, and the purpose of that as well.
One should have the door-keepers fashioned according to one's wealth.

(45) [This may be] by the measurement of the inner sanctum (*garbhālaya*), or according to the fixed image (*dhruvabimba*); it may be by the measure of the inner sanctum or by the fixed measure, and one should construct them with four proportions according to one's wealth.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Fixed Image and Other Forms," in the Śrī Puruṣottama-saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
In the venerable *Purushottama-saṃhitā* within the illustrious *Pañcarātra*.
The Ninth Chapter:
The Rules for the Characteristics of Chariots and Other Vehicles;
The Characteristics of the Chariot.

I shall now describe the characteristics of the chariot of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow; likewise, the height of the celestial vehicle (vimāna), the height of the gate-towers (gopura),
the height of the flagstaff (dhvajastaṃbha), and the height of the pavilion (maṇṭapa).
One should have an excellent chariot made either of iron or even of wood;
if it is made of wood, it must have a solid inner core and be adorned with gold and silver.
Or one may have it fashioned from bell-metal according to one's means;
it should be inlaid with the nine gems and surrounded by a hundred door-pillars—
whether sixteen, twelve, or eight, according to the extent of one's wealth.

One should fashion the fourteen [levels] beginning with Atala and ending with Bhūḥ, or else one should determine the extent [of the structure] according to the height, such that the three worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ correspond to the base [of the edifice]. (One should determine the length in accordance with the height. 4–5.
On the first part of the base, one should fashion the wheels;
on both sides, one should construct them in accordance with the chariot.
And at its front, there should be a large crest-pitcher (śikhā-kumbha) resplendent with a wheel.

Equipped with a hundred bells and adorned with banners and flags, one should arrange horses or even elephants in the front part; in their midst, one should station a charioteer holding a bow and a goad. 7–8.
In the artistic design, one should imagine the inhabitants of the respective worlds situated in the levels of Atala and so forth:
the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and likewise Garuḍas. 9.
He should likewise fashion the Siddhas, the Vidyādharas, the gods, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, the Piśācas, Guhyakas, Sādhyas, and the Munis who are supreme Vaiṣṇavas;
and he should manifest the divine incarnations and pastimes of the Lord in the forms of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others.
One should fashion the characteristics of the central pedestal of the chariot; in its center, upon the altar, one should arrange a tortoise-pedestal (kūrmapīṭha).
Upon that, indeed, is Ananta, adorned with a thousand hoods.
One should fashion a golden pedestal in the center of that [altar],
and in its middle, a lotus with eight petals, complete with a pericarp and filaments;
one should prepare a golden throne for the seated deity.
This is the specific fruit of constructing the chariot:
having thus fashioned this divine chariot for Viṣṇu, whose splendor is supreme, those who worship it with great devotion go to the highest state. 14.

Beyond this, I shall describe the other vehicles and their characteristics, as well as the characteristics of mounts in general: the Sun, the Moon, the Lion, the Tiger, and the Lord of Birds (the Eagle) serve as seats. 15.

One should have the Hanuman, Hamsa, Mattabhā, Hayasyandana, and Śibikā, as well as the vehicles of all the kings, constructed in due order, or one may have the vehicles made equal in size to the inner sanctum (garbhālaya). 16.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Chariot and Other [Vessels]," in the *Puruṣottama-saṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the glorious *Pañcarātra*.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ. In the Śrī Pāñcarātra, in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, this is the tenth chapter.
The procedure for determining the auspicious moment for consecration;
having heard the procedure for consecration,
Brahmā said:
O Lord of gods, Lord of the universe, if you are pleased with me, O Master, please explain in full detail the question regarding the *gṛhabrahman* and the characteristics of its foundation.
The Blessed One’s reply: The Blessed One spoke the *Pratiṣṭhāvidhikārikā* (the Verses on the Ritual of Consecration).
Now I shall describe the supreme procedure for installation in its specific details:
first, one should construct the pavilion; second, the ritual immersion in water; third, the ceremonial bathing; and fourth, the laying to rest on the bed.
The fifth is the placement of the fire, the sixth is the feeding of Brahmins;
the seventh is the peace-offering (śāntihoma), the eighth is the touching (sparśana);
the ninth is the purification of the house, and the tenth is said to be the [offering of] jewels.
Eleventh, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* for the completion of the ritual action;
