twelfth, one should perform the installation (*sthāpana*); thirteenth, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*); fourteenth, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*); and thereafter, the offering of the oblation (*sarivāra*).
The sixteenth [chapter] is declared to be the supreme indication of ritual action (kriyā).
Now listen to the determination of the auspicious moment (muhūrta) for consecration (pratiṣṭhā): the solstice (ayana), the fortnight (pakṣa), and the characteristics of the moment for consecrations.

"The northern course is the most excellent; it is said that the southern course is to be abandoned. Having relinquished the southern course, the northern course is supreme. Regarding the fortnights, whether it be the bright fortnight or even the dark fortnight, the days to be avoided [are as follows].
One should avoid [these acts] when Jupiter has set, when Venus has set, and during the Vyatīpāta yoga (8).
During a solar transit, on an inauspicious day, and during lunar or solar eclipses,
one should avoid them for sixteen days before and after [the event] (9).

Likewise, on days of transgression, during the month, on full-moon and new-moon days, as well as on other forbidden occasions such as the beginning of months and so forth, one should not perform [the practice];
these are the unsuitable days.
For the king, the kingdom, and others, for the village and likewise for the preceptor,
for the sacrificer and the sacrificial hearth— during auspicious and favorable times, on lunar days, asterisms, and weekdays, and during auspicious moments.
The lunar days— the first, the second, the fifth, the thirteenth,
the tenth, and the full moon— are auspicious dates in the bright fortnight.
The days of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury are considered the most excellent of days. 13.
[Regarding] the lunar mansions (nakṣatras):
One should perform the installation of the Lord Viṣṇu, which brings about prosperity, under the asterisms of Uttarās, Revatī, Aśvinī, Dhātṛja (Anurādhā), Puṣya, Punarvasu, Hasta, and Śravaṇa.
The benefic planets are Soma, Bṛhaspati, Bhārgava, and Budha; such is the determination of the auspicious lagna. 15.
These are declared to be the benefic planets (saumya-grahas) recommended for installation;
however, Rāhu, Saturn, and the Sun are censured. If they are situated in the third or sixth house from the lord of the Lagna, they indicate auspiciousness.

The Moon is auspicious when situated in the second, third, as well as the fifth and sixth houses; likewise in the seventh, tenth, and again in the eleventh house; however, it is not so when situated in the sixth or seventh house.
If the Moon is aspected by malefic planets, it should be known as causing fear; however, if Mercury, Venus, Saturn, Rahu, the Sun, and Ketu are situated in the ascendant,
they are respectively remembered as bestowing death, longevity, prosperity, and sons.
In the second house, benefics bestow wealth, while neither the Sun nor the Moon bestows what is desirable; others [malefics] are not so.
Malefics situated in the third house are known to grant home, prosperity, and sons.
Benefics in the fourth house bestow auspiciousness, as does the Moon, whereas malefics cause suffering.
In the fifth house, malefic planets cause mental anguish, while benefic planets bestow sons and wealth;
however, therein, a waning moon (kṣīṇendu) becomes a source of trouble for one's sons.
The sixth house is said to grant suffering, whereas the tenth house bestows wealth.

If the gentle planets are situated in the house of dharma (the ninth house), they bestow the excellence of sons; if all the planets are situated in the house of gain (the eleventh house), they grant wealth, sons, and grandsons;
if all the planets are situated in the house of expenditure (the twelfth house), those planets cause great expense.

Sunday is declared auspicious if it is joined with Hasta or Puṣya; Saturday is beneficial for the performer when conjoined with Svātī or Rohiṇī. The third lunar day joined with Mercury, and the sixth joined with Jupiter [are likewise auspicious].

The eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) conjoined with the Moon causes danger to life. However, the seventh lunar day (Saptamī) joined with the asterism Puṣya destroys living beings like fire; yet, Monday conjoined with Uttarāṣāḍhā is auspicious.

The muhūrtas known as Vṛṣa, Matsya, Mṛgendra, Kumbhaka, Dhanu, Meṣa, and Mithuna are considered excellent; those beginning with [the remaining] Meṣa and Mithuna are recorded as middling, provided they are endowed with the strength of the Sun for the agent and possessed of the strength of the Moon and the stars. 28.

If the fifth house from the ascendant is occupied by five bricks (pañceṣṭaka), and the eighth house is endowed with purity, being aspected by or joined with a benefic planet, during an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction—what more need be said here? For the Guru [Bṛhaspati] has declared this to be the best of all astrological moments (muhūrta). 29–30.
One should perform the installation of the God of gods at the proper time according to the prescribed rule; one should construct a pavilion half that size, facing the desired direction.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, the Great Upaniṣad, in the *Śrīpuruṣottamasaṃhitā*.
The Tenth Chapter, titled "The Determination of the Auspicious Moment for Consecration," Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
The Eleventh Chapter of the Śrī Pāñcarātra Puruṣottama Saṃhitā:
The Procedure for the Sacrificial Hall, the Fire-pits, and the Arches.
Regarding the procedure for the construction of the sacrificial pavilion and other rites, the inquiry of the Brahman priest:
The Brahman said,
"O Blessed One, O Lord of Gods, please describe the characteristics of the sacrificial pavilion."
In which country should it be performed? All other matters are very extensive.
This is the response of the Blessed One; the Illustrious Lord [spoke].
The characteristics of the sacrificial pavilion (yāgamaṇḍapa) are as follows:
it should be located to the east, in the northeast, or even to the north of the temple,
either in the second enclosure (varaṇa) or in the third enclosure.
For the purpose of the sacrifice, one should construct a pavilion provided with sixteen pillars,
measuring sixteen cubits in width and likewise measured in length;
it should be equipped with four doors and adorned with four archways.

Having divided that ground into nine parts, one should construct an altar (*vedi*) in the central square of Brahmā, and then arrange sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) in the surrounding directions; this is the characteristic of the square pit (*caturaśra-kuṇḍa*).
One should dig the ground one cubit deep so that it becomes square; in its center there should be a lotus pedestal four finger-breadths high,
surrounded by an eight-petaled lotus twelve finger-breadths wide.
Outside the pit, there should be three girdles in the four directions; according to an additional reading, these should be,
in order, the *pārvatī*, the *rājasī*, and the *tāmasī*.

[The determination of the girdles for all the kutas: The first girdle should be made four finger-breadths in height and twelve finger-breadths in width; the second should be raised to the same height.
The second girdle should be eight finger-breadths wide;
the third girdle should be made four finger-breadths wide and endowed with a height of two finger-breadths; above that, the yoni is prescribed.

In the fifth part of the *kuṇḍa*, one should fashion a *yoni* fifteen *aṅgulas* in size, shaped like a *pippala* leaf; or the construction of the *yoni* may be on the southern side. (10) If the *hotṛ* priest faces north, he should perform the rite without the *yoni*.
One should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the measurement of the diagonal line; having drawn four lines in the four directions to form a square,
one should place a line from the center touching the corners by means of its side portions.
With the third [line] drawn in excess, one should rotate it like the full moon; having stretched the cord across the center of the bow-shaped pit, one should mark out the northern line. 13.
Having accepted the three girdles as before for the sake of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
this should be the bow-shaped (cāpa) pit, square like the previous one;
[the other] is the circular (vṛtta) pit.
From the center of the field, one should rotate the diagonal cord as before; then,
at the position of the full moon, that [shape] shall be provided with a girdle as previously described— this is the lotus-shaped sacrificial pit (padmakuṇḍa).

Having measured out the area for the *aśrāvṛtta* (the non-circular shape) as before, one should construct a lotus-shaped pit (*padmakuṇḍa*) along the path of the thread in the place of the girdle (*mekhalā*),
and a triangular pit (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*).

Having joined the sixth part of the width of the *aśravis* at the upper and lower points of the north and south [sides], and having fixed a thread by joining it to the western corner, one should mark the *mekhalā*. 17.
*Mekhalā*.
The Guru should construct the triangle by following the measurement of that [central] sūtra;
the girdle (mekhalā) must be exactly the same as the shape of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
This is the procedure for the five pits.

The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be square in the east, bow-shaped in the south, circular in the west, and a lotus-shaped pit is prescribed in the north; in the north, there is also a triangular pit.
(In the region of fire, it should be triangular); a lotus-shaped pit should be made for Śiva when performing the rite of the five fires.

For those [gateways], one should prepare four arches (toraṇas) of the following dimensions: the Aśvattha, the Udumbara, the Nyagrodha, and likewise the Plakṣa—these four for the purpose of the arches. 20.
I shall now describe the height of those [arches] and of all the toraṇas below:
it may be equal to the door of the pavilion, or half as long, or twice that staff-measure, or even equal to the height of the pillar. 21–22.
One should have the arches (toraṇas) made in the shape of a plank, measuring five cubits, or again four cubits, or half of that;
these are for the construction of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), including the pillars and other components.
The pillar should be ten *tālas* in height, and the fillet (*paṭṭikā*) half of that; the circumference at the base of the two pillars is said to be thirty-two *aṅgulas*,
while the circumference in the middle is twenty-eight *aṅgulas*.
I shall not be at the top of that; [the pillar] should be twenty-four finger-breadths in height.

Having divided the length of the pillar into three parts, the base portion should have eight corners (octagonal), the middle portion should have six corners (hexagonal), and the upper portion should be circular.
Alternatively, for the purpose of immobilization (staṃbhana), the circumference at the root, middle,

and tip is desired to be twenty-four, twenty-two, and sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) respectively; or else, the circumference at the base may be sixteen finger-breadths, and from there it should be equal to that at the tip.
Then, one should fashion the two pillars so that they are released [from the base] according to what is beautiful;
28. In front of the two pillars, one should make them like the bud of a lotus, or alternatively, one should have them made like flames of fire, according to what is beautiful. 29.
One should make the pillars equal in height to the width of the two bands;
the width of the two bands should be exactly twelve finger-breadths,
or eight finger-breadths, or sixteen finger-breadths in length.
The lotus for the sake of the fillet (paṭṭikā) should have a width of four finger-breadths.
One should divide the pillar into four parts and cast one part into the ground; having gathered sacrificial trees as desired, or otherwise, [one should proceed]. 31–32.
One should not make the measurement of the door less than the measure of a man;
likewise, one should have the archways (toraṇas) constructed endowed with these characteristics, according to the marks of the eight auspicious signs.
33. [End of] the section on the characteristics of the eight auspicious signs.
I shall describe the characteristics of the eight auspicious objects as they are;
having prepared sacrificial trees, especially those that yield milky sap,
the length should be one cubit and the width six finger-breadths.
A solid [mark] three finger-breadths wide is declared to be of red hue and white color;
one with a yellow luster or the appearance of a lotus brings auspiciousness to the king and the kingdom.
[Marks resembling] the Śrīvatsa, a full pitcher, a kettle-drum, and a circular mirror [are likewise auspicious]. 35–36.
One should likewise draw a pair of fish, a conch, a discus, and the son of Kāśyapa upon the panels as auspicious symbols in their proper sequence. 37.
[The] sacrificial fuel-sticks.
The fuel sticks should likewise be of *pālāśa*, *duṃbara*, *aśvattha*, and *plakṣa* wood;
then one should bind twenty-one such bundles of fuel with two *kuśa* grasses. 38.

A pair of fuel-sticks (samit) measuring twenty finger-breadths should be made with kuśa grass; likewise, the brahmakūrca and other vessels are prescribed to be made with twenty-four darbha blades. 39.
The wise should discard the root and the tip of the grass; the knot of the *pavitra* should be like a braid, and its form should be fashioned accordingly.
The enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) should be three *prādeśas* in length, and the *pavitra* itself should be one *prādeśa*.
The wise man should have the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles made of *khādira* wood as part of the sacrificial implements;
they should be twenty-four finger-breadths in length, with their tips shaped like lotuses.
The cavity should be exactly one finger-breadth wide; thus is the *sruva* described.
The handle of the *juhū* should be twelve finger-breadths long and its cavity four finger-breadths wide;
the *sruc* is said to have an eight-finger-breadth handle. 42–43.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sacrificial Hall, the Fire-pits, the Arches, and so forth," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, which is a Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ.
The twelfth chapter in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Puruṣottama Saṃhitā.
The procedure for collecting the clay from the preceptor’s residence; the selection of the preceptor;
on the day the installation arrives, the patron, remembering Lord Hari—
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and performed his daily obligatory rites, being pure and having likewise completed his daily duties,
he should be accompanied by his wife, sons, and others, together with Brahmins and kinsmen,
amidst dancing, singing, and the like, and with umbrellas, banners, and canopies.
At the outset, after the installation of the deity, one should enter the residence of the preceptor; having offered fruits, flowers, and other gifts with devotion upon the ground,
one should prostrate fully with eight limbs and make this formal request.

"O Blessed One, by the power of your mantra, please cause [the devotees] to enter that [state] for the sake of attaining liberation; O you who are fashioned as an image for the sake of the liberation of devotees.
Having thus prayed and worshipped with flower garlands, sandalwood paste, and other offerings.

Thinking, "To the worshipper, Hari is manifest in person; of this there is no doubt," [one should place] that one of great wisdom upon a vehicle. Having placed him upon the vehicle, accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, he should be escorted by Brahmins learned in the Vedas.

Having led [the image] around the village in a clockwise direction, one should cause it to enter the sacrificial hall (7). When an auspicious moment has arrived, one should perform the worship of Viṣvaksena, the recitation for a holy day, and the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), and then worship Viṣvaksena.
Having sprinkled all the ritual materials with water from the auspicious day (puṇyāha),

the preceptor, together with the sacrificer, should perform the formal declaration of intent (saṃkalpa) according to the divisions of place and time, while wearing the marriage bracelet, garments, and other ornaments.

Having honored the officiating priests with the ritual fee for the assembly and having worshipped the deities with the madhuparka offering, he should then cause the priests to wear the auspicious threads and perform the worship of the assembly. 10.
Having obtained his permission and having invited the Vaiṣṇavas according to the scriptures, one should afterwards feed them at midday along with one's kinsmen.
In the evening, the collection of the clay and its ritual procedure [should take place].
When evening has arrived, the preceptor and the patron should begin the collection of clay amidst the sounds of singing and instrumental music,
accompanied by a great multitude of people and preceded by the chanting of the Vedas.
Having gone to the eastern or northern direction, in a pure place there, one should sprinkle it with water while reciting the mantra from the Śāstra and smear it with cow dung. Then,
with the mantra "Bhūmir bhūmnā," one should draw a circular mandala.
In the center of that, having drawn the goddess Medinī, who is endowed with nine days [of youth],
with her two lotus-feet placed in the northeast and northwest respectively, and with her face turned upwards— one should worship her preceded by the ritual placement (nyāsa). 15.
One should worship the discus with the *kūrca* in the west, Viṣvaksena with honey in the north (16), Garuḍa in the eastern part, and Śeṣa with a spade in the south.
[Additional readings]
Having drawn an image of Bhūvarāha, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers;
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of Varāha, one should mutter the Vārāhānuṣṭubh mantra.
Then, having meditated upon Bhūvarāha, the Guru, holding a spade, [should proceed].
Saying "I dig you," he should then bury it in its belly while facing east;
having gathered the earth, iron, and so forth, in a vessel made of metal or bamboo, and having covered it with a new cloth, he should offer a bali-oblation into the womb of the earth. 18–19.
Having placed an earthen vessel upon an elephant, a vehicle, or the like; or,
according to additional readings,
while crossing a river, [placing] sand, chaff, or powdered dung [into it].
Accompanied by Brahmins who recite the *Bhūnūkta*, *Medinīnūkta*, and *Śākunānūkta*, as well as those who recite the *Śrīsūkta*, *Pāvamāna*, and other hymns,
he should lead [the image] around the village clockwise and cause it to enter the pavilion.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Collecting Clay," in the *Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā*, the Great Upaniṣad of the *Śrī Pañcarātra*.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ. In the Śrī Pāñcarātra, in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, this is the thirteenth chapter.
The ritual for sowing the sprouts (*aṅkurāropaṇavidhi*):
the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) is performed by the protector of the village and its outskirts; [this is] the pavilion for the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇamaṇḍapa*).
Having entered, the Guru should stretch out threads moistened with sandalwood paste; the Guru should stretch out the threads,
first twelve straight lines extending eastward for the construction of the maṇḍala.
One should lay out fifteen threads extending from north to south;
having cleared that area for the sake of the grid, there shall be thirty-six squares.
Therein, within the central group of twelve, one should place the water-pots (ghaṭikās) in sequence.
As before, one should place the water-jars (ghaṭikās) in the eastern and western directions; in the southeast, southwest, and south, one should place the earthen bowls (pālikās) as before.
In the northwest, northeast, and north, one should place the shallow dishes (śarāvās) as before.
The preparation of the grain-seats (dhānyapīṭha) for the consecration of the vessels should be performed with rice, husked grains, and sesame seeds;
each of these seats should be prepared individually with the root-mantra.
The *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva* are considered to be of three kinds [of material].
The characteristics of the *pālikā*, *ghaṭikā*,
and *śarāva* are that they may be made of gold, silver, copper, or indeed clay.
The width of the opening of the *pālikā* is said to be sixteen finger-breadths (16).
One should make the opening of the *śarāva* twelve finger-breadths wide;
for those with faces situated on the four sides, the width is four finger-breadths (8).
The middle opening of the jars should be six finger-breadths in width;
the width of the footstool for all of them is ten finger-breadths;
its height is four finger-breadths, and the neck is desired to be one finger-breadth.
The face is like the *dhattūra* flower and resembles a lotus.
(10) The height of the *pālikās* is recorded as twenty-five finger-breadths;
that of the jars (*ghaṭas*) is twenty-two, and that of the shallow bowls (*śarāvas*) is twenty. (11)
Having brought bowls endowed with these characteristics, the preceptor,
having sprinkled them with the root mantra according to the ritual for placing the *pālikā* vessels and so forth, [should place] a blade of *dūrvā* grass and a leaf of *aśvattha*. 12.

One should tie *śirīṣa* and *sahadevī* around their necks with a thread wound around them, using the mantra "taṃ tvā anvehi. With the mantra "bhūmir bhūmnā," one should cast earth that has three layers.

In the aforementioned locations, one should place the water-jars (ghaṭikās) with the *parameṣṭhin* mantra; one should deposit the jars in the center with the *brahmajijñāsa* mantra, and one should arrange twelve jars with the *yata indra* mantra. 14–15.
One should place the earthen bowls (pālikās) in the eastern quarter with the mantra "tvamagne," and likewise in the south-eastern quarter with the mantra "yamāya soma.
One should place the bowl in the southern quarter with the mantra "mūṣaṇuḥ paramaṃtreṇa," and in the south-western quarter with the mantra "yamāya soma. (Verse 16)
Saying "Tat tvā yāmi," the preceptor should place the water-pots in the western direction as before;
he should place the shallow bowls (śarāva) in the north with the Vāyu mantra, and previously place the shallow bowls in the east with the Soma mantra. 17–18.
(One should place the shallow bowls in sequence with the mantra of Īśāna. With the mantra of Īśāna, one should deposit the shallow bowls in sequence upon the *raudra* [vessels].
One should worship Viṣṇu in the *pālikās*, and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) in the *ghaṭikās*.
Having meditated upon Śiva in the shallow bowls (*śarāvas*), one should invoke him and perform worship.
One should place the jars in sequence in the eight directions of the *pālikās*. Then, having established [the deities] upon heaps of grain, one should worship the world-protectors (*lokapālas*).
Thereafter, the Guru, having invoked the deities of the archways, banners, and so forth, should proceed. (20–21)
Having placed the water-pitcher in the western position and having deposited the vessels upon a heap of grain measuring ten *droṇas* with the mantra beginning "dhruvanta," [he should proceed]. 22.
One should place a water-pot upon that [altar] and fill it with water mixed with perfumes; one should deposit the five products [of the cow] and the five gems.
Having invoked the Moon-god (Soma), fashioned from gold, into that [pot], one should worship him. 23.
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) to the north of the Soma-pitcher,
one should place a water-jar (karaka) there and worship Hetirāja; this is the installation of the jar and the pitcher.
The thirteen [grains] ending with muddga, ādi, and veṇubīja are unsurpassed. [They are]:
washed grain, muddga, narpa, nīvāra, śimba, māṣa, and likewise yava.
The wise person should wash with milk the priyaṅgu, black chickpeas, green gram, and sesame seeds; likewise, the grains such as rice and bamboo-seed should be washed nine times with fresh water.
Sesame, mung bean, barley, rice, black gram,
wheat, mustard, chickpea, and kidney bean— these are proclaimed as the nine grains (*navadhānya*).
This is the location for the seed-vessel (*bījapātra*).
Either nine kinds of grains, or thirteen, or even more,
should be collected for the purpose of sowing sprouts in a metal vessel; that vessel should then be placed upon a pedestal of rice measuring nine *droṇas*.

The preceptor, having performed the invocation of the presiding deities of the seeds with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, should worship Viṣṇu as the lord of mung beans and Umāpati (Śiva) as the lord of mustard seeds. 30.
For wild rice (nīvāra), Jagatprāṇa is prescribed; for pulses (śimbā), Hari; for black gram (māṣa), Yakṣarāja; and for barley (yava), Brahmadaivata.
For millet (priyaṅgu), Mahāsena is prescribed, and for chickpeas (caṇaka), Bṛhaspati. 31.
Having worshipped the goddess Śrī of the śyāmāka grains and the tortoise of the kuluttha beans (32), the wise one should wash these lords of the grains with milk;
this is the consecration of the seeds.
The consecration of the seeds is performed with the mantra "yājātā" (33).
Having placed that vessel upon the head of the disciple amidst the sounds of musical instruments,
he should then circumambulate the temple in a clockwise direction (34).
Having set down that vessel, one should cover it with a new cloth;
this is the ritual for the offering of sprouts and the fire-oblation (homa).
Therein, one should perform the rite for the auspicious day (puṇyāha), whether at the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon the altar (sthaṇḍila). 35

Having established the fire according to the rules, the preceptor, having offered fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge with the root mantra, should offer the porridge with the *Nṛsūkta* (Ṛgveda 10.90).
He should then offer one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter with the Soma mantra.
Having touched the *pālikās* with the *saṃpāta* clarified butter while reciting the *sparśamantra*,
one should pour the remainder of the clarified butter into the seed-vessel and perform the recitation (*japa*) of the Creator’s mantra one hundred times, following the permission of the Brahmins.
At an auspicious moment, one should sow seeds in the *pālikās* and other vessels according to the sequence of Brahmā, Indra, and Agni, using the twelve-syllable mantra. (39)
One should cover [the vessel] gradually with earth while reciting the mantra "ūrdhvaṃ dhṛtāsi";

then, one should offer oblations (bali) from the Soma-pitcher using mantras containing the word "liṅga," as well as the Pāvamāna hymns and other sūktas, in all directions. 40. Then, one should present the bali offering.

One should perform the worship and offering of the Soma-jar until the conclusion of the sacrifice (verse 41). One should offer oblations to the groups of deities beginning with Kumuda day and night, and one must protect the lamps so that they do not go out until the completion of the ritual. (Verse 42)
"Beginning from the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one is declared to be an initiated preceptor (guru).
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Offering of Sprouts," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
In the Puruṣottama-saṃhitā of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Chapter Fourteen: The Ritual Procedure for the Vāstuyāga; An Exposition on the Occasion for the Worship of Vāstu.
Then one should perform the Vāstuyāga for the propitiation of Vāstunātha;
if Vāstunātha is not worshipped, the performed rite will become demonic (āsura).
Therefore, this should be done at the commencement of rites such as the sacrifice to the gods.
One should worship the guardian deities of the site (vāstu) even beforehand; I shall now describe that procedure.
One should prepare the layout of the vāstu-maṇḍala there, and having purified the ground with the Bhūsūkta, one should smear it with cow dung.
One should fashion colored streaks with red, yellow, and white powders.
Upon that mandala made of rice-grains on a new cloth,
[one should place the image] with gold weighing one karṣa, or half of that, or even half of the latter.
O wise ones, one should fashion the image of the door-keeper without stinginess regarding wealth;
ten lines should run upward and likewise ten lines should run crosswise.
One should draw this mandala so that it consists of eighty-one squares.
The ritual for the purification of the image:

one should perform the purification of the image with the essences of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) individually. Then, in that central position, one should perform the worship of the Vāstu-deity and the image.
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity— reciting the two mantras beginning with "Vāstoṣpate" as much as possible.
Whether ten thousand, a thousand, or one hundred and eight times,
one should perform the installation of the water-pot (*kumbha-sthāpana*).
On that very spot, having placed the Vāstu-pitcher (vāstukuṃbha), one should install a tuft of grass (kūrca) provided with the five barks and salts,
wrapped with a thread, and adorned with perfumes and other offerings;
and having invoked the Vāstu-deity into the pitcher, one should place the image within the pitcher.
One should perform the consecration of vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for the Vāstu-pūjā and worship the Vāstupuruṣa with sixteen or thirty-two ritual offerings (*upacāra*) in due order. 10.

The construction of the Soma-maṇṭapa and the arrangement of the maṇḍala should be performed according to the rules; having established that Soma-maṇṭapa to the east or the north, one should [arrange] grains, cloths, and so forth, as well as rice, in their proper order. 11.
In the center of that, having drawn a sixteen-petaled lotus together with its pericarp,
and having worshipped the lotus with the sixteen types of offerings (upacāras),
one should perform the installation of the water-vessel (kumbha) and the purification of the image.
Having fashioned a reddened image of Soma measuring one *karṣa* along with a *maṇi* and a brush (*kūrca*) within a water-pot (*kuṃbha*) containing a *soma* plant placed upon the pericarp,
one should purify it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and install it in the pot according to the scriptures.
The consecration of the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and worship:
the preceptor should perform the consecration of the vital breaths while reciting the Soma mantra,
and he should worship Soma with the sixteen types of ritual offerings.
The procedure for the worship of the eight guardians of the directions beginning with Brahmā: O Brahmā, starting from the square situated in the center of the Vāstu-maṇḍala and proceeding outward,
one should worship Viriñci (Brahmā) in the nine squares and Indra and the others in the eight squares.
Having himself recited the mantra "brahmajijñānam," the Guru [should worship] Prajāpati,
the Creator, Brahmā, the Lotus-seated One, the Unborn, Vidhi, Śatānanda, Druhiṇa, and the Progenitor of the Universe. 16–17.
Having uttered "āvāhayāmi" (I invoke), one should worship the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin);
then, with the six preceding words, one should worship Māhendra.
Likewise, one should worship Āryaman and Bhāskara with the mantra "ā satyena."
One should worship Āditya, who has seven horses, Mārtaṇḍa, the kinsman of the world;
and one should properly worship Dharmarāja, who possesses six banners and is the lord of the southern quarter,
while correctly reciting the mantra beginning with "yamāya soma."
One should worship Yama, the wielder of the staff, Kāla, Kālāṃśa, the son of the Sun (Yama),
and the one whose vehicle is a buffalo in six places.
After that, one should worship the Lord of the Aquatic Creatures (Varuṇa) in six places.

Then, according to the prescribed rite, he should worship Varuṇa— the wise lord of the waters, possessing a beautiful form, riding upon a sea-monster (makara), holding a noose in his hand— with the mantra beginning "imamme varuṇa," while circumambulating him clockwise. 22-23.
One should worship Kubera while reciting "Āpyāyasva" and "Śveta," [addressing him as] Kubera,
King of the Yakṣas, Lord of Wealth, and Sovereign of the Guhyakas;
one should worship the wielder of the mace, the Lord of Riches, with six steps.
Having recited the mantra for Agni— the messenger, the smoke-bannered,
the consumer of oblations, the seven-tongued, and the bearer of sacrificial offerings— one should utter the fourfold Agneya mantra of liberation, which has Naravāhana as its source.
Then, in the group of four in the southwest, [one should worship] Karbura, who holds a sword in his hand; thereafter, having uttered the word "Vāyu," the life-breath of the world,
the wind, and the measure of the wind, one should [worship] in the group of four in the northwest.

Having invoked that Īśāna, the Great Lord who is the husband of Gaurī, one should perform the invocation of the deities in the fourfold [direction] of Īśāna, where Īśāna is mounted upon his bull. 28. In the northeast (Īśānī), in the group of four, is the invocation of the deity.
The wise one should worship starting from the northeast corner and continuing outside of that;
according to the rules, he should worship in the thirty-two squares in a clockwise direction, using the mantras beginning with the name of each deity, preceded by the Praṇava (Oṃ). 29–30.
And likewise Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, and Āditya;
Indra, who is crowded with truth, and Bhṛśa, the lord of the intermediate space (Antarikṣaka); and there Agni, Uṣṇāṃśu, Pūṣan, and Vitatha as well. 31.
Yama, Graha, Kṣata, followed by Gandharva and Bhṛṅgarāja (32); then the Ṛṣi, Nirṛti, and thereafter Dauvārika;
then Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and likewise Saritkṣnā and Asura (33).
Poṣaṇa, Nāgaja, and Nāgamukha; beyond that, Guhyaka, Bhallāṭa, Soma, and likewise Anargala—this is the invocation of the thirty-two pitchers. 34.
One should worship Aditi and the Sun-god (Sauradeva) on those outer [sections]; having thus completed the worship, one should place golden or silver jars,
or else jars made of copper, within the water-jars.
Combined with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), along with the five barks and five sprouts;
combined with the seven earths and endowed with the nine gems;
combined with the fourteen medicinal herbs and endowed with the nine gems. (36–37)
Having established [the deity] surrounded by the thirty-two [deities], one should then encircle it with thread; then,
having placed eight jars in the eight directions according to the prescribed sequence, one should place Kumāra outside in the east and Bhāskara in the south.
O King, one should place Jaṃbuka in the west, Pilipiṃcaka in the north,
Diṅgiśravas in the northeast, Biḍālaka in the southeast, Pūtanā in the southwest, and the sinful Rākṣasī in the northwest. 39–40.

One should worship in this manner within the jars, [using] their respective mantras individually or their name-mantras individually; then the preceptor, having established the fire in either the sacrificial pit or on the altar, should perform the Vāstu-homa. 41.

Having performed the laying of the sacrificial bricks (iṣṭakādhāna) and the butter-portions (ājyabhāga) according to the path prescribed in the scriptures, one should then meditate upon Vāstu in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the rule,
offering ten thousand, or a thousand, or one hundred and eight oblations.

Or else, one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) amounting to a tenth part of the recitation (*japa*). Then, having offered the Soma-mantra one hundred and eight times, one should offer [oblations] for the deities situated in the pavilion according to the specific number of their respective positions.
One should cause the oblation (homa) to be performed with ghee mixed with honey for the sake of all success;
one should perform the oblation with fuel-sticks (samidh) of *śamī*, *apāmārga*, and *khadira*.
Then, one should [worship] all the attendant deities with their respective mantras.
Having offered oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, one should perform the rites up to the final full-oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

Then, according to the prescribed rule, one should offer the bali-offering to the presiding deities of the site (vāstu). Thereafter, the Vāstukuṃbha [should be placed] upon the grounds of the sacrificial pavilion.
One should sprinkle [the area] with the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta for the purification of the two doors. 47.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ,
in the Puruṣottama-saṃhitā of the Śrī Pāñcarātra.
Fifteenth Chapter:
The Ritual for the Circumambulation with Fire and the Immersion in Water; The Procedure for the Circumambulation with Fire.

Then follows the fire-consecration (*agnikaraṇa*); for that purpose, one should choose a *brāhmaṇa*. [The sacrificial pit] should be as thick as an elephant’s trunk, measuring five cubits by three cubits, consisting of a heap made of *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass, and joined with a triple-pointed tip.
Having ignited that heap in the Vāstu-homa fire according to the prescribed rite (2), one should perform a circumambulation while reciting the Paryagni mantra,
moving it everywhere throughout all parts of the hall and the entire area of the temple (3).
Then, proceeding in a clockwise direction with the chanting of the Vedas preceding him,

he should perform the sprinkling of the sacrificial grounds with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). The declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) should be performed by Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas.
Those reciting the *śāntisūkta* mantras should sprinkle [the area] with purified water;
one should light lamps there filled with cow’s ghee and incense the directions on all sides with fragrances such as black agallochum (*kṛṣṇāguru*).
One should cover the pillars with white cloths and canopies,
and adorn them with banners, beautiful flags, pearl necklaces, sprouts, other flowers, fruits, and ornaments of gems and gold.

One should adorn the entire pavilion, as well as the sacrificial hall, with plantain trunks, betel-nut trees, archways, and so forth, according to one's financial means; let it not be fruitless. 8. [The sacrificial hall]...
Then, O Four-faced One, after the worship has been performed in the sacrificial hall,
one should cause pillars to be erected on both sides of the doors, measuring two *tālas* in height, and likewise install the arches (*toraṇas*) according to the prescribed rule.
An *aśvattha* tree should be placed in the eastern quarter, likewise an *udumbara* in the south, a *vaṭa* at the western gate, and a *plakṣa* in the north;
a banner should be established on both sides of every gate.
In the east, two yellow-colored [vessels] should be placed upon red banners;
in the south, two blue-colored ones; and in the north, one should place full jars with white banners, provided with lids and cloths.
Filled with water from golden pitchers adorned with jewels, and encircled by threads—
these are Suśobhana, Subandha, Subhadra, and Suhotraka;
these shall be the deities of the archways (toraṇas) and the presiding deities of the banners.
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana,
Śaṅkhakarṇa, Sarpanetra, Sumukha, Supratiṣṭhita, Pūrṇa, Puṣkara, Ānanda, and Nanda.
Then, having invoked Vīrasena, Suśeṣa, Saṃbhava, and Prabhava,
as well as the presiding deities of the water-jars (kumbha), one should worship them in sequence.
One should worship the lords of the directions upon the banners in the eight directions with their respective mantras.
One should perform the intermediate worship and invoke the wise ones; between Indra and Īśāna, one should invoke and worship the Vasus (18).
Between Agni and Indra, one should invoke and worship the Rudras.
In the intermediate space between Yama and Agni, one should worship the Ādityas in their proper order.
In the middle between Yama and Rākṣasa, the wise man should worship the Sādhyas; then, having worshipped them, Marut should be worshipped in the direction between Varuṇa and Kubera.
One should worship the two Aśvins in the space between Marut and Jaleśa;
one should worship the Viśvedevas in order between Kubera and Marut (verse 21);
and one should worship the Moon-god in the space between Īśāna and Soma.

In this manner, one should worship each respective deity in due order. When midday has arrived, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, shall proceed to the workshop and perform the worship of the artisans.
Having gone to the workshop of the artisan, one should examine it thoroughly without hesitation.
When an auspicious moment has arrived, with the permission of the Vaiṣṇavas,
[one should proceed] regarding the image fashioned by the artisans according to the method seen in the scriptures.
Having correctly examined the characteristics, one should wash [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*);
then, having rinsed it with scented water, the preceptor should thoroughly smear the ground and scatter flowers thereupon. 25.
There, one should lay the image down; thereafter, one should worship the artisan. One should satisfy the master craftsman with wealth according to the nature of the work.
Indeed, the opening of the eyes (the consecration) should be performed by a skilled artisan.

Having diligently performed the rites of weighing, measuring, and standardizing, as well as the fire-oblations (homa) and so forth, and having given a cow according to the rules to the artisan, one should likewise perform the propitiatory rite (śāntihoma) at the time of afternoon. 28.
When the Śānti-homa is performed, the loss of honor, measure, and weight that occurs for men goes to dissolution along with that loss.
One should personally offer a caru-oblation with sesame seeds mixed with śamī leaves and ghee.
The preceptor should offer oblations with each of the seven vyāhṛtis individually;
thereafter, he should offer sixteen oblations of caru with the Nṛsūkta,
and he should offer one hundred oblations of clarified butter with the mantras of the five Upaniṣads.
Having offered oblations in the presence of the image, the preceptor should then perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) while worshipping with this mantra:
"Salutations to you, the Blessed One, whose nature is Jātavedas. 32.

Just as that [offering] belongs to Nārāyaṇa, so let this oblation for the gods and the ancestors be for Him who is the enjoyer, the one to whom the gods are to be sacrificed, the Self, and the Supreme Self; O Lord,
establish it for a long time within Your image for the sake of our welfare.
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods with the mantra "devasya tvā," he should touch [the disciple] with a white woolen thread combined with silk cloth and white mustard seeds;
then, having wound it around with gold, he should bind it on the right hand.

Having properly placed the images upon a chariot, an elephant, or a palanquin— whichever is preferred— consecrated seven times with the mantra "viṣṇorarāṭam," and having circumambulated the village, [one should proceed]. 36-37.
The ritual for the consecration in water is performed with white parasols, white fly-whisks,
and canopies made of Chinese silk as well as those made of silver. 38.
With auspicious fans, various kinds of sacrificial ladles,
and the sounds of conchs and drums, accompanied by dancing and singing,
the preceptor, together with the Brahmins, performed other great ritual services.
[With additional readings: accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments, reciters of Vedic auspicious hymns, shouts of victory, and praises, together with devoted followers of the Bhagavat.]
One should lead the deity very slowly to the water's edge as previously described.
Having reached the place for the ritual immersion in water by means of a palanquin or similar conveyance,
one should set the deity down near the water upon a water-shed or a lion-throne.

Having established a level site facing east that is suitable for the preliminary consecration (*jalādhivāsa*), or alternatively facing north, one should perform the rite in rivers, natural pools, tanks, mountain springs, or lakes. 42.

When possible, one should perform the ritual immersion in water according to the prescribed rules; however, those places unsuitable for the preliminary consecration in water include locations with very little water, cremation grounds, and places defiled by salt water. 43.

Furthermore, one should not perform the consecration (adhivāsana) of an image in places such as near a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), on low ground, in saline soil, in places covered with moss, or where there are people of other castes. 44. One should not install an image in such defective locations as these.
Regarding the characteristics of the consecration of water and the water-shed (*prapā*):
one should construct a water-shed in the midst of the water, provided with many pillars, endowed with four gates, and adorned with four archways (*toraṇa*). 45.
It was provided with canopies and banners, adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass,
furnished with strings of pearls, decorated with wreaths, and illuminated by incense;
it was filled with various kinds of fruits, square in shape, and most beautiful.

The procedure for the consecration of the water (*jalādhivāsa*) occurs prior to the recitation of the *puṇyāha* formula; the self-possessed Guru, having properly prepared the waters on the Sadyas or other [auspicious days] and having joined them with the *Puruṣasūkta* mantra, [proceeds]. 48.
Then, having dried that water with the *agni-mantra*, the Guru should subsequently fill it again with the *amṛta-bīja* mantra for water and the other elements.
Within that water, he should establish the great pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*), which is equal in size to the image.
One should place a very firm, smooth image made of wood [according to the mantra] in a reservoir of water;
having placed it upon an auspicious covering, one should prepare a new,
beautiful yogic seat provided with a pillow, and arrange it upon that in the proper sequence.
Having worshipped the pedestal with flowers and other offerings from the sacred texts while remaining composed,

one should thereafter worship the door, the archway, the water-pot, and so forth. Then, one should consecrate the image with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) using the five Upaniṣads in their proper sequence.
Facing the east, one should bathe [the deity] and perform the pure ablution (śuddhasnāna).
One should act in this manner according to the prescribed rule, beginning with the offering of ghee,
followed by the arghya, pādya, ācamana, garment, and sacred thread (yajñopavīta).

Having offered all the ornaments with the twelve-syllable vidyā-mantra, one should then withdraw the image by means of the dissolution path alone; this is the sequence for the withdrawal of the principles (tattvas). 55. The Sequence of the Withdrawal of the Principles.

I shall describe the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhāra): facing either east or north, having first withdrawn [the senses] starting from the east, and thereafter [withdrawing] the ears and other [senses],
one should then meditate upon sound and the other [objects], followed by earth and the other [elements] in their proper order.
The mind is dissolved into the principle of the mind (manas-tattva), and the Great One (mahat) is dissolved into that which is designated as the Unmanifest (avyakta).
Earth is dissolved into water; likewise, water has its abode in fire;
fire is dissolved into the paths of wind; and the principle of wind is dissolved into space.
Space is dissolved into the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra); the ego-principle is dissolved into the Great Principle (mahat);
the Great Principle is dissolved into the Unmanifest (avyakta); and the Unmanifest is situated within the Self (ātman).
Having thus withdrawn the principles (tattvas), one should meditate upon the God who is free from all affliction.
Having covered [the pedestal] with auspicious *darbha* grass, new garments, garlands,
and so forth, the wise preceptor, together with the image-guardians (*mūrtipa*), should wrap it without gaps from the base to the crown, while it remains in the midst of water. (60–61)
Then, with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, the preceptor should cause the image to be brought;
he should then lay the image down facing north with its head toward the east. To the right of the reclining image, he should place a large water-pot.

One should perform the worship with the seed-syllable of Brahmā; thus one should cause the rite to be done. (Having established the pitchers of the world-protectors in the eight directions, the preceptor) should install the guardians of the worlds in their respective directions.
Having placed auspicious items all around, he should then perform the ritual of fragmentation (śakalīkaraṇa).
(Regarding the water as the Ocean of Milk) having meditated upon the water as the Ocean of Milk, one should remember the seat as Śeṣa;
having emerged from the water, the knower of mantras should perform protection according to the rule—he should prescribe protection there.
He should display the wheel-mudrā and the protection-mudrā.

The duration for the water-rite (*jalādivāsa*) is limited by time; in the absence of rivers and the like, the method for the water-rite is as follows: "A stay in the water for three nights, or one night, or even a watch (*yāma*), half a watch, or even for the duration of a *muhūrta* is prescribed. One should perform the water-rite for three nights or one night.
In the absence of rivers and the like, the consecration of the image (*bimba*) in water shall take place.
Having drawn out a great quantity of water into a wooden trough or a cauldron— or, as may be possible, into another earthen vessel or the like—
the expert in the ritual should immediately perform the water-consecration.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Dwelling in Water," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, which is a Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pañcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ.
This is the sixteenth chapter in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Puruṣottama Saṃhitā.
The characteristics of the Bhadrā-maṇḍala;
Brahmā’s inquiry regarding the appropriate times for rites such as those performed in water and so forth.
O Lord of Kamalā, what is the proper time for the ritual immersion in water, for the consecration, for the bed, and for the altar? The Blessed One said:

One should determine the suitability for the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the Śrī Bhagavat with water; the preliminary consecration may take place at evening, while the laying to rest (śayana) is prescribed for the dead of night, and the installation (pratiṣṭhā) should be performed during the day at a moment enjoined by the scriptures. 2.
Now the characteristics of the *bhadra* [maṇḍala] will be correctly explained:
having made the ground square, one should then divide the square field into eight parts. This is the procedure for constructing the *bhadra* maṇḍala.
Indeed, there shall be one hundred minus one squares;

from the center, one should draw a lotus divided into nine parts, provided with a pericarp and filaments, and adorned with twelve petals. (The pericarp is joined with filaments. It is endowed with a pericarp and filaments, and beautified by twelve petals.
Indeed, there are nine doorways in each pair of squares.
One should erase six squares at a time in each corner;
thus, the doors are formed with half a square for the threshold. 5–6.
Regarding the arrangement of colors: one should then fill the mandala with powders of five colors. One should fill it in sequence with five-colored powders;
the eastern gate with white color, and the southern with black. 7.
The western [direction] should be filled with red color, and the northern with yellow; likewise, the eight secondary doors should be filled with dark blue color.
The lotus should consist of five colors, and its pericarp should be of the second [color].
One should draw four corners with the syllables [of the colors] blue, yellow, white, and black;
having thus filled [the mandala] with powders for the writing of the seed-syllables, one should write the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the center.
One should write the names of Keśava and the others on the twelve petals of the twelve-syllable mantra;
one should place the names of Vāsudeva and the others at the four gates,
and write the names of Indra and the others at the eight subsidiary gates.
In this very manner, the wise one should color the auspicious [liṅga];
he should then invoke the deity into it and worship with the root mantra. 12 [Additional Readings]
For those who worship Hari by reciting the twelve-syllable mantra,
this maṇḍala is highly praised as it quickly bestows success; however,
for those devoted to the eight-syllable mantra, the number of petals is said to be eight.
"That alone is their vehicle; among those, the eight-syllabled [mantra] is supreme.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Bhadraka Maṇḍala," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra. Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ. In the Śrī Pāñcarātra, in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, this is the seventeenth chapter.
The ritual procedure for the Vāstuyāga:
thereafter, at the clear dawn, the Preceptor, together with the image-makers (mūrtipās), performs the invocation of the Vāstupuruṣa.
On the southern part of the ground within the sacrificial pavilion, on a clean spot,
one should draw the body of Vāstu there with powders of five colors;
it is depicted face-down, with its head toward the east and its hands and feet at the two corners.
Having placed a tuft (*kūrca*) made of seven *darbha* grasses upon that [seat], one should worship it.
This is the procedure for the Vāstu-worship; after worshipping Vāstu with perfumes and other offerings, thereafter—3.
One should worship Daṃśumālin in the region of the head of the site-deity (vāstudeva); having invoked Kāma at the right armpit, one should worship him there;
and one should worship Kumāra at the elbow and Vināyaka at the hand.
He placed the two Aśvins at the two feet, and the Moon in the middle of the body; Durgā in the right hand, the Mothers likewise at the elbow,
Sthāṇu at the root of the left arm, and [Brahmā] in the lotus of the heart.

"Place me, Hari, at the navel; likewise place Brahmā at the navel. Having worshipped the guardians of the directions in the eight quarters, and having worshipped the Kṣetrapāla in the north, the best of teachers should worship that Vāstu in the western region."
Having established the fire according to the rules, one should offer oblations with clarified butter one hundred or one thousand times, as desired, using the five Upaniṣads; thereafter,
one should offer oblations of Apāmārga, Śamī, and Khādira wood.
One should offer sixteen oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) with the breaths (samīraṇas), the root mantra, according to the number of syllables in each respective mantra, and the Puruṣa Sūkta;
and one should offer the deities of the quarters (dvāstudevas) one oblation of caru each.
One should offer the bali-oblation to the Lord of the Field and to the deities in the proper sequence.
Having performed the worship of the Vāstu deity according to this rite, the procedure for raising [the structure] out of the water follows.
When the afternoon has arrived, the preceptor, together with the image-keepers (mūrtipās), should lead [the deity] to the riverbank accompanied by dances, songs, and instrumental music; then,
recalling the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama), he should lift the image out of the water.
Then, one should perform the dismissal of the deities residing in the *kalaśa* and the *kumbha* (the vessel for the deity's ablution).
Having seated them upon the grass mat (*viṣṭara*) on the bank, facing either east or north,
one should effect the purification of the metal images by means of the *samāvartana* rite.
Having purified the image with the juice of *tiṃtriṇī* fruit, [and having performed the opening of the eyes and displayed auspicious objects].
(15) [Additional readings: having performed the opening of the eyes and displayed auspicious objects].
Having beautifully adorned the images with garments, ornaments, flowers, and various auspicious perfumes, and having placed them upon a vehicle,
one should lead them to the sacrificial pavilion accompanied by the auspicious sounds of musical instruments.
One should cause [the deity] to be seated upon a cushion in the northern part of the pavilion. 17.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Invocation of Vāstupuruṣa and the Removal of Water," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
In the venerable *Purushottama-saṃhitā* belonging to the glorious *Pañcarātra*.
Chapter Eighteen:
The Ritual for Installation and Consecration Bathing; The Opening of the Eyes.

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the procedure for the installation and ceremonial bathing; one should perform the opening of the eyes of the image according to the ritual manual. With the mantra "madhu vātā," one should carry out the opening of the vision.

The binding for protection is for the purpose of bathing; therefore, one should perform the binding for protection first, prior to the bath. (One should do so with golden, silken, or cotton threads according to one's preference)—whether it be a golden thread, a silken one, or otherwise, simply a cotton one.
It should be made pure with five or seven threads,
and joined with one hundred and sixty betel nuts, or four times that number of betel nut shells, or furnished with fruits such as plantains.
The Guru, having filled a golden, silver, or copper vessel measuring two *khāris* with rice,
and having covered it with a cloth, places it upon the head of the attendant.
Having performed the ritual placement [of the deity], accompanied by dance, song, and the like, with the splendor of parasols and fly-whisks, joined by many lamps, adorned with canopies and banners,
and provided with a canopy while Brahmins recite the *Śākuna* and other great *Sūktas*.
Having circumambulated the temple three times, one should place that vessel on ground smeared with cow dung in the eastern direction of the image within the sacrificial pavilion,
and worship it with the Sūtra-mantra.
Having sprinkled that thread with water and taken it in both hands with the thumbs and ring fingers,
one should smear sandalwood paste upon the thread to the right of the image while reciting the Aparājita mantra.
One should bind the thread for Śrī and the others on the right hand with the left hand,
while touching it with the right hand and with a one-pointed mind.
Having recited the Astra-mantra, one should then worship the deity with water for the feet (arghya) and other offerings.
One should construct an auspicious pavilion for the purpose of the ablution, endowed with the proper characteristics; it should be ten cubits in width and twice that in length.

Having divided that pavilion into three parts— shining with four gates in the four directions and adorned with archways— construct in the western third a beautiful, square bathing altar measuring four cubits. 13–14.
Having fashioned [the deity] adorned with fire on the head and with severed hands,
one should arrange a stream of water on its northern side;
and in the northeast of that pavilion, [one should place a vessel] filled with fragrant water.
Having placed a water-vat or a basin there, one should cover it with water (verse 16).
Wrapping it with a new cloth while reciting the *pavamāna* hymns,
one should then consecrate it and prepare the materials for worship, such as the *arghya* offering and the rest (verse 17).
Regarding the characteristics of the mandala for the placement of eighty-one jars:
one should lay down fourteen lines moistened with sandalwood paste; thus, there shall be seventy-nine squares extending northward. 18.
The thread-spanning should be one hundred [units] in width and sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) in measure;
having gathered nine pieces of wood for each of the eight directions as well as the center— thus for the nine grounds— one should erase the remaining squares.

In this manner, upon the eighty-one squares, one should prepare separate pedestals using rice, husked grains, and sesame seeds respectively, each occupying a fourth part [of the space]; likewise, having laid down *kuśa* grass upon the pathways, one should place golden and silver [images].

Regarding the characteristics of the jars: the jars made of copper or clay should be endowed with the proper marks, resembling ripe *bimba* fruits in luster, without cracks, and free from blemishes. 22.

Having washed the jars— which are resonant, unbroken, and devoid of dark spots— with the Viṣṇugāyatrī mantra, one should wrap them with nine threads on the western ground while reciting the mantra "tanuṃ tanva."
One should perform the consecration of the water-pots (kalaśas) upon the sacrificial seat (dhyānyapīṭha) in this manner.
With the Viṣṇu-mantra, one should place blades of kuśa grass with their tips pointing eastward and northward; upon those kuśa blades, one should set down the pots, turning them face downwards. 24–25.

Having correctly uttered the *praṇava*, and having strewn [the grass] around that water-pot as before, he himself, facing eastward, should sprinkle it with the *arghya* water using the *Puruṣasūkta* and the *Parameṣṭhi* mantra. (26)
Having performed the placement of unbroken rice grains with the *viśve* mantra,

and having then turned those jars face upwards, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times with clarified butter using the *Viṣṇugāyatrī* and the *Śu* mantra, accompanied by the *Nivṛtti* and *Hvaya* vidyās.
Mixing it with the *saṃpāta* clarified butter, one should not accumulate other materials; this is the procedure for the installation of the pitcher (*kalaśa*).
One should fill half of the pitchers with water while reciting the *iṣṭavidyā*. (29)
Having placed ghee in the central pitcher, one should place warm water in the eastern direction;
the jewel-pitcher in the southeast, the fruit-pitcher in the south,
the metal-pitcher in the southwest, and the cleansing-water in the west.
One should place fragrant water in the northwest and water with unbroken grains (akṣata) in the north; likewise, one should place blood-water in the northeast.
Outside of that, in the central group of nine situated in the eastern direction, one should install the pitcher for the water for washing the feet (pādya). 31–32.
One should place the *arghya* in the south, the *ācamana* water in the west, and likewise the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in the east;
one should place a jar of curd in the center, milk in the southwest, and a jar of honey in the northwest.
One should place a pitcher of decoctions in the northeast, and sixty-four pitchers filled with pure water, along with eight more, all around; then,
having fashioned a *kūrca* of twenty-four *darbha* grasses, one should place it in the center.
One should place this [mantra] into a jar of ghee and into all the jars of water;
one should cast into them bunches of kuśa grass made of seven or five [blades].
Having covered the jars with lids, one should surround them in sequence with wheels or shallow bowls.
With garments, he should cover these vessels for the materials and these cloths with mantras (37).
Reciting the mantra, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests, should cover the others, each with a single cloth, having reached the presence of the deity in my vicinity (38).
While the Vedic instruments are being played and the dancing and other performances have commenced,
one should offer oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra, equal in number to the jars. 39.
One should perform the invocation of the deities into the jars using the *saṃpāta* clarified butter;
this is the procedure for invoking the presiding deities of the jars:
Vāsudeva in the jar of ghee, and Puruṣa in the jar of hot water. (40)
One should worship Satyadeva in the fruit-pitcher, Acyuta in the water of cat-feces, Ananta in the seed-pitcher, and Keśava in the jewel-pitcher (41).
One should worship Nārāyaṇa in the iron-pitcher and Mādhava in the fragrant water.
One should worship Govinda with barley-water, and Viṣṇu with milk;
one should offer the arghya to Madhusūdana, Trivikrama in the water-pot, and likewise Vāmana and Śrīdhara in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). 42–43.

One should worship Hṛṣīkeśa in a jar of curd and Padmanābha in a jar of milk; then, in a jar of honey, and subsequently in water infused with the decoction of bark, one should worship Dāmodara, preceded by the worship of the pedestal (pīṭhapūjā). 44.
Having worshipped the Earth in the jars placed upon the grains,
the Weapon-mantra in the grass-bunches (kūrca), and the King of Weapons likewise in the small bowls (cakrikā),
and having worshipped Viṣṇu in the cloths, one should bathe them according to the prescribed method.
Holding in his hand the water-pitcher (pādyakuṃbhaka) drawn forth from the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī-ṛc, he performs the bathing with the water contained in that pitcher using a kūrca. 47. Bathing.
Having sprinkled [the deity] with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should bathe Puruṣottama;
then, one should worship the Lord with the root mantra (mūlamantra) and the offerings beginning with arghya and ending with the lamp.
At each substance used for the jar-bath, one should recite the verse "mūrdhānaṃ divaḥ."
Having smeared [the image] with twenty-one kinds of clay, the preceptor, seated upon a lotus, should wash it with water while reciting the five Vāruṇika mantras;
then, as before, he should bathe the Lord with the arghya water, reciting the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā. 49–50.
The sprinkling with that water for sipping [the mouth] is performed with the mantra "tadviṣṇoḥ";
the consecration with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) is performed with the mantra "pavitraṃ te";
and the consecration with the central jar of ghee is performed with the mantra of ghee. 51.
The consecration with curd should be performed with the *dadhikrāvṇ* mantra;
one should perform the sprinkling with clarified butter using the *āpyāyasva* mantra, and [the sprinkling] with honey using the *madhu vātā* mantra and the *oṣadhīḥ* mantra. 52–53.

The bathing of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, should be performed with decoction water; then, with the mantra "mā nastoke," one should perform the consecration with hot water from a jar,
and with the verse beginning "vaṣaṭ te," one should perform the consecration with precious gems and water.
One should perform a bath with fruit-water using the *phaninī* anuvāka;
an ablution with metallic water using the *hiraṇyagarbha* mantra;
and one should bathe [the deity] with alkaline water using the *trātāram* mantra.

One should perform the bath with water while reciting the "Idam Viṣṇu" mantra; thereafter, one should perform the turmeric bath with the Śrīsūkta. Following that, one should perform the pure bath with a thousand streams using auspicious materials.
Having thus bathed the Lord of Gods, one should perform the worship of the maṇḍala.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation and Bathing," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pañcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
In the Śrī Pāñcarātra, the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā.
The nineteenth chapter: The Procedure for the Consecration of the Bed.
The Blessed One said:
Next, I shall explain the ritual for consecrating the bed and the procedure for dwelling upon it; by this,
the rite of installation will undoubtedly reach perfect accomplishment.
First, one should construct a pavilion endowed with all auspicious characteristics, supported by sixteen pillars, and adorned with ornaments. 1.
Likewise, [he should offer] trees such as the plantain, the areca nut palm, the punnāga, and the betel nut;
garlands of kuśa grass and flowers; canopies, banners, and flags; and, in due order, door-pitchers, archways, and mirrors.
Then, having adorned the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalā) on all sides, one should prepare incense of guggulu and agaru, as well as rows of lamps; furthermore,
one should anoint [the area] with fragrance and draw decorative patterns (raṅgavallī).
Having arranged various colored powders, one should draw a mandala in the center—
either a Svastika, a Bhadraka, a wheel-and-lotus, or some other design. Upon the mandala, one should prepare a bed according to the prescribed method.

Having prepared the bed with the twelve-syllable mantra, one who knows the mantras should then sprinkle the altar; then, having spread out abundant *darbha* grass— both with tips pointing eastward and tips pointing northward— he should strew it profusely.
One should prepare an extensive grain-seat (*dhānyapīṭha*), consisting of nine loads of *śāli* rice, half as much unhusked rice, and half as much sesame seeds; upon that,
one should place a tiger skin and then a cotton mattress.
One should spread a soft mattress, place woolen blankets upon it, and over those,
one should lay silken cloth; thereafter,
one should spread variegated garments and, following that, white, well-washed cloths everywhere with great care.
Having prepared the bedding, scented with the fragrance of musk,
strewn with various flowers, and adorned with various ornaments,
[he arranged] the bed of the Blessed One.
Having prepared the bed, one should then cause the Lord of Devas to lie down upon the couch according to the prescribed rite (verse 7).
While the Brahmins chant the Puruṣasūkta as appropriate,
accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments and auspicious songs, the image-bearers and the preceptor [should perform the ritual] (verse 8).
Having carefully raised the image with mantras beginning with "uttiṣṭha" (Arise),
and having led it from the bed to the ground of the altar along the path outside the sacrificial pits,
the Guru should place it upon the bed in a clockwise direction.

With the mantra "viśvataścakṣur" and others known as Vaiṣṇava, one should awaken the Lord with the mantras of His forms, facing the temple; one should then place the images of Śrī and the other deities at His sides. 10–11.
Then, with the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ," he should clothe [the deity] with a garment;
having worshipped the banner, the archway, the water-pot, and so forth in their proper order,
he should likewise cover the archways with new cloths.
Having stationed Brahmins who recite the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures at the locations of the eastern and other doors,
the preceptor, being composed, should place the deity within his own heart;
having performed meditation and visualized [the deity], he should then distribute the water-pots in the eight directions.
One should cast a conch, a discus, a lotus, and likewise a mace,
as well as the Śrīvatsa, Garuḍa, the tortoise, and a golden banner into the piles of earth;
and in the intervals between the jars, one should place the eight auspicious objects (maṅgalāṣṭaka).
Having placed the *sākurā* and *pālikā* vessels all around the altar (16),

one should worship the eight forms of Viṣṇu and the others upon the eight jars. Then, having invoked the deity in the northwestern direction, [one should place] a ninefold cloth upon the zodiac sign (17).
Having established the great pitcher,
which is provided with a lid, filled with divine fragrant water, and adorned with jewels and gold, one should place a spout at its side. 18.
Equipped with a *kūrca* grass-bundle, sacred threads, and garments, and filled with water from holy pilgrimage sites—
[according to an additional reading: provided with fruits and flowers, and accompanied by a golden image].
Having seated them, one should skillfully feed the Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa);
thereafter, the officiating priests should perform the fire-oblation (homa) by the command of the preceptor.

One should honor either the churned fire, the fire from a jewel, or even a worldly fire with the twelve-syllable mantra; having sprinkled it with the water of the "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha), one should meditate upon the divine fire in the mind and place it within the western sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). 20–21.

One should perform the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*) using *darbha* grass around all the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), and one should cause the fire from each pit to flow toward the western pit. (22) [Additional Readings]
One should mutter [the respective mantras] in order: the Āhavanīya fire in the east, the Dakṣiṇāgni in the south,
the Gārhapatya fire in the west, the Sāvitranāma fire in the north,
and the Āvasathyāgni in the southeast.
One should worship the Āghāra and other offerings in sequence within the lotuses situated in the midst of the fires;
Vāsudeva in the eastern fire, Saṃkarṣaṇa likewise in the southern,
Pradyumna in the western sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and Aniruddha in the northern.

One should worship Nārāyaṇa in the lotus-pit according to the prescribed rule; having invoked the goddess Śrī into the lotus-pit, one should worship her according to the ritual. Then, one should meditate upon Mahālakṣmī in the lotus-pit and worship her.
[Additional reading: The wise man, recollecting the Vāyu-mantra, [should perform the rite] with the seed-syllable of Agni.]
One should place four cows on the right side of the hall and worship Gaṅgā, Sarasvatī, Godāvarī, and Yamunā within them.
Having released them, the wise man should have milk-rice (pāyasa) cooked.
One should offer oblations with milk one thousand and eight times in the eastern fire-pit (26).
One should offer milk-rice (pāyasa) with the mantra of the deity residing in the pit;
likewise, one should offer kṛsara-rice in the southern fire and molasses-rice in the western fire (27).
In the north, one should offer *haridrānna* (turmeric rice); in other fires, *mudgānna* (mung bean rice) or *dugdhānna* (milk rice);
and with sesame, *śāli*, barley, and bamboo seeds, respectively, all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should perform the oblations following the instructions of the preceptor.
The procedure for the invocation into the pitcher (kumbhāvāhana-vidhi):

while the officiating priests are thus offering oblations into the great pitcher, the preceptor should worship Hari, the infallible one, having invoked Him as the Supreme Light, the mass of consciousness.
Having prepared the offering water (arghya) and other materials with the root mantra, one should worship [the deity].
Sudarśana, surrounded by flames, resembling a thousand suns and possessing a thousand spokes, should be worshipped according to the prescribed rite within the water-pot (karaka). 30–31.
Having invoked [the deity] with the six-syllabled mantra, one should personally perform worship;

[one should also perform] the dissolution of the principles (tattvasaṃhāra), ritual placement (nyāsa), fire-oblation (homa), and so forth, as well as the placement of the deity upon the couch and the dissolution [of the deity]. 32
Having performed the creation in the proper sequence, the preceptor should again emanate the principles (*tattvas*).
Then, he should offer oblations into the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) previously prepared with cow’s ghee;
this should be done either one hundred and eight times or twenty-eight times.
Or else, one should perform eight oblations according to one's capacity; then the Guru should offer the supreme oblation.
Having thus performed the homa of the tattva-nyāsa, immediately thereafter, one should perform the nyāsa of the ten vital airs, beginning with prāṇa, in the iḍā and other channels. 33–34.
The sequence of the sixteen-fold placement (ṣoḍaśanyāsa):
for those other than Matsya and the rest, the sixteen-fold placement is proclaimed;
first is the placement of the Praṇava, and second is that of the Vyāhṛtis. 35.
The third is the deposition of syllables (*akṣara-nyāsa*), and the fourth is that of the constellations (*ṛkṣa*).

The fifth is to be known as the deposition of time (*kāla-nyāsa*), the sixth as that of the day (*vāsara*), the seventh as the deposition of phonemes (*varṇa-nyāsa*), and the eighth as the deposition of water (*toya-nyāsa*). 36.
The ninth is the placement of the Vedas (nigamanyāsa), the tenth is beneficial for the gods;
the eleventh is the Virāj, while the twelfth is the placement of the wheels (cakratunyāsa);
the thirteenth is the placement of the qualities (guṇanyāsa), and the fourteenth is the placement of the forms (mūrtinyāsa). 37–38.
Then the placement of the powers (śaktinyāsa) is proclaimed; the placement of the worlds (lokanyāsa) is the sixteenth.
Having thus performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should perform the sixteen-fold placement and the peace-offering. 39
Having offered oblations of honey into the eastern fire-pit with the mantra "Bhūḥ Svāhā" one hundred times,
and having collected the residual drops of clarified butter (saṃpātājya), he should touch the feet of the deity.
In the same manner, he should do so in the southern fire-pit with the mantra "Bhuvaḥ Svāhā."
Then, having offered milk oblations, the wise one should touch the heart.
Thereafter, in the western pit, having offered curd with the mantra "suvaḥ svāhā," he should touch the face; and then, in the northern tri-angled pit— 41–42.
The preceptor should perform the oblation with clarified butter using all the *vyāhṛtis*; with the remnants of that offering, he should touch the head of the disciple.
Furthermore, in the eastern sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), he himself should likewise offer oblations of clarified butter, jaggery, and honey.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, the preceptor,
having touched his face with the residue of the offering, [should perform] the invocation of the Kalās using the water-pots situated at the directions of the altar.

All the image-protectors (mūrtipās) should sprinkle [the area] with water from branches of the Khadira, Aśvattha, Pālāśa, and Bilva trees, as well as with purifying waters containing the Ābliṅga mantras. Then,
the Guru [should perform the rite] with a branch from the Vaitasta tree placed in the pitcher at the corner of the altar.
One should sprinkle the images and the *nakala* vessels with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī mantra.
Having performed the rite of enlivening (*sajīvakaraṇa*), one should offer the sacrificial food (*naivedya*) according to the fivefold rule. 47.
[Additional Readings]
One should worship the immutable Lord with the services due to a great king;
having performed the worship with the Thousand Names and having praised Him again and again,
the Guru himself should then recite the Mūrti-mantra according to his ability.
By the power of his own austerity, having caused the deity seated within the heart-lotus of the Guru to ascend into the [divine] image via the path of the *brahmarandhra*,
he should bow his head to the ground and offer everything up to the final food offering (*naivedya*).

Having offered the water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and the attendants such as the fly-whisk and fan, the preceptor (*ācārya*), pure in soul, should pray to the Lord:
"May the binding of the bracelet, the bestowing of the [sacred] thread, and the lying down for the dream-portion [be performed]."
One should tie the *kautuka* (protective thread) on the right hand with the root mantra;
