then, having offered oblations (*bali*) at the doors, one should perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings and finally offer the *pūrṇāhuti* according to the mantra of the Lord of Dreams. 48.
[Regarding the additional readings:

Having performed the binding of the eight directions, having covered the deity with a seat, and having [honored him] in ten ways with the chanting of the Vedas, the sounding of musical instruments, and various kinds of hymns.

One should conclude the remainder of the night with dancing, singing, the sounds of victory, the chanting of the Lord’s names, and the recitation of the mantras for the [deity’s] forms (the preceptor,
the patron, and others). The preceptor, the patron, and the others should spend half the night on a bed of *darbha* grass.
Rising early in the morning, uttering the name of the Blessed One, he circumambulated the village of Adhikaṭhāṇi accompanied by a great festival.
Having entered the temple and completed the daily rites,
the preceptor himself should perform a propitiatory rite for the pacification of bad dreams, even if no dream has occurred.
If the rite is auspicious, the wise one should commence [the main ritual] according to the prescribed rules.
Thus, the characteristics of the bed have been declared in brief.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Sleeping on the Bed and so forth," in the *Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā*, the Great Upaniṣad of the *Pāñcarātra*.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
In the venerable Puruṣottama-saṃhitā within the divine scripture of the Śrīmad-pāñcarātra.
The Twenty-Fifth Chapter:
The Ritual for Consecration (Pratiṣṭhāvidhi)
Then, at dawn, on an auspicious lunar mansion and weekday, when the *lagna* has been determined,
the preceptor— being the best of the twice-born— should perform the fire-oblation for the site (*dvāravāstu-homa*) and the procedure for establishing the pits;
he should then perform the consecration of the deity together with the patron.
One should perform the *homa* sacrifice as before; then, on the southern side of the gateway,

one should perform the ritual placement of gems (*ratnanyāsa*) according to the scriptures within the pits of the pedestal situated in the center of the womb-chamber (*garbhagṛha*) and in the eight [directions] of the first enclosure.
Immediately thereafter, one should place eight seeds in the pits; then,
the wise man should deposit gems in the third [set of pits] and minerals in the fourth, while he should place the eight metals in the central pit.
O best of the twice-born, having placed mercury, vermilion, gold, and *śāli* rice seeds above that, and having installed the pedestal of the woman-stone (*strīśilā*),
the wise man should make it firm with lime and then have the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited.
The eight grains are proclaimed to be rice, barley, niṣpāva, priyaṅgu,
nīvāra, śāli, māṣa, and sesame.
The eight precious gems are indeed lapis lazuli, pearl, coral,
diamond, topaz, moonstone, crystal, and sapphire.
These eight are the eight minerals and these eight are the gems: yellow orpiment, realgar, 8,
saurāṣṭra, gorocanā, śyāma, lead, red ochre, and collyrium.
The eight elements have been thus described; one should install them in their proper sequence. This is the order of installation:
in the center of the stone slab of the woman, one should perform the installation of the *praṇava* (the syllable Om).

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the prescribed rule upon these very [lotuses], placing the vowels in the pericarp (*karṇikā*) and the consonants on the petals, beginning with Vimalā and the others;
thereafter, one should worship the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) in sequence with perfumes and flowers.
Having meditated upon Śrī in the *piṇḍikā* and covered it with a new garment,
one should assign the Weapon-mantra (*astra*) according to the rule at each door, and so forth, including the spreading of another cloth.
Then the Guru, having arrived, dismissed the deities of the banner and the archway; having placed the fire within his heart, he should, together with the Brahmins,
lift up the great pitcher and thereafter the pitcher containing the image.
The Guru, together with the image-bearers (*mūrtipas*), should carry forth all the images starting from the base;

holding the *galaṃtikā* himself, he proceeds with a continuous stream [of water], accompanied by the auspicious sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and all other instruments, as well as various other auspicious sounds such as those of conchs and kettledrums. (14–15)
With banners, umbrellas, flags, and the like; with shouts of victory, chowries, Vedic recitations, networks of hymns, and the chanting of Hari’s names—
moving [the image] in a clockwise circumambulation— one should enter the inner sanctum.
At the door, the preceptor himself should worship with the *arghya* and other offerings.
This is the procedure for the installation of the Blessed One: having circumambulated the pedestal, he should cause the deity to enter within.
When an auspicious moment has arrived,
one should install the immutable Lord with the mantra "dhruvā dyauḥ," with the ṛc "cātvā hāruṣam," and with the sāman "pratiṣṭhāsi" into the center of the neck of the pedestal.
Having filled [the vessel] with the eightfold binding, one should place the ritual peg (śaṅku) upon the full disc;
then, reciting the Pauruṣa Sūkta, one should set down the image for the rite (karmārcā) in front.
To its east, one should place the festive image (utsavārcā), and to the south, the bed and the offering (bali).

In the north is the bathing-tirtha for worldly goals and the stages of attainment. Having thus established [the deities], one should perform the worship of the Lord of Gods; this is the procedure for worship.
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) before the primary image, the Guru,
having performed three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), should meditate upon the eternal Brahman—
upon that Viṣṇu within the lotus of the heart, established in the mental sacrifice (mānasayāga).
Having worshipped Śrī and Bhūmi with the mantra whose essence is the Puruṣa-sūkta,
he should then invoke Hari onto the seat held in his joined palms;
being well-composed, he should then project that Viṣṇu into the image.
Having recited the *nivṛtti* mantra, one should meditate upon [the deity] residing within that image (25).

Having prostrated and offered a welcome, and having tied the *amutra* [cord], one should show it and perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*)— the one [deity] who is identical in creation, maintenance, and dissolution— in accordance with the prescribed rule (26).

One should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) of Śrī and the other goddesses, as well as the installation of the fire for Śrī and the other deities; one should sprinkle them with the water from the great pitcher (mahākumbha) using their respective mantras, preceded by the ritual assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa). 27.
The preceptor should establish the Gārhapatya fire in the sacrificial pit and upon the cooking vessels; standing with palms joined in reverence,
he should pronounce the *prahava* while the sacrificer stands before the deity and recites this profound mantra.
O Lord who is affectionate toward devotees, the fulfillment of the desired aims of devotees occurs through the recitation of this hymn;
O God, I pray to you with the desire for your grace.

"Be present for a long time in this place prepared by me with faith. Be gracious, O Lord of the gods; accept even this worship, O Indirāvara, for the sake of the village, the king, the kingdom, and the subjects. (30-31)
"Grant satisfaction to my body, nourishment, and likewise the supreme goal"—
having thus informed the God, the sacrificer, with a serene mind,
proceeds with the sequence of granting land as a gift to the priest for the sake of eternal worship under the name of the deity.

Having inscribed the name of the deity upon the earth provided with grain and water, one should provide for half the livelihood of the family of the officiating priest, ensuring that the worship and offerings to the Slayer of Madhu continue uninterrupted as long as the moon and sun endure. (33)
Then, having summoned the worshipper into the presence of the deity, the patron, with palms joined in reverence (*añjali*), should make this request:
"For the purpose of worshipping the deity and for the livelihood of your family... (34-35)

Saying, "Take this land given by me," he should then write the deed of gift (*dāna-śāsana*) upon a stone slab or a copper plate and place it into the hand of the officiating priest (*arcaka*), along with gold, fruit, and water.
Alternatively, one may cause the gift of land to be made under the name of the worshipper;
the gift of land in the name of the deity is said to yield the highest fruit, while that in the name of the worshipper is said to yield middling fruit. (37–38)
One should always provide wages only after first making a gift of land;
for if one provides wages without a gift of land, his lineage will perish, and both his life and prosperity will be destroyed. (39)
The nine devalakas have been excluded from all ritual activities (sarvakarma).
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause the ground itself to be offered; this includes the appointment of the site-preparer (sthānācārya) and others.
Then, for the purpose of utilizing the excellent water of the Bhagavat-bāda-tīrtha,
one should appoint a presiding teacher (sthānācārya) to that place, as well as attendants for the hands, instructors, and performers of dance, song, and instrumental music. 41–42.
Then, for the sake of increasing the worship of the deity, he should appoint those others who perform the purification of the site as well as the purification of the vessels;
and for their livelihood, he should grant land and wealth. 43.
One should then employ them in various services, each according to their respective names.
He who installs the Lord with the groups of attendants goes to the supreme abode, where he dwells like the Blessed One himself.
According to the means of the patron, one should arrange for all of these;
otherwise, the twice-born devotee should respectfully choose at least one reciter.
He obtains the full fruit [of the rite] until the dissolution of the universe (ābhūtasaṃplava).

To the preceptor, those seeking sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and other devotees performing dance, song, and so forth; to all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), as well as to ascetics (*yati*) and the learned— 47.
One should satisfy each [of them] individually according to one's means.
Then, at the conclusion of the installation, the patron, with devotion, should worship the master artisan who performed the installation upon a prepared seat. 48–49.
With golden waist-bands, armlets, and bracelets, as well as with necklaces of gems, earrings made of jewels, and finger-rings;
with upper garments of fine linen and wealth consisting of living beings and their possessions.
Having gratified him according to the rule while remembering him in the heart like a god,
one should place him upon a vehicle or similar conveyance preceded by the sound of musical instruments, and after circumambulating the village, cause him to enter his own home.
Whoever should thus install the Lord according to the Pāñcarātra ritual, as declared in the Pāñcarātra Āgama,
goes to the supreme abode— which is beyond past history and characterized by the absence of rebirth—
and purifies twenty-one generations of his lineage.
Thus, the beautiful rite of installation has been briefly explained. (Padmaja) 54.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Installation," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, a great Upaniṣad within the glorious Pañcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
In the divine scripture of the illustrious Pāñcarātra, in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā.
The Twenty-First Chapter: The Ritual for the Consecration of Vimānas and Other Structures.
The Blessed One said:
Regarding the consecration of celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and the characteristics for the consecration of temples, pavilions,
and so forth: one should duly construct a sacrificial pavilion (*yāgamaṇḍapa*) in front of the temple.
The preceptor should construct a structure provided with four gates and adorned with four archways; furthermore, he should arrange eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) all around the palace,
and he should fashion one pit on the ground area of the sacrificial altar.
The best of the twice-born should perform the homa of all the forms and fashion a mound (vapra) upon that [ground].
At night alone, he should duly carry out the sowing of sprouts; having prepared a mountain-like structure as before, or rather, a vessel made of metal.
Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) according to the rule for that linga-measure together with the mantra-image, and having provided all the necessary implements,
he should cause everything required for the bath to be prepared by those two according to the prescribed ritual.
Having placed the image within that [pedestal] which is endowed with jewels and other such things,
and having covered it with flowers, ornaments, and garments— just as one would with the *arghya* flowers—
he should slowly ascend to the pinnacle of the temple together with the *mūrtipas*.
Then, having performed the placement of the jewels according to the path prescribed in the scriptures and following the sequence previously mentioned,
one should install the image together with the crest-pot (śikhā-kuṃbha).
Having worshipped it and covered it with cloth, one should perform the rite of offering the milk-rice (pāyasa).
Thereafter, one should establish the temple with six items beginning with white mustard seeds (siddhārthaka).

Then, having tied the marriage-thread (kautuka) upon the beam of the celestial chariot (vimāna-paṭṭikā) with twenty-five threads, one should subsequently perform the rite of shadow-consecration (chāyādhivāsana).
O best of preceptors, one should perform the ceremonial bathing in a mirror as previously described;
if images have been fashioned for the four directions of the temple,
one should then open their eyes according to the sequence prescribed in the scriptures.
One should also perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the pedestal and the door of the celestial chariot (vimāna).
In the eastern sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the preceptor himself should personally perform the entire oblation (homa);
then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should offer the excellent oblation for the destruction of obstacles to the Cakra.

Having established and thoroughly worshipped [the deity], one should immediately thereafter install the *astra* (weapon-mantra) at a height of three parts above the *śikhā* (crown) using the *śikhā-mantra*.
O Brahmin, the installation of both the temple (*prāsāda*) and the image (*biṃba*) should take place simultaneously.
The consecration of a celestial chariot has thus been briefly described by me. O best of sages, listen now to the consecration of pavilions and other such structures.
First, the Maṇḍapa, and likewise the Āgrya and the Āsthāna-maṇḍapa;
the enclosure wall, the residence for the attendants, the treasury, the storehouse for garments, the water-hall, the flower-hall, and likewise the Yāga-maṇḍapa. 16–17.

One should purify the fire-sanctuary and all other areas with abundant water; having performed the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), one should perform the rites of sprinkling and smearing, and especially sprinkle them with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and decorate them with canopies and other ornaments.
Then, having perfumed with incenses and offered lamps,
one should decorate with powdered rice and scatter unbroken grains upon the ground;
having had the "Auspicious Day" (Puṇyāha) recited, one should then worship the Vāstu deity.
Having prepared another pedestal, one should place a great water-pot (kumbha) there;
having worshipped the deity there along with his limbs and retinue,
one should then establish the fire either on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa).
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with additional verses according to the scriptures, following the very path previously described.
Having offered oblations to Taurkhya, the presiding deity of the pavilions, with his own mantra one thousand, ten thousand, or even one hundred and eight times, [one should offer] fuel-sticks,
clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge, each separately and individually.
Having fully gratified the deity in the fire, one should then perform the offering of wool (ūrṇāhuti).
When an auspicious moment arrives, one should perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) with water from the ritual pitcher (kumbha) for the installation of vehicles,
chariots, gate-towers (gopura), and so forth, as well as the installation of door-frames, panels, and the like.
Thus has the procedure for the consecration of pavilions and the like been described.
(23) For chariots, great gates, city-gates, and other vehicles, the same [procedure] is prescribed. O Lotus-born One, two door-panels should be fashioned at each gate. (24)
One should sprinkle the door-frames with water from the auspicious day (puṇyāha),
and having sprinkled them with water and covered them with cloths,
one should then place the door-panels and door-frames upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and worship them with the water-pot (kuṃbha).
One should place eight jars all around with the mantras beginning with Vāsudeva.
To the north of the jar, the preceptor should place a water-pot;
having worshipped the archways and so forth, he should then perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).

Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the rules, one should sprinkle [the area] with the residual clarified butter (saṃpātājya). At an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary alignment, one should place gems into a pit situated beneath the threshold stone; thereafter, one should have the day of merit (puṇyāha) proclaimed.
Having sprinkled [the area] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the twice-born should place the door-panels.
Then, he should invoke the deities with water from the pitcher using a *kūrca* grass-bundle;
likewise, he should invoke Śānti in the lower part and Vāgdevī on the right.
One should place Rati and Lakṣmī above; O Brahmā, on the right door-panel one should establish Viśvadṛk and Bhūtabhāvana,
and on the left door-panel one should station Viśvavaktra and Pratāpavān.
Having likewise invoked the forms of the ten avadānas in due order [into the arrows],
one should place the Vedic scriptures and the Purāṇas in sequence upon the bamboo shafts;
thereafter, one should invoke the thirty-three deities into the iron-headed arrows (nārāca).
Having assigned the sages to the stakes (kīla), one should worship Gaurīśa on the surface of the lintel (paṭṭikā) and Viśvabhāvana on the door-panel (kavāṭa) made of jasmine wood. 34.
[Additional readings]
Having invoked and diligently worshipped Vāyu, the lord of the door-panel, one should perform the recitation (japa) according to the rules with the "Avāta-vāyu" mantra.
The installation of the door-panel has been declared; now hear the installation of the wheel (cakra).
Now I shall specifically describe the excellent installation of the Sudarśana [discus], namely the supreme consecration of the wheel. (35) [Additional readings]
For the sake of destroying calamities in the village caused by fire, thieves, disease,
and the like, for the protection of the temple of the gods, and for the welfare of the country,
the installation of the Sudarśana Bhagavan’s abode must be performed.

O best of the twice-born, the characteristics of the Sudarśana, the king of wheels, shall now be described in brief: [the characteristics] of the gate-towers, the village, and the pillars in sequence.
One should again make it wide by ten cubits, or five cubits, or even by two cubits; or it may be thirty-two finger-breadths,
or twenty-four finger-breadths, or likewise sixteen or twelve.
Equal to the face of the primary image, it may be provided with a thousand spokes, or a hundred spokes, or twenty-four spokes;
or likewise, it may have twelve spokes, eight spokes, or even five spokes. (38)

One should have a wheel fashioned from gold and other materials, adorned with various gems, consisting of six spokes and three sides, surrounded by flames, and embellished with a central hub-mandala. 39–40.

The procedure for its consecration is as follows: having gratified the artisan with wealth, grain, and so forth, and having collected all the necessary materials and sacrificial substances without exception according to one's means. 41

On the northern side of the temple, one should construct an excellent pavilion provided with sixteen pillars; in its center, one should prepare an altar. Around that altar, in all four directions, one should cause four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made.
Alternatively, one should construct a beautiful hexagonal pit (kuṇḍa) there;
near that, in the region of the northern door, is the bathing pavilion (snānamaṇṭapa),
and in the Raudra pavilion is the pavilion for the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇamaṇṭapa).

Having prepared the interior area, one should decorate it with lime powder; at an auspicious time when the sun has risen in the east, the image-bearers (mūrtipās), having churned the fire, should establish it within all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas). 45.
Having performed the Vāstuhoma and other rites as previously prescribed, one should proceed;
all materials should be circumambulated with fire from the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and sprinkled with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and the water of the Puṇyāha rite. 46–47.
Having soaked that wheel in milk, one should bathe it with seven jars [of water] according to the previously mentioned method; likewise, one should cause it to be immersed in water and so forth.
Then, at the time of afternoon, one should lift the wheel out of the water.
Having entered the sacrificial hall, the Guru should cause the ceremonial bathing to be performed in due order. Having opened the eyes with the mantra, he should lay [the deity] upon the bed;
then, having invoked Hetirāja into the pitcher placed upon the grain-seat (dhānyapīṭha), he should summon him. 49–50.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) according to the prescribed method, one should cause the propitiatory oblation (*śāntihoma*) to be performed and make the *cakra* "living" (endowed with consciousness) in the previously mentioned sacrificial pavilion.
Then, provided with a bed of *darbha* grass, one should sleep together with the guardians of the images (*mūrtipās*).
When dawn had arrived, the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images (mūrtipās),

worshipped the deities of the site (vāstudevas) and other gods, and having performed the ritual dismissal (udvāsya), the teacher then offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and made the fire over to [the disciple].

When an auspicious moment has arrived, the sacrificer, having subdued his senses and accompanied by the officiating priests and the preceptor, should enter the upper chamber while preceded by the sound of musical instruments,
performing a circumambulation of the temple.

One should install the Wheel-King (cakrarāja), preceded by the placement of the jewels (ratnanyāsa). Having uttered the mantra "dhruvanta," one should cast the sacrificial offering (bali) in the four directions.
The patron (yajamāna) should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor (ācārya) according to his pleasure.
Thus, he who with devotion constructs the great Sudarśana-cakra shall enjoy all pleasures in this world and, at the end, attain union [with the Divine].
57. Thus ends [the section] in the glorious *Pāñcarātra*, the Great Upaniṣad, in the glorious *Puruṣottama-saṃhitā*.
The twenty-first chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Consecration of Vimānas, Gopuras, Maṇḍapas, and so forth.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
The twenty-second chapter of the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, within the glorious and divine scripture of the Pāñcarātra,
entitled "The Procedure for Initiation into the Cakra-abja Maṇḍala."
Brahmā said:
Regarding the inquiry of Brahmā for the purpose of hearing the rules for initiation:
"O Blessed One, I desire to hear about the supreme and auspicious initiation of the gods."

In whom should the fitness for propitiating the deities be established? For those who have not been initiated, there is no entitlement to worship and the like, as previously stated. Therefore, O you of excellent vows, please explain the procedure for initiation correctly.
The Blessed Lord said:

Listen to the reply of the Blessed One regarding the excellence of the initiation rite (dīkṣā-vidhi) and the etymological definition of the word "initiation" (dīkṣā). With a concentrated mind, I shall explain initiation according to the scriptures.
By performing which all men become composed of the Blessed One (Bhagavat);
by means of this, liberation is attained and worldly existence is diminished;
it bestows and destroys [suffering], and is thus designated as *Sādīkṣā*. 3–4.

One who is a Vaiṣṇava, a devotee of the Blessed Lord, skilled in the meaning of all Tantras, the initiating preceptor (dīkṣā-guru), characterized by these qualities, proficient in the Tantra of Installation (pratiṣṭhā-tantra), and born of the Pāñcarātra tradition. 5.
One should invite a venerable and great devotee of the Lord (the preceptor). O Lotus-born One, having summoned him,
the instruction for the site of the divine initiation should take place in a beautiful temple or in the house of the teacher and the disciple.

One should commence the rite of initiation during an auspicious *lagna* and at a favorable moment (*muhūrta*). One should perform the divine initiation (*devadīkṣā*) under an auspicious *lagna* and a favorable lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*).
It is essential to receive instruction on the deity’s mantra from the mouth of a Guru; a mantra that is received by chance, through deception, or by force [is ineffective]. 7.
If one were to examine them independently, it would result in misfortune rather than benefit;
for all mantras and all rituals have emerged from the mouth of Kuruvaktra. Therefore, mantras must be received from the mouth of a guru alone by those who possess wisdom.
In the initiation for the worship of Viṣṇu and other rites, at self-manifested sacred sites and the like,
the auspicious time for initiation— consisting of the solstice, month, lunar mansion, lunar day, weekday, and so forth— is prescribed.
In the same way, the preceptor should not investigate [the disciple's] enemies, friends, and so forth.
This is the instruction regarding mantras from the lotus-mouth of the teacher; initiation is for one who approaches [him], and by that, the disciple is purified.
To a disciple who is indeed humble, who abides by the duties of his own caste and stage of life,
who is endowed with devotion and faith, whose mind is constantly attached to the very actions prescribed [for him],
and who further understands the essence and non-essence of the Vedas, Vedāṅgas, and Yoga; 12.

The mantra should be imparted to one who is learned, virtuous, and constantly devoted to the elders; it should never be given to one who is unrighteous, O Four-faced One, nor to one who has not undergone initiation and the stages of life.
In his own home, at the time of Puṣkara during the evening, the best of mantra-knowers,
having first performed the laying of the lines (sūtrapāta), should then construct the pavilion (maṇṭapa) in due order; this is the procedure for the construction of the initiation mandala.

One should draw either a mandala of a wheel and lotus, or one that is auspicious (bhadra), or one that brings well-being (svastika), using five kinds of colored powders according to the injunctions of the scriptures; then,
the most excellent knower of mantra and tantra should perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).

One should worship [the deity] individually with the sixteen services, beginning with the prayer to the Blessed One; then, having placed the Guru at the forefront, one should be intent upon the propitiation of the deity. 17
Accompanied by various auspicious hymns, the practitioner should enter the temple;
having prostrated before the God of gods, he should then circumambulate him three times. He may proceed on a chariot, an elephant, or a palanquin, according to his preference.
Having mounted the God and the Goddess [onto the vehicle] and performed a circumambulation of the village,
one should reach the site of initiation and, accompanied by dance, song, and other arts,
seat the God upon the pedestal near the mandala.
O twice-born one, having performed the rites up to the *nīrājana* preceded by the offering of *arghya*, *pādya*, and so forth,
and having thus worshipped according to the rules, the preceptor should then duly install [the image] within the mandala of his own house using the *Dhruva-sūkta*.
Then, having performed the entire sequence of rites beginning with the *puṇyāha* and ending with the *pūrṇāhuti*,
one should request permission from the elders and the great-souled ones (or from the elder and the great-souled one).
Prior to the *puṇyāha*, one should perform the sowing of seeds (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) and other preliminary rites.
And having placed the discus and lotus in the northwest, one should place the great pitcher (mahākuṃbha) to its north;

having approached the small pitcher (karaka), one should place Janārdana in the great pitcher and Sudarśana in the small pitcher, while Viṣṇu and the others are in the secondary pitchers (upakuṃbhaka).
Having invoked and worshipped according to the rules, one should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*);
the installation of the fire (*agni-pratiṣṭhā*) should be performed according to the procedure stated in the *Sūtra*.
One should cause the rites of sowing sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth to be performed by one seated upon a lotus.
Then, having performed the *mūrti-homa* and offered oblations to the attendants (*pārṣada*) of Vaikuṇṭha (verse 26),
and then having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* ending with "vauṣaṭ," O Lotus-born One,
follows the procedure for examining the tooth-stick (*daṃtakāṣṭha*) and other items of the disciple.
Then, having summoned the disciple, he should have him clean his teeth with a wooden stick (27).
Having examined that wood, he should bind the eyes with a cloth;
having applied ash to the forehead while reciting the Astra-mantra (28).
Then, having performed the binding of the disciple's eyes and the binding of protection, one should have him consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
these are the procedures beginning with the binding of protection.

Then, for the sake of purifying the body, the disciple should consume the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the syllable Om; thereafter, the self-possessed Guru, having taken the Lord of Devas in his hand and having prostrated, should contemplate [the disciple] as purified.
I offer this petition to the Blessed One; O Lord seated upon the lotus, please release the noose of saṃsāra that binds us mortals. 31.
O Lord, you alone are my refuge; no other goal is known to exist.
You are the cause of liberation from the bonds [of saṃsāra], consisting as you do of the very means for your own propitiation.
Therefore, [I seek you] for these beings born as animals, who are bound by the fetters of birth.
"O Lord of Gods, I shall perform the *vipāśā* [untying]; you should grant me permission. Having thus informed him, one should wrap the remaining portion with a thread.
O twice-born one, having doubled a thread that is white, red, and black— these three colors—
and then making it threefold, one should proceed from the crest-lock to the feet along that thread twenty-five times.
One should envelop the body of the disciple nine times with the root mantra;
this is the procedure for the oblation (homa) with clarified butter performed one hundred and eight times, followed by the final offering (pūrṇāhuti). 36.

With the mantra of Svapnādhipati, one should offer an oblation (*bali*) of ghee one hundred and eight times, and especially with black gram (*māṣa*) water, to the spirits (*bhūta*s). For the disciple whose eye-bandage has been removed, there is the binding of the body.
Having taken up the thread of illusion and placed it in a shallow bowl, O Lotus-born One,
the Preceptor should cover the side of the water-pot with one bowl and prepare his bed for the purpose of the dream.

Having spread darbha grass upon that bed, the disciple should take rest. The Guru should not cause the Deity residing in the mandala and the pot to emerge [from them] until the second day, when the peace-offering (śānti-homa) is performed.
Then, at the clear dawn, having bathed with the preceptor at their head,
and having duly completed the daily rites, they should perform the propitiation for the pacification of dreams before Janārdana situated within the maṇḍala, and then bind the eyes once again.
Having performed this, one should offer a hundred oblations of the root mantra into the fire.
This is the sequence for the withdrawal of the *māyāsūtra*.
Then, having severed the *māyāsūtra* and resorted to the sequence of withdrawal—42.
Having thus indicated the principles, the preceptor should perform the rites beginning with drying and ending with the primordial nature (prakṛti) within the body of the disciple;
that is, he should carry out the actions such as drying and so forth upon the disciple's body. 43.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five upaniṣads upon the body, preceded by the rite of emanation (sṛṣṭi); one should sprinkle [the disciple] with the root mantra and release the blindfold. 44.
Having displayed the wheel and lotus below, the Guru, accompanied by the disciple, [worships] the glorious Lord Nārāyaṇa, the teacher and sovereign of the worlds. (45) The instruction of the mantra.

Having meditated, he should impart the mantra accompanied by the *praṇava* into the right ear of the disciple, as well as the seer (*ṛṣi*), the meter (*chandas*), the deity (*daivata*), and the limbs (*aṅga*) [of the mantra]. Following that, the instruction including the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*) and so forth should be given. 46.
Having taught the eight-syllabled mantra, he then [taught] the twelve-syllabled one in due order;
then the six-syllabled mantra of Viṣṇu, and thereafter the Gāyatrī,
O Lotus-born One, as well as the other root-mantras of the four forms.

Thereafter, having instructed him in the mantras of the deities according to the prescribed rule, the Guru should, at that time, impart instruction on Dharma to the disciple while he is under his observances. 49.
The mantra must not be disclosed to another, nor should one display the rosary;
one should not revile the guru with speech (and having prostrated to one's own guru), nor should one eat *kalañja*.
One should not speak falsehood with one's voice, nor should one approach the wives of others. 50.

One should perform circumambulation from afar for the temple of the God of gods, for the teacher who follows the Pāñcarātra system, for a horse, a banyan tree, gold, a community of virtuous people, and the house of one's guru; however, when near an image of Hari, one should perform it close by.
"I shall always honor one who is devoted to the vow of Viṣṇu, who worships the abode of Viṣṇu, and who eats only what remains from the food of Viṣṇu, just like Viṣṇu himself.
Having thus commanded all these and other such rules, the best of teachers—
Having announced the disciple's name—
having thus announced the disciple's name to the venerable Guru and others—
the disciple, having prostrated before that Guru, should proceed in this manner.
And one should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given to one's own teacher according to one's ability.
[Additional readings: one should offer everything—cows, land, grain, and so forth—according to one's ability.]

The excellence of the initiated one is as follows: "A Brahmin who thus attains this Vaiṣṇava initiation with firm conviction, knowing it in this way, is the best among those belonging to all stages of life (āśramas). (56)
One who performs sacrifices for the sake of others for their own benefit is proclaimed as an *ācārya*;
he is not merely a *sūri*, nor a *suhṛt*, nor a *sātvata* learned in the *Pāñcarātra*.
An *ekāntika* who follows his doctrine, a *deśika*, one who has received initiation (*dīkṣita*), and a worshipper (*arcaka*) [are distinct from such a person].
The Guru, the Bhāgavata, the Pūjaka, and the Sādhaka are all Hari;
they are to be addressed by such titles as Bhaṭṭāraka and so forth. O Kamalāsana, this concludes the initiation.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* oblation, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the deity.

Having led the Lord of Gods around the village in a clockwise direction preceded by Vedic chanting and musical instruments, and having placed him upon a vehicle, one should cause him to enter the temple.
Thus, the ritual procedure for the initiation of the deity has been correctly explained by me; now,
in this context, I shall describe the procedure for the five purificatory rites known as the *pañcasaṃskāra*.

O twice-born one, those who desire to perform worship—whether they seek liberation or merely wish to offer praise—should undergo initiation which generates my pleasure and makes one fit for worship; [I shall now describe] the five purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*). 62.

For them, there is no other way [to liberation] than this initiation (*dīkṣā*), which consists of five elements: the *puṇḍra*, the name, the mantra, the sacrifice (*yāga*), and the fifth, the *saṃskāra*. This initiation of the five purifications brings delight to the God of gods.
One who possesses the initiation of the five purificatory rites (pañcasaṃskāra) is remembered as a great devotee of the Lord (mahābhāgavata).
Having performed the rites beginning with the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), the placement of the jar (kumbhāvāhana), and the fire-ritual (agnikārya),
and having brought the great jar (mahākumbha) together, preceded by the offering of sprouts—
One should establish the fire and perform the two libations (āghāra) as before.
Having offered one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, one should indeed offer sixteen oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru).
Then, having offered the *nṛsūkta*, one should offer the expiatory oblations (*prāyaścittāhuti*).
After that, following the consecration of the disciples and so forth, and having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should grant permission even to the twice-born. 67
Then, having approached the water-pot, he should consecrate the disciple with it;
thereafter, having adorned that disciple with white garments and other ornaments,
the disciple, with palms joined in reverence, should prostrate like a staff upon the ground.
The disciple prays to the Guru with the firm resolve that is about to be described:
"O Guru, [grant me] the prayer to the Guru, the worship of Viṣṇu, and the excellent initiation through the path of the five purificatory rites. (69)
Having granted permission, [the preceptor] says, "Protect me, protect me, and likewise for the pleasure of Viṣṇu.
Then, the sequence of the purificatory rites (*tāpa-saṃskāra*) is requested for this disciple near the sacrificial fire-pit (*homakuṇḍa*).
On the southern side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), he should sit facing north (71).

O best of those who know mantras, he should properly worship the discus (cakra) and the conch (śaṅkha), worshipping them with offerings up to the food-oblation (naivedya); at the conclusion of the fire-sacrifice (homa), the Guru should heat them (72).

[According to the additional readings: Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) of the weapons, such as the Sudarśana and others, according to the ritual procedure, he should then place it upon the upper arm of the disciple at the right shoulder.
One should place the discus and the conch on their respective [bases] with their own mantras.
(73) Afterwards, the Guru himself should wash those two with cow’s milk. Thereafter, O Brahmin, having washed them, he should install them in the place of worship.
[This concludes] the rite of the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*).
Then, one should perform the application of the *puṇḍras* according to the previously mentioned rite (74).
Having bestowed upon the disciple a name ending in *-dāsa* according to the path prescribed in the scriptures, this constitutes the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
The consecration of mantras serves all purposes; they reside within the womb of the Vedas, and the Veda itself is established in the eight-syllabled mantra.
(Praise of the Eight-Syllabled Mantra)

Therefore, the eight-syllabled mantra is remembered as the root of all mantras; the Guru should likewise instruct the eight-syllabled mantra preceded by its ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the prescribed method, as well as the two final [mantras].
By the mere instruction of this eight-syllable mantra, the instruction of all other mantras is accomplished;
therefore, the instruction of all mantras is [contained] individually within it. 77–78.
For the sun does not depend anywhere upon a lamp;
likewise, the consecration of the sacrificial rite, the installation of the Śrī-mūrti, and the gift of the knowledge of sacrifice to the disciple [do not depend on external aids]. 79
O Brahmin, while the teacher performs the additional recitations with a stainless mind,
he should then summon the disciple and cause him to receive the blessing.

But the disciple, regarding his own guru as the Lord alone, should worship him according to the prescribed rite; [in some cases] he should offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). These five purificatory rites have thus been described in brief.
By which a mortal, shaken free from sin, attains liberation (this is certain) and reaches the supreme goal. 80.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for Initiation into the Lotus Mandala," in the *Śrīpuruṣottamasaṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpañcarātra*. Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ.
In the glorious Pāñcarātra Divyāgama, within the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā,
this is the twenty-third chapter.
The ritual for raising the banner and invoking the deity,
according to Brahmā, in the performance of the great festival.
O Lord, O lotus-eyed one, you who are affectionate toward those who have sought refuge, this question regarding Brahman is a great festival for me:
how does one become a *mahotsava*, what is its nature, and what is its fruit?
O Lord of virtuous vows, speak at length to me, whose mind is filled with inquiry; thus [requested],
the Blessed One gave this reply.
O Brahmin, this most excellent great festival, performed by those desiring the highest good,
is a propitiation that generates my pleasure; it is auspicious and has been celebrated as a great festival.

O dear one, listen to that great festival performed by Indra in the past for the purpose of releasing himself from the sin incurred upon the slaying of Vṛtra, and for the pacification of that sin—O child, listen to that great festival. This great festival was performed even by the Lord of the Gods for my pleasure;
it is half the meaning of the word "festival" (utsava).
I shall describe the procedure for that festival in detail.
By means of this ocean-like festival, the wise cross over all worldly suffering and attain liberation. 4-5.

The varieties of festivals: (It is traditionally taught that a festival is threefold—daily, occasional, and optional. The great festival is of three types: daily, occasional, and optional; it serves exclusively to remove sins and to extend the lifespan of the performer.
It brings about all prosperity for the subjects of the kingdom,
is the supreme pacifier of terrible calamities such as famine and ill omens,
and is auspiciously bestowing the goals of human endeavor, including virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation.

The Determination of Long Constellations: (The northern solstice is auspicious; one should indeed commence the sacrifice to Hari. For the commencement of divine sacrifices, the northern solstice is most excellent.
On the new moon day, the full moon day, the twelfth lunar day, or under the Śravaṇa constellation.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, Rohiṇī, and Punarvasu—
[according to other readings: on other auspicious lunar days, during eclipses, and at other festival occasions].

Having determined the day of the pilgrimage by consulting the birth asterism of the patron (*yajamāna*), as well as the asterism of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and the asterism of the banner, one should commence the sacrificial rite;
this is the determination of the festival day.
O Four-faced One, the determination regarding the duration of the great festival for the raising of the banner is twelve days, or nine, or seven, or five, or three, or even a single day.
One should not have the work on the banner performed for one day, three days, or even four days.
Regarding the characteristics of the sacrificial pavilion:
the sacrificial pavilion is to be constructed as before to the northeast of the temple.
One should have a pavilion constructed measuring ten cubits in length, or nine cubits, or even five cubits, with its width and length proportionate, and provided with four doors. 12–13.

One should cause a large water-shed (prapā) to be constructed on all four sides of the pavilion; in its center, one should fashion a beautiful great altar (mahāvedī) one cubit in height. While it is being built, one should arrange sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) on the four sides.
The bow-shaped [altar] is likewise circular, and the three-pointed one is as described from the beginning in sequence;
or else, one may fashion it as either a single [triangle] or a square according to the desire of the builder— this is the decoration of the hall.

Then, one should construct the horse-stalls, the archways, and so forth, as previously described. One should have sacrificial ladles and spoons fashioned, and arrange the eight auspicious symbols in their proper order.
One should decorate the pavilion and the water-shed with variegated cloths made of fine cotton.
One should wrap the pillars with silken cloths and hang garlands of pearls from them;
having placed lamps upon the pillars, one should adorn them with banners.
One should fasten white canopies and beautify them with flower garlands.
Having thus decorated the hall, one should then choose the preceptor (ācārya) and others. Regarding the selection of officiating priests (ṛtvij-varaṇa):
there should be sixteen priests, O Brahmin, or eight, or even four.
And those [images] should be adorned according to one's means with golden necklaces, garments, and the like (20);
and with applications of fragrant substances, turbans, and vertical *puṇḍra* marks,
they should be decorated with devotion by the patron according to his wealth (21).
The commencement of the festival:
one should perform the ritual bathing of the deity at both the beginning and the end of the festival.
Prior to the commencement of the festival, the hoisting of the banner (dhvajārohaṇa) is prescribed. 22.
On the day before the hoisting of the banner, one should perform the rite of depositing the sprout (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
One should have Garuḍa painted on a cloth made of silk, jute, or cotton;
[this] is the characteristic of the banner-cloth (*dhvajapaṭa-lakṣaṇa*). (23)
Ten cubits in length and five cubits in width,
in its center one should depict Garuḍa, possessing a golden luster and nine tālas in height;
he has a blue tip on his nose and his right foot is slightly bent.
The omnipresent Lord, clad in white garments, was joined with the flapping of wings; he had the appearance of moving through the sky, with curls of hair arranged upon his forehead,
adorned with necklaces and armlets, and radiant with anklets as ornaments.
The Guru, having had the Lord Garuḍa— who is adorned with ornaments of the lord of serpents— carefully drawn by another artisan and painted with five colors;
27 [additional readings].
One should paint auspicious objects such as the parasol, the chowrie, and the water-pot in their proper sequence on the sides of the cloth painting, according to the prescribed method;
[this is] the abode of Garuḍa.

Taking that cloth, the preceptor should cause it to enter the sacrificial ground by circumambulating the temple and other structures from left to right; he should then install the cloth and perform the consecration.
Or, he may perform the rites such as the opening of the eyes during the formal installation ceremony.
Having performed the ceremonial bath in a mirror, the preceptor should cause [the image] to rest upon the bed (29).
Having placed the great pitcher upon a mandala of grain and rice to the northwest of that cloth-painting, he should set down the *karaka* vessel to the north (30).

Having established eight water-pots in the eight directions, endowed with the characteristics prescribed by the scriptures, one should invoke Garuḍa, who is the embodiment of the Vedas, into the central pot. Then, having invoked the discus and [the deities] beginning with Ananta in the respective order, one should properly worship them in the pots according to the path already described, as well as Indra and the others in the eight directions.
Then, having fully worshipped Garuḍa depicted on the cloth up to the offering of food (naivedya),

one should perform the preliminary consecration (ādhivāsa) and the fire-oblation (homa); after performing the purification, drying, and other rites, one should then kindle the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having performed the circumambulation with fire using the root of *darbha* grass, the best of preceptors should perform the installation of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*),
the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the principles (*tattva*) along with their emanation and reabsorption, and the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Having taken up the Śakti residing in the pitcher with the *kūrca* [grass-bundle], one should place it upon the cloth (34).
Then, having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* preceded by the *gāruḍanyāsa*, one should, with palms joined in reverence, pray to the Son of Vinatā (35).
Prayer to Garuḍa:
Come, O divine portion of Viṣṇu, O Vainateya of great strength! O Lord of Birds, manifest your presence; be gracious here. Homage to you! 36.
"O son of Vinatā, being summoned by this rite, bring about success;
the three worlds must be summoned for the prosperity of the festival of the Lord. One should worship the Lord with the offerings prescribed in the Gāyatrī. (37)
At dawn, having placed that cloth [icon] upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, one should perform a circumambulation of the village at daybreak,
accompanied by the sounds of dancers, singers, and musical instruments, as well as the resonance of Vedic recitations.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village along the path for raising the banner, one should cause [the deity] to enter the temple;
then, having gone to the ground near the flagstaff, with the banner-cloth... 39.
The Guru himself should appropriately decorate the additional recitations, the place of the banner,
and the pillar with garlands of *darbha* grass, flowers, and sprouts.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) accompanied by the sounds of musical instruments,
and having sprinkled the image with water while reciting meritorious mantras containing the word "Bhaga," one should recite the Viṣṇu-sūkta and encircle it with a cord of darbha grass.
One should deposit gems, metals, minerals, and seeds into the pit at the base of the pillar (41).
Having tied a cloth to the top of the pillar with the *suvarṇosī* mantra,
one should firmly secure the base of the pillar in the pit for the purpose of installing the gems (42).
The supreme preceptor should install [the image] with the consecration mantra (pratiṣṭhāpanamantra),
having placed the son of Vinatā depicted on the cloth facing the deity;
then, he should invoke the four deities in the four directions according to the prescribed ritual.
There, one should pray to Garuḍa with this profound and moving prayer: "O Lord of Birds,
by the abundance of the wind from the waves of the flapping of your wings..."
"O destroyer of enemies, having cast off your armor in battle,
wait until we have reached the vicinity of the festive ritual bath (avabhṛtha).
Having thus informed the lord of birds, from that time forward, day after day," 45–46.

It should be worshipped during both times until the conclusion of the holy day; having performed this, one should carry out the invocation of the deity in the evening. (47) [This concludes] the purification of the drum and the place of worship.
Having sat down on an auspicious seat on the right side of the deity, one should wash the foot with water using the *pavitra-mantra*, and wash the ground with water;
then, one should sweep [the area] in due order with *darbha* grass while reciting the *viṣṇorarāṭa-mantra*. 48.
One should smear [the ground] with cow dung using the mantra "gaṃdhadvāram" (49).
One should fashion decorative colored lines (raṅgavallī) adorned with the five powders using the mantra "āpa undantu.
Then, one should scatter unbroken rice grains (akṣata) on the ground with the mantra "devasya tvā" (50).

One should prepare a seat of grain with the mantra "dhānyamasī," and adorn it with lotus leaves using the mantra "śanno devī. Having recited the "trātāram" mantra, one should draw a lotus in the center.
With the mantra "dhanvanā gāḥ," the preceptor should spread darbha grass [on the ground] and cover it with darbha grass facing upwards.
With the mantra "mūrddhānam," the Guru should consecrate the ground and place four lamps filled with ghee in the four corners.
The worship of Viṣvaksena, the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāha), and so forth:

having first worshipped Viṣvaksena, one should then cause the declaration of the auspicious day to be recited; thereafter, one should sprinkle the drum with those waters while reciting the mantra beginning with "māpavuṃdantu. 54.
One should sprinkle all the musical instruments with the mantra "Agni rāyuṣman.
With the mantra "Aryamāya," one should place the drum upon another pedestal;
having established the drum there, one should invoke the deities in their proper order into its center.
Then [he worshipped] Agni, the deity who carries oblations; Bhūteśa, the great element; Viṣṇubhakta, the wielder of the mace (Gadādhara);
Prajāpati; Sūrya and Candra; Śeṣa; and then the Mothers of the Earth (Bhūmātṛkāḥ). 56.
One should worship Vācaspati, the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis), and Nandīśa; likewise,
one should provide musical instruments such as the mardala,
the kāhala, the conch, the mṛdaṅga, and the vallakī.

Having placed a *saṭaha*, a *jhallarī*, a bell-metal cymbal (*kāṃśya*), and a *tāla* in order around Indra and the other deities (verse 58), one should station dancers and singers outside of that; then, having worshipped Garuḍa depicted on a cloth and having surrounded the drum with musical instruments (verse 59).
One should perform the beating of the drum with the mantra "kad viṣṇoḥ" (RV 7.99.1),
and having recited the Śrīsūkta, one should cause all musical instruments to resound. (60) [This is] the invocation of the deities.
Then, one should properly perform the invocation of the groups beginning with Kumuda, as well as the sages, Brahmā, and all the Rudras;
for the sake of satisfying each respective deity and others, one should sound their corresponding musical rhythms (tālas).

Then, having placed the image— accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi— upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, and having adorned it with special ornaments, one proceeds with the festive procession for the offering of oblations (balipradānavithi). 62.
Bound by the neck with the sacrificial offering (bali), one should cause it to be whirled according to the sequence of steps (63).
Together with all the attendants, accompanied by instrumental music, dance, and song,
[one should worship] with water for respectful offering (arghya), perfumes, garlands, betel, incense, and lamps (64).
Starting from the gate of the celestial mansion (vimāna) and extending as far as the village street,
one should offer an oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa), preceded by the invocation of the deities.
The oblation should be performed in the eastern part of the village.

Standing facing the east in the eastern direction of the village, the Guru, the preceptor, should perform the invocation of the deities with this mantra: "O hosts of immortals, come hither; you who preside over the eastern quarter. (66)

May those who are deformed and those who are beautiful, having accepted this offering prepared for us, drink [the water] and be satisfied; may the followers of Kumuda approach me with joy—salutations to them! 67–68.
With this mantra, one should worship the Kumudas along with their attendants in due order,

offering everything from perfumes to lamps (and casting an oblation of milk-rice). One should cast the oblation of milk-rice (pāyasa), and then offer betel leaf accompanied by various musical rhythms and songs.
Thereafter, having reached the southeastern direction, the Guru should satisfy [the deities];
this is the bali offering for the southeastern region:
"O hosts of immortals who dwell in the southern quarter, come hither!"

May those followers of Kumudākṣa, who are terrifying, fierce-faced, and formidable, accept this prepared worship; may they, never satiated, drink of us and come to me with joy—homage, homage to them! 71–72.
Having thus gratified Kumudākṣa as before, [he should say]:
"O hosts of ancestors, come from the southern region and occupy your seats in the direction of Yama. (73)
May those followers of Puṇḍarīka, who are of most cruel conduct, accept this prepared offering and, being satisfied, come toward me; salutations to them! 74.
May they approach me with affection; salutations to them!
Having invoked the lotus-eyed one (Viṣṇu) as before,
[one should know that] the Yātudhānas come from the northwestern direction and lie down upon the lords of the corners.
May the flesh-eaters of cruel intellect, having taken this sacrificial offering raised by us, be satisfied and protect us; may they come to me with pleasure—salutations to them! 76-77.
Having thus worshipped Nirṛti, one who has taken recourse to the western direction should come from the western part of the region, for those who first lie down in the west [are the ancestors]. 78.

May the great serpents with venomous fangs, having received this prepared worship and being satisfied, protect us; may they come to me with pleasure—salutations to them. 79. May they come to me with joy; salutations to you.
Having thus worshipped Varuṇa, one who has taken refuge in tranquility [should proceed];
the hosts of Gandharvas arrive in the northwestern quarter and reside in that direction of Vāyu.

May those whose speed is formidable at the mere sight of them, who are never satiated even after receiving this prepared worship, and who move with eyes like serpents—may they come to me with pleasure; salutations to you all! 81-82.
Having thus worshipped Vāyu, he took recourse to the direction of Kubera;
then the host of Yakṣas arrived from the northern quarter and lay down in the north. 83.
May those of deformed appearance, staff in hand, having accepted this prepared offering, being satisfied, drink from us as the followers of Sumukha. 84.
[Additional Readings]
Having thus worshipped Kubera, he proceeded toward the direction of Maheśvara, [saying]:
"May the hosts of Piśācas come; may they abide in the fierce quarter.
With tridents and weapons in their hands, let them accept this prepared worship. 85.
Having taken water for sipping and being satisfied, may those who follow the well-established path approach me with joy;
salutations to them! May they approach me with joy; salutations to them! 86–87.
Having thus performed the worship, the preceptor went into the center of the village and said:
"O hosts of Siddhas who dwell in the sky, come hither! O pure ones whose hearts are rooted in truth, attend to this rising rite of hospitality."
"Having taken water, may those who are satisfied and follow Pṛśnigarbha come here;
they are great, and salutations be to them. Having thus worshipped the sky, one should then worship the earth. 89-90.

O hosts of lower worlds who dwell upon the earth, you who possess many forms and vast knowledge, come hither; having accepted this offered worship, drink [of it] with satisfaction, you followers of Mānava. 91.
"May the great ones come to me; salutations to them who are pleased.
Having thus invoked and gratified [the deity] for the satisfaction of each respective god, the preceptor should then please [them] with dances and rhythmic claps. 92-93.

First, having struck the drum, one should perform the invocation of the deities (*devatāvāhana*). Having thus wandered through the village and entered the temple, the Guru should reach the place of the banner and worship Garuḍa; then, having fully worshipped Garuḍa.
One should satisfy Him from all sides with cymbals and other musical instruments, as well as with dance and song (95).
Having thus performed the invocation of the deity, one should worship the great pitcher (*mahākumbha*).
Thus [ends] the *Śrīpuruṣottamasaṃhitā* within the *Mahopaniṣad* of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The twenty-third chapter, titled "The Ritual for Hoisting the Banner and Invoking the Deities.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
The twenty-fourth chapter, on the procedure for the Brahmotsava festival, in the Śrī Puruṣottama-saṃhitā within the glorious and divine scripture of the Pāñcarātra.
The Blessed Lord said: O Lotus-born One, listen; I shall now describe the procedure for the worship of the pitcher (kumbha).
In the central part of the pavilion, which is provided with sixteen pillars and adorned with ornaments, one should perform the invocation of the pitcher (kumbhāvāhana).
For that purpose, one should draw a mandala consisting of a lotus within a wheel using five colors.
Regarding the sequence for constructing the mandala of the wheel and lotus:
one should divide the extent of the square field, measuring two hundred and fifty-six units, into that many squares. 3.
In the center of the thirty-six squares, one should draw five circles:
the first is the field for the pericarp (karṇikā), the second is the location for the petals, the third is the location for the hub (nābhi), and the fourth is the field for the spokes (ara).

The fifth is the *nemi* (rim) ground with twenty-eight corners. Having fashioned the outer pedestal (*pīṭha*) below, one should then perform the creeper-design (*latāvidhi*) with two rows on the outside. One should fashion four gates; [thus] one should provide four gates. 5–6.
Furthermore, for the purification of the conch shells, one should then sweep out two squares in each corner by means of the prescribed method; then,
for the sake of aesthetic beauty and for the purpose of establishing the boundaries, one should sweep out three squares in each [corner].
Furthermore, for the sake of adornment, four items should be swept separately. Regarding the method of coloring, one should beautify the maṇḍala there with five colors, beginning with white.

Then one should decorate the maṇḍala with powders produced from jewels, or from the earth, or even with fragrant powders; or else, with white and variegated flour of śāli rice. One should then color the pericarp yellow and adorn it with white dots.

One should draw the pericarp with pale-red (*pāṭala*) or black; the ground of the filaments with dark-blue (*śyāma*); and the three lines of the navel with yellow, red, and [dark] colors respectively.
The petals should be white in color, and the enclosures red.
One should adorn the ground around the rim with black [materials] and the pedestal with yellow ones. Then, one should beautify the walkway with variegated creepers and canopies;
likewise, one should arrange the beauty of the upper part with red and yellow [materials]. 12–13.
Having painted the four gates of the maṇḍala as white, red, yellow, and black, one should indeed begin the worship of the maṇḍala; one should commence the ritual adoration. 14.
Maṇḍalārcana.

One should worship the path of mantras in the pericarp, the path of phonemes on the petals, the path of principles (tattvas) on the filaments, and the path of kalās on the stamens; one should worship the path of words in the region of the navel and the path of worlds (bhuvanas). 15.
Having invoked the syllables upon the rim and the pericarp (16),
and having invoked the Supreme Self and performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should worship; then, one should worship the Śakti on the twenty-second petal and in the filaments (kesaras) (17).
Then Hari should worship Śrī and the others at the tips of the petals;
Brahmā is in the second circle, while the three-eyed one (Śiva) is in the third.
Viṣṇu and the others are to be worshipped on all twelve spokes.
On the Matsya and other [seals], worship is performed on the rim;

on the pedestal (pīṭha), in the four directions, Varāha, Narasiṃha, Ananta, and Hayagrīva are worshipped, and in the intermediate directions starting from the southeast (indrāgni), Indra and the others are worshipped in sequence. 19–20.
The gatekeepers are to be worshipped, and then one should worship Chaṇḍa and the others;
one should worship Viṣvaksena in the north-east and Garuḍa in front. To the south, one should worship Hetirāja, and the mace (Gadā) at the western gate.
In this manner, one should worship in the immediately following petals according to the sequence:
from Vāsudeva to Kṛṣṇa, performing the worship of the twelve Ādityas.
One should perform the placement of the eight syllables upon the eight dots. 22–23.

Having invoked the twenty-four deities corresponding to the twenty-four forms within the twenty-four lotuses, one should perform the installation of the jar (kumbha-sthāpana); one should then place the great jar (mahākumbha). 24.
Installation of the Jar.

Having placed the sacrificial pitcher along with the water-jar in the center of the maṇḍala of the wheel and lotus, one should perform the mental sacrifice; [one should worship the Lord within the pitcher] and worship the Radiance (Prabhā) in the outer pitcher. One should then perform the oblation of great sacrificial offerings upon the altar according to the prescribed rule.
With fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge, the preceptor [should perform the rite] with the root mantra—
either one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times— or surrounded by one hundred and eight recitations of the Gāyatrī.
The Procedure for the Vaikuṇṭha-Pārṣada Homa:
An expert in the Tantras should perform the Vaikuṇṭha-Pārṣada Homa, beginning with the Lord Ādinārāyaṇa, accompanied by Śrī, Puṣṭi, and Nīlā. 28.
The three eternal sages, the five-armed Puruṣas, as well as the Śrīvatsa, the Kaustubha gem, the forest garland, the crown,
the pair of jeweled earrings, and the divine Vaikuṇṭha chariot.
Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Bhuvaṅga, Pataṅgaka, Maṇika, Tāpasa, Siddha, and Sādhya; and thereafter Matsya, Haṃsarūpa, Hayagrīva, and Kūrmaka. 30–31.
Varāha, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana, Bhṛgu, Rāma, Śrī Rāma, Jānakī, as well as Lakṣmaṇa and Bharata;
Śatrughna, Hanumān, Balarāma, and Revatī.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Rukmiṇī, as well as Satyabhāmā; Buddha in the form of Kalki, Dvāralakṣmī, and likewise the Banner; Brahmā the creator of the universe, Vāṇī, and Sanaka and the others. 33–34.
Furthermore, Nārada and Bhṛgu, Mārkaṇḍeya thereafter, Vedavyāsa and Śuka, as well as Agastya and Kāśyapa;
Aditi and Atri, together with Anasūyā. 35.
[He should worship] Bhāradvāja, Kauśika, Gautama, and Vasiṣṭha;
then Arundhatī, Jāmadagnya, and Reṇukā; and thereafter the eight guardians of the quarters beginning with Indra, using two Gāyatrīs for each.
Pārvatī and Gaṅgā, followed by the two Gāyatrīs, then Uṣā, Padminī, and Chāyā, preceded by Āditya; [these],
along with the nine planets and the oceans, [are worshipped] with one hundred and eight repetitions of the Gāyatrī.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa) according to this procedure, the best of teachers [should worship]:
Vāsudeva in the eastern square, Saṅkarṣaṇa likewise in the south, Pradyumna in the west, and Aniruddha in the north. 39–40.
With milk-rice, *kṛsara*, sweet rice with molasses, turmeric-rice, and *maudgala* dishes,
one should offer oblations separately into the fires while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*.
In a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), [one should worship] the deities beginning with Brahmā and Rudra, as well as the eight guardians of the directions.
Having uttered the mantra ending in "svāhā," consisting of each respective name in the dative case followed by the word for the retinue,
one should offer oblations in due order to Brahmā, Prajāpati, the Rudras, and all the gods. 42–43.
The Vedas, the Ṛṣis, the Gandharvas, and the Līlās;
the Yakṣas and the Apsarases, along with the months and the years;
the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, and likewise the streams.
Beings, domestic animals, wild beasts, as well as plants, are so designated;
likewise, trees, those born from sprouts, those born from sweat, those born from eggs, and those born from wombs, as well as the seven worlds beginning with Bhūḥ. 45–46.

One should offer oblation materials to these—the seven worlds beginning with Atala and their respective deities beginning with Caṇḍa—using the root mantra (mūlavidyā). This is the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti). 47.
Having sprinkled [the offerings] with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," one should perform the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
One should do this every day, especially in the evening and morning. This is the procedure for offering the bali during a festival.
Then, one should perform the offering of the *bali* in the pavilion of the sacrifice;
the *bali* image may be a discus (*cakra*), a palanquin (*śibikā*), or other such objects. Having departed from the temple, [one should place] the *kumuda* and other offerings at its door.

Having performed worship, one should again offer the *bali* on a clean patch of ground. On the first day and subsequent days, one should perform the *bali* according to the rules for the daily festival, with the specific distinctions of materials for the deity's offering.
On the first day, one should scatter an offering consisting of sesame-seed powder, turmeric powder, and parched grain mixed with *caru*;
on the second day, having combined [sesame and rice] with *caru*— that is, sesame and rice along with *caru*— one should offer it.
On the third and fourth [days], one should offer mixed parched grains (*lāja*), various grains, and cakes along with coconut water; likewise,
having combined groats (*saktu*) and rice flour with the cooked sacrificial oblation (*caru*).
On the fifth day, one should offer lotus seeds and milk-rice made with śāli rice; on the sixth, having combined cakes with sacrificial porridge (caru), one should cast the offering (bali);
on the seventh day, in all cases, [the offering is made] together with the four kinds of food.
Having joined the cakes at night with unprecedent ornaments, garlands, and garments, the offering of the bali is prescribed as equal [to the previous] in eight and nine locations as before. (56)
One should perform the festival every day until the conclusion of the holy day (tīrthadina).
O Lotus-seated One, listen now to the procedure for the village festival.
At the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform a special festival (viśeṣotsava). For that purpose, having placed the festival image upon the auspicious throne,
one should proceed with dances, songs, musical instruments, umbrellas, chowries, and banners.

Together with Brahmins reciting all the benedictory hymns (*svastisūkta*) and so forth, and having performed the rite of bathing and the circumambulation of the temple (*dhāma*), one should lead [the deity] to the bathing pavilion (*snānamaṇṭapa*). 60.
Then, in front of the deity, the preceptor should have a mandala prepared for the ritual bathing using sesame seeds, rice, and other grains; thereafter,
he should arrange nine or five jars endowed with the proper characteristics in due order.
Having arranged them, one should fill all the jars with filtered water (62).
Having cast the respective substances into them, one should worship the respective deities;
having performed the ritual bath according to the rules with turmeric and the Śrīsūkta (63).
One should perform the ritual bath with the *Nṛsūkta* using a thousand-spoked [wheel],
and having wiped [the deity] with a cloth and a garment, one should adorn the Blessed One with clothes, ornaments, and garlands, and offer incense and lamps.

Having offered all the various kinds of food, such as hard and soft delicacies, according to the prescribed manner, and having then given a roll of betel leaves (*tāmbūlavīṭikā*), one should perform the waving of lights (*nīrājana*).
Then, having distributed the offered food and other edibles among the devotees... 65–66.
Regarding the sequence for the procession during the festival:

having then established the deity upon the previously mentioned auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha), one should have the vehicle proceed along the ground nearby accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments. 67.

Having established the *vibhava* [mantras] and performed the ritual placement of mantras (*maṃtranyāsa*) according to the rules, one should worship the deity with offerings such as the *arghya* and other services.
The attendants of the deity are mounted upon their vehicles, carrying parasols, chowries, and weapons.
The attendants, intent on devotion, should remain by the side of the deity. Then, one should properly perform the village festival for the Blessed One with dance,
instrumental music, song, the chanting of the Vedas, and the great multitude of people.

With umbrellas, banners, flags, canopies, and auspicious yak-tail fans; with the sounds of lutes and flutes, and the resonant blasts of conchs and kettledrums; and by the forms of Siddhas and Gandharvas moving through the sky.

One should celebrate the festival of the Lord with various diversions that produce joy for the spectators, along with diverse riches, and with other such [means]. At that time, the devotees of the Blessed One should offer flowers, fruits, and so forth.
Taking all of that, the worshipper himself should sprinkle it;
having offered flowers and other items to the God of gods, the Guru should scatter them. (74) This is the sequence for the vehicles.
On the first day, the swan-vehicled one (Brahmā) is desired;
on the second day, the lion; on the third day, the lord of birds (Garuḍa);
on the fourth day, Śeṣa; and on the fifth day, the son of Añjanī (Hanumān).
In the sixth [house], both the Sun and the Moon shall mount the chariot; in the seventh, there shall be a horse;
in the eighth, a horse; and in the ninth, an elephant.
[Additional readings]
With palanquins adorned with jasmine flowers and other vehicles [arriving] at will, the nine-day festival of the God is thus proclaimed in due order.
(At the conclusion of the festival, the Lord of Gods should again be bathed. After the festival, one should perform the bathing of the God once more.
(One should worship according to the prescribed ritual up to the offering of food. Having worshipped the Blessed One, one should present cakes and other offerings.
(78) Then, with Śrī and Bhūmi, one should lead the Lord inside with a garland.
This is the sequence for the special festival; it is not a festival lasting for many days.
On the first day, there is an auspicious excursion to the forest; on the second, [the festival of the swing];
on the third day, the festival of the boat; on the fourth, the festival of the palanquin;
on the fifth, the filling [of the vessel] is prescribed; and on the sixth, the wooden trough for water.
When the seventh day arrives, one should perform the mounting of the chariot;
on the eighth day, the hunting expedition, and on the ninth, the great festival is prescribed. Thus, O Brahmin, has the procedure for the nine-day festival been described.
Brahmā said: O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, you are the path to auspicious festivals and the bestower of the desired fruits of devotion. 82
O best among speakers, please explain all of that in detail: the inquiry regarding Brahman during the hearing [of the Vedas], and the marriage of Śrī and the others, if you have grasped it. 83.
The Blessed One replied with these words concerning the ritual for the auspicious festival: the Glorious Blessed One spoke.
Now, the supreme marriage ceremony of the goddesses, beginning with Adhaśrī, is described;
listen to it all with an attentive mind. (84) By the mere hearing of which, one shall attain the fulfillment of birth.
The determination of the day for auspicious festivals:
on the day of anyone’s descent [into an incarnation], one should perform their auspicious rites (kalyāṇa). Among all incarnations, this applies to the birth-star of each successive one.
And on the eleventh day, one should perform the Kalyāṇa [rite] with a spirit of devotion (86).
For the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world, one should cause this festival to be celebrated every year; such is the sequence for the Kalyāṇa festival.
First, having worshipped Viṣvaksena on an auspicious day,
one should sprinkle all the ritual materials with water and put on protective threads (rakṣāsūtra) for the primary images, such as Dhruva and others, as well as for Śrī and the rest. 87–88.
At the time of binding the protective threads (rakṣāsūtra) according to the rules for all the teachers and officiating priests,
let the festival proceed for the destruction of the defect of creation. 89
For the purpose of avoiding impurity (āśauca) and for the sake of attaining spiritual fitness, they should each individually wear threads made of gold. 90.
[The section on] the fire-oblation (homa) and so forth.

One should establish the fire according to the prescribed rule; then, having performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*), one should offer the two *āghāra* libations. Then, for the sake of the success of the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice, one should offer oblations in sequence with the five hymns (*sūktas*).
Likewise, one should offer sixteen oblations with the Mūrti-mantra (92).
Having offered twenty-eight fuel-sticks and clarified butter with the twelve-syllable mantra, one should complete the remainder of the fire sacrifice (93).
The entry into the auspicious pavilion:
that very night, having caused the Lord to enter the excellent wedding chamber preceded by the sounds of musical instruments and the festivities of the city, (verse 94).
Regarding the ritual for taking the hand in marriage:

having worshipped Viṣvaksena, one should then cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made; thereafter, one should respectfully inform the presiding deity of the marriage rite. 95

The determination of the cause for the marriage festival must never be neglected; it is certain that it should be held every year, and if it is devoid of the regular festival, an expiation is prescribed. 96.
