Filled with devotion and faith, one should perform the annual festival of the investiture of the *akṣata* grains and the marriage rite for the Lord; one should perform all the rites prescribed in the ritual for taking the hand in marriage.
97. One should perform every action as ordained by the rules for the ceremony of taking the hand.
Having seated Hari, the Lord of Gods, facing east near the square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) along with the two Goddesses, being well-composed, [he performs] the principal oblations and so forth. 98.
Having performed the preparatory rites beginning with the placing of the sacrificial fuel (idhmādhāna) up to the end of the Āghāra offerings according to the rule,
one should perform the primary oblation known as the Praveśa, which is supreme;
then one should perform the Lāja-homa and likewise the Tantric Homa.

Having performed the seven oblations for the removal of obstacles, one should perform the Śrīsūkta-homa for the attendants of Vaikuṇṭha, as well as for the presiding deities of the lunar days (tithis), the weekdays (vāras), and the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), and one should offer oblations to Jayā and the others in their proper sequence. 101.
Having performed the ritual up to the end of the worship with excellence according to the rules,

having placed the deity upon the vehicle preceded by dance and instrumental music, and having led [the procession] around the temple, one should enter the shrine after circumambulating the village. 103.
Thus, the marriage ceremony and its festive celebration have been correctly described;
following that, the procedure for the festival known as the "Forest Excursion" (vana-vihāra) will now be told. 104.
On the second day, one should place the deity in the vehicle for the purpose of bringing prosperity and wealth to the earth, at the conclusion of the daily worship,
with the mantra "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ" along with the goddess Savarṇaprabhā. 105.
Having adorned him with flower garlands and the auspicious sounds of musical instruments as before,
he should lead him to the garden grove and seat him upon an auspicious throne within a pavilion situated in its center, together with the two goddesses.
One should bathe [the deity] with twenty-five jars of filtered water;
[according to an additional reading:
or having performed the fire-sacrifice (homa) as prescribed, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila)].

Having offered ornaments, seats, forest roots, fruits, and so forth, as well as cool, refreshing water, green gram soup mixed with *guḍūcī*, and betel leaf, one should then perform the *nīrājana* ceremony. 108–109.

Having praised the Lord of Gods with hymns and prostrated with the eight-limbed salutation (sāṣṭāṅga), one should thereafter offer a handful of flowers at the feet of the God. In front of the God, [the rite should be performed] by those skilled in dance, song, and instrumental music.
You should repeatedly display various kinds of musical instruments and dance performances.
At the conclusion of the Vedic recitation, as before, together with auspicious rites,
one should place the deity upon a vehicle and lead him into the temple.
Having thus performed the forest festival (vanotsava), one should then perform the boat festival (plavotsava).
Regarding the procedure for the boat festival:
when the third day has arrived, [one should worship] the God together with the Goddess. 113
Having placed [the image] upon a palanquin and adorned it with ornaments and decorations, one should bring it to the shore of the lake by way of circumambulation. Then,
[one should place it] in a most beautiful pavilion situated in the middle of that lake.
Having placed [the deity] upon the lion-faced [pedestal], one should perform the excellent worship up to the offering of food (naivedya).
Then, taking a divine boat, made firm with wooden planks, adorned with various ornaments, and beautified with garlands of flowers— 115–116.
It was adorned on all sides with banners of various shapes, mirrors, and chowries,
as well as with heaps of coconuts, betel nuts, and plantains,
along with bells and small tinkling bells.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and having consecrated the raft with sprinkling water, the preceptor,
having invoked the Lord of Birds (*khageśa*) upon it and worshipped Him according to the ritual rules, should offer an oblation (*naivedya*) with devotion and pray to the Lord of Birds.
The man, having consecrated the water through rites such as burning and nourishing,
should invoke the Ocean of Milk therein and satisfy Indra and the other deities.
Having established the fire according to the prescribed rule either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a mound of sand (staṇḍila), [he should proceed].
Having completed the rites ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the preceptor should, with the remaining mantra,
offer one thousand and eight, or one hundred and eight,
oblations of *caru* using the *Puruṣasūkta*, consisting of sixteen offerings.
Taking the *saṃpāta* clarified butter, he should sprinkle it from the *tarpamathya* vessel; having sprinkled it, the Guru should then duly place the Lord of the Gods upon that float. 123.
[Additional Readings]
With the mantra "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ" and the mantra "dhruvā dyauḥ," the officiating priests,
the initiated ones, and the attendants should all stand around the deity on that very day, filled with devotion. 124.
In front of the deity, one should perform dancing, singing, and so forth upon a small boat;
then, having circumambulated the pavilion three times, one should place the Lord therein. Having worshipped the deity there with offerings such as rice cakes and other foods, [one should proceed].
After offering coconuts, cakes, and other such items, one should place the deity upon a vehicle and,
following the previously mentioned path, lead it clockwise around the village and cause it to enter the temple. 126–127.
Having thus performed the festival of the boat, one should perform the daily worship.
This is the procedure for the swing festival;
on the fourth day, one should perform the most excellent swing festival. 128.
In the pavilion constructed for the purpose of installing the swing, the preceptor,
having beautifully adorned it, should worship Viṣvaksena. Then, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, he should sprinkle the swing with consecrated water.
One should worship Ananta and the Vedas upon the ropes of the swing.

Having offered the bali-oblation to Indra and the other deities, and having seated the Lord in the vehicle, the Guru should place Him upon the swing amidst the sounding of conchs and kettledrums. 130–131.
[One should have dances, songs, and diversions performed in the presence of the deity. There, having worshipped the deity, [one should offer] various foods, fruits, and water.
Having offered the beverage, one should then present the betel-leaf (tāmbūla).
Then, together with Brahmins reciting the Puruṣasūkta and other hymns,
one should take hold of the ropes of the swing and move it slowly and steadily.
Then, having placed the Lord of the Gods of gods upon the palanquin and having circumambulated it three times, one should enter the temple. 134.
This is the procedure for the festival of completion.
When the fifth day arrives, one should perform the Pūraṇa festival;
for the purpose of filling [the eyes], one should make a cage [for the insects] out of gold, silver, copper, or even bamboo. 135.

One should construct the cage in exact proportion to the image. The height of the image is said to be four finger-breadths [above the base], and its circumference should be ten finger-breadths. 136–137.

Having sprinkled this cage, which is endowed with these characteristics, with water, and having placed it upon a heap of grain, the most excellent preceptor should seat that cage upon a pedestal made of grain and other materials.
Having worshipped the Yoga-pīṭha, he should cause the image to arise by means of the "uttiṣṭha" mantra.
The preceptor himself, taking [the image], should place it within the cage;
with the mantra "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ," he should perform the binding of the protective thread while the sounds of musical instruments and Vedic recitations proceed, remembering Lord Hari. 139–140.
The determination of the difference in fruits based on the difference in filling materials:
one should perform the filling with gems for the pacification of all defects;
by filling with gems and worshipping the image of Hari with devotion, [one attains the desired result]. 141.
Having attained the fruit of all sacrifices, he shall go to union with Viṣṇu;
he who worships Hari with devotion using a core of gold or other metals attains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. 142.

Whoever fills the excellent image of Hari with fruits out of devotion attains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and rejoices in the abode of Viṣṇu. Whoever, with devotion, fills the imperishable Lord with *ghṛtapūra* (ghee-filled sweets), [attains the same]. 143–144.
Having obtained the fruit of the Cāturmāsya vow, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
but he who, with devotion, fills Madhurā with Lord Janārdana, immediately obtains the fruit of a sacrifice and attains union (sāyujya) with Viṣṇu. 145.
The distinctions of mantras will now be explained through the addition of supplementary recitations and the differentiation of substances:
gold and other materials [are offered] along with gems and jewels, and silver from the source of gold.
Reciting the mantra beginning with *yāḥ phalanti* and ending with *phalaiḥ*, and then reciting the mantra *madhu vātā* while pouring honey, the Guru should perform the filling.
Thus has the supreme festival of filling (*pūraṇotsava*) been correctly described. 146.
I shall describe the festival of the water-vessel (*jaladroṇī*); listen attentively as I explain it.
One should have a water-vessel made—either of gold, silver, copper, or bronze—in accordance with the dimensions of the image, and having two openings. (147)
One should fill the water-vat with fragrant water scented by camphor, saffron, flowers, and collections of aromatic substances. Then,
having performed the rites of drying and so forth, one should worship Gaṅgā and the other [deities].
Then, having brought the deity forward while the recitation of the Vedas and the sound of musical instruments have commenced, the Guru, chanting the Svasti-sūkta,
should then immerse the deity along with the two goddesses.
Having placed the deity, whose garments are still wet from bathing, upon a palanquin or similar vehicle,
one should smear him from head to foot with fragrant saffron;
then, having paraded him through the village, he should be brought to the assembly hall.

At the conclusion of the festival, having performed the ritual bath for the deity with devotion, the best of preceptors should worship the Lord according to the prescribed rites using the thirty-two modes of service; then, having entered the temple, he should perform the daily worship of the All-pervading Lord.

In the manner thus described, one should perform the sixth festival (Ṣaṣṭhī-yātrā). Regarding the ritual for the chariot festival (Rathotsava-vidhi): one should conduct the chariot festival on the seventh day according to the prescribed sequence.

It was adorned with umbrellas, banners, flags, and the like; with garlands of flowers and canopies; with strings of pearls and golden ornaments; together with clusters of tinkling bells, gongs, and celestial beings; and with golden water-pots. 155–156.

Having sprinkled the chariot with water and with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) [as prescribed by the sages]. (157) It is joined with beautiful peacock-feather ornaments, endowed with various colorful designs, and provided with rows of lamps and other decorations. 157. Having sprinkled the chariot with water, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should worship the respective deities located from the base to the pinnacle of the chariot and other vehicles;
one should worship Satya, Susarṇa, Garuḍa, and Tārkṣya upon the wheels. 158.
One should worship Māyā and Ananta upon the two discs and the staff;
one should worship Keśava and the others on the base, Dharma and the others on the foot-sections, the weapons on the pillars, and Hari always on the pinnacle. 159–160.
In the halls, one should worship Vāsudeva and others; on the altars, Kūrma and others;
and on the pinnacle, Ananta, and above that, Padmanābha.
One should also worship the door-keepers such as Chaṇḍa and the groups beginning with Kumuda.
Having worshipped the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) in the eight quarters in due order, and having worshipped them in the corners as well, one should then worship Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta,
and Ananta; thereafter, one should worship the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) upon the horses.
Then, within the intermediate spaces of the worlds beginning with Atala,

one should worship the King of Weapons (Hetirāja) both inside and outside the chariot (ratha). Having fully honored Viṣvaksena in the form of the charioteer, the Guru [should worship him] in his embodied form as the driver.
Then one should perform the *balidāna* (offering) around the sacrificial ground (*rahas*) in due order;
[according to an additional reading: one should perform the *bali* with *caru* mixed with sesame, parched grain, and unbroken rice].
Then the guide, having caused the Lord and the two goddesses to ascend the vehicle,
performed the ritual for the Blessed One’s installation in the middle of the chariot amidst shouts of victory and the sounds of dancing, singing, kettledrums, and small drums. 166
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, trumpets, drums, and the like, as well as the notes of lutes and flutes,
and reciting the Śākuna Sūkta while circumambulating the chariot,
one should then cause the Lord to ascend it with the mantra beginning with "dhruvanta."

Having worshipped the Lord there according to the rules up to the offering of food (naivedya), women shall obtain progeny; therefore, one should give the food from the offering to women for the sake of attaining offspring. 168. The grace offered to the Blessed One while seated in the chariot [brings this result]. One should then give the food of the offering to women for the accomplishment of progeny.
One should cause that chariot to circulate through the village so that it may be easily accessible.
By seeing the Lord of the Gods seated upon the chariot, one is liberated from sins; there is a special merit in beholding the Blessed One while He is stationed on the chariot and in worshipping Him.
O Lotus-Seated One, this world and its certainty must be understood: whoever, having gone to me who am situated at the base of the *ara*, is satisfied through a state of devotion with wealth,
horses, cities, villages, elephants, flowers, fruits, and so forth— 170–171.
Having eaten all those enjoyments with great respect along with many offerings, he shall at the end attain equality with me.
Then, having established the Lord in his chariot and so forth, as before—
(With the circumambulation of the temple itself,) one should cause [the deity] to enter from there by means of that very sequence of circumambulation.
173 Thus has been described the procedure for the chariot festival of the Lord who wields the Śārṅga bow; [now follows] the ritual for the hunting festival.
Now I shall describe in detail the supreme festival of the hunt (mṛgayotsava),
which generates delight for the Blessed One and destroys the danger from serpents.
For the procession of the hunt festival, on the eighth day, [one should worship] the Lord.
Having specially adorned the caravan with the requisites for the journey and having mounted him upon the jewel of a horse, which was resplendent with various ornaments,
he should cause him to go to great Viṣala accompanied by a vast multitude of people.

There, having performed special worship, he should then cause a hunt to take place; having stationed the army all around with bows for binding deer and other equipment, he should position a fierce beast in the center.
Having done so, the soldiers there would drive the deer before the city;
they would show those various deer and release them one by one outside.
By this, there would be infinite merit from the cruel creatures that were killed. 178–179.
One should worship the bow and the five arrows in front of the deity;
one should discharge four arrows in the four directions and one upward.
Then, having worshipped the deity with full elaboration according to one's means.

Having circumambulated the village clockwise, one should cause it to enter the temple. (181) This is the ritual for the Avabṛdha festival; then, during the latter part of that night, the consecration of the sacred image at the holy site (*tīrtha*) takes place.
The Guru should bind the *kautuka* (sacred thread) on the right hand of the image;
having placed it upon another heap [of grain], he should worship it according to the prescribed rite, including the rubbing with powdered *niśā* (turmeric) and other substances. 182.
Having placed the mortar upon a heap of grain in front of the deity, the Guru should then meditate upon Lakṣmī according to the method of the Śrīsūkta;
he should then wash the pestle with water and consecrate it with the root mantra.
The image-worshippers (mūrtipāḥ), having taken the powder of turmeric (niśācūrṇam), should grind it with four Vaiṣṇavas or with Vaiṣṇavī women; in this way,
they should grind the turmeric powder so that it becomes exceedingly fine.
Having placed that powder in a jar, one should wrap it with a new cloth (186). One should place that jar upon a pedestal of rice while reciting the root-mantra;
having worshipped it with scents, one should consecrate it with the Śrīsūkta and those powders (187).

Having mounted [the image] upon a vehicle, preceded by the ritual bathing at a sacred site (*tīrtha-bimba*), a person should perform the special rite (*viśeṣa*)—namely, the ocean bath—at a holy ford such as a river, or alternatively, on the bank, on the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) or the new moon day (*darśa*). 188. (The Ocean Bath)
On the full moon day and on the new moon day, if there is a space between people, Madhava, having led [the deity] to the shore of the ocean, should remain there in a pavilion,
at a water-station (prapā), or on an auspicious throne, facing either east or north.
Having removed the vehicle and other items, one should then install the deity there.
In front [of the deity], twenty-five, ten, or seven jars [should be placed]; this is the procedure for the purificatory ablution (*avabhṛtha-snāna*).

Having established nine or five [vessels], one should consecrate the deity with those jars; this is the procedure for the wheel-bath (*cakrasnāna*). Then, having duly invoked the Gaṅgā and other rivers into those sacred waters (*tīrtha*), one should proceed.
Taking up the discus, the eminent leader of the community,
having gathered [the assembly], should immerse it in the sacred water (tīrtha) three times according to the prescribed rite,
preceded by the recitation of the *Abliṅga*, *Pavamāna*, and other hymns.
Regarding the description of the specific fruits of bathing with the discus:
those who immerse themselves in the lakes at that very time, having shaken off all their auspicious merit as well as the entire accumulation of great sins (mahāpātaka), [attain liberation]. 194.
They certainly go to that station which is difficult to attain, remaining there as long as the moon and stars exist.
Then, having invited the Deity and seated him within the pavilion,
one should worship Him there with water for the guest-offering (arghya) and so forth, using the Puruṣasūkta.

Having offered food and other items there, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas. Then, having placed the deity upon a vehicle, one should convey him to another temple. That night, one should worship the deity in a mandala known as Puṣpayaśas.

During the great festival, the Ācārya may perform the rites of initiation and so forth according to his own will; however, during the great festival, it should be carried out in a highly skillful manner by the Lord of Teachers following the path favored by him, through the application of reasoning and deliberation. 198.

Even amidst the festivities of a wedding, the preceptor should perform, as appropriate, the "Great Benediction" (*mahadāśīrvāda*); and that which pertains to festivals not specifically mentioned for the assembly hall and so forth is called the "Great Benediction," known by the name of the "Assembly Hall Festival. 199.

One should arrange the playful display of flower garlands, the detailed distribution of ornaments according to their splendor, the closing of the doors, the conversation between the God and the Goddess, and many other various wonderful diversions. 200.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Brahmotsava Festival," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, the Great Upaniṣad of the Śrī Pañcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ. In the glorious Pāñcarātra, the divine scripture, in the Śrī Puruṣottama-saṃhitā, this is the twenty-fifth chapter.
The ritual procedure for the flower-sacrifice;
the inquiry to Brahmā for the purpose of hearing the ritual procedure for the flower-sacrifice;
Brahmā.
O God of gods, O Lord of the world, O cause of creation, preservation, and destruction!

For the sake of fulfilling the desires of your devotees, please initiate the sequence of festivals; even when there is the touch of those who are untouchable during that festival, [let it be auspicious].
O Lord of the Universe, O best among speakers, please explain in detail how that fault may be avoided;
for you previously described the festival for the purpose of granting the desires of your devotees.

During its festival or while wandering about, if there occurs any fault such as touching what is untouchable or drinking [forbidden things], for the sake of pacifying whatever defect may have arisen— especially during a great festival— for the purpose of pacifying those respective defects and for the accomplishment of atonement (niṣkṛti) for that:
"O God of gods, O Lord of the universe, tell me what is the means for this. To this, the Blessed One gave this reply: the Blessed One said—

Listen to the ritual procedure for the Śrīpuṣpayāga; I shall now explain this festival known as Puṣpayāga, which must be performed for my satisfaction. It burns away all defects and removes every blemish. 4.
Therefore, having become composed, at the end of the day during the night,
or on the following day during the night, one should perform the flower-sacrifice (puṣpayāga) either in the assembly pavilion or in the center of the sacrificial pavilion.
Having first prepared an earthen altar (vedi) three *tālas* high and equal in width and length to two *tālas*, one should install the deity upon it;
and on the ground directly in front of that, [one should prepare an area] two cubits in length and width.
One should prepare an altar (*vedi*) five *tāla* units in height and as level as the surface of a mirror;
to its south, one should arrange powders of five colors and flowers—
this is the sequence for the construction of the flower-sacrifice mandala (*puṣpayāga-maṇḍala*).
Having sprinkled [the site] and cast [the materials], the Guru should construct a mandala upon that altar;
first, he should fashion the pericarp with black powder,
and then, above that, he should likewise form another part with yellow powder.

One should fill the four petals in the four directions according to the divisions of the quarters starting with Indra—white, red, yellow, and dark—with colored powders. Then, between the petals and in their center, there should be two lines, white and yellow. 10–11.
Above that, one should perform a circular motion with white powder;
then, having drawn an eight-petalled lotus, the colors in the directions are as before,
with yellow in the northeast, dark blue, white, and black.
Within the lines at the edge of the petals, fill the center with reddish-smoky color (13).
Encircling it with red powder, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus above that;
filling it with the colors of the *vīta* pattern, the tips of the petals are black (14).
One should divide the interior with white-colored powder;
having made the rim, one should draw around it with smoke-colored powder. Above that, [one should draw] a twelve-petaled [lotus] with colors mixed together. 15. With colors mixed together.
Having filled the lines of the petals with white and red [powders], the interior of the petals should be yellow using mixed powder;
having made a beautiful circle around it with black powder— 16–17.
Around that, one should place the three powders— white, red, and black—
and having joined them with the four doors, one should invoke the deities in their proper order. (18) This is the sequence for invoking the deities in the mandala.

First, in the center of the pericarp, one should meditate upon the eternal God of gods, whose body is dark and tender, as dark as a peacock's neck, clothed in yellow silk, adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark, a forest garland, and so forth, and endowed with the conch, discus, and other [emblems]. 19. Endowed with the discus and other [weapons].

One should worship Vāsudeva— the Lord of the universe, the enchanting one, higher than the highest, and the bestower of desired fruits— by means of the twelve-syllable mantra. Then, on the four petals, one should worship [the deities] starting from Indra in their proper sequence.

One should worship Vāsudeva, who resembles a pure crystal, with a body blazing with light and a red complexion; then Saṃkarṣaṇa in the second [position], and in the third, one with the luster of gold. 22.22-23ab.

Having likewise worshipped Pradyumna, who possesses the common qualities of knowledge and so forth and is yellow in color, and the god Aniruddha, who resides within the [inner] array, is dark-complexioned and of great splendor, upon the four petals; 23–24.

One should inscribe the eight-syllable mantra on the eight-petaled lotus, the syllable of the *tāraka* (Om) on the six-petaled lotus above that, and the twelve-syllable mantra on the twelve-petaled lotus;
starting from the circle of the pericarp, this is done upon the five circular lines.
One should invoke and worship the five elements, beginning with earth; thereafter, one should worship them together.

Then, upon the lines situated at the tips of the petals, within the four enclosures, one should likewise worship those consisting of the three qualities: the sāttvika, the rājasa, and the tāmasa. 26–27.
In the sections at the tips of those petals, one should worship the Ṛgveda and the others in their proper order;
and above them, in the enclosure, one should worship Brahmā and the others in sequence.
[One should represent] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa with red, pale yellow, and dark blue colors respectively.
Having invoked [the deities] according to their colors and qualities within the three enclosures (āvaraṇas),
one should place the four pitchers at the gates of the first enclosure,
and the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgalāni) at the gates of the second enclosure.
Likewise, one should worship individually with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings the four *kumuda* lotuses at the doors of the third enclosure,
according to the respective colors and forms of the deities situated within the mandala. 31.
One should worship with fragrant flowers according to the path of the scriptures.
Having established the festive worship within that maṇḍala and having meditated upon it, one should worship in due order with flower-offerings; this is the procedure for the twelve-fold propitiation.
One should perform this supreme sacrifice named the Śrīvaiṣṇava Mahāyāga at night, preceded by Vedic instruments, with sixteen types of offerings repeated twelve times. 33–34.
Having offered milk-rice and other foods, as well as mangoes and other fruits, and various delicacies cooked in ghee in great abundance (35),
and having given water for drinking and sipping along with excellent camphor, [he should proceed].
One should devoutly offer betel-leaf and cast handfuls of flowers at his feet.
Having placed the Lord upon a vehicle, one should proceed to the bedchamber of the two Goddesses,
which is adorned with all ornaments and resplendent with nets of pearls.
It was adorned everywhere with lamps of jewels and gold, perfumed with incense of musk and aguru, free from all impurities, and provided with every kind of bedding, seat, and necessary article. 38.
Having placed the deity with effort upon a floral bed within a well-canopied gateway (toraṇa),
and having worshipped him, the preceptor should perform seven circumambulations by means of a vehicle.
Having circumambulated the temple seven times with the *saptadhātu* mantra,
or alternatively, having led it twelve times, one should perform the circumambulation of the sacred site (*dhāmadakṣiṇa*).
With the sound of each musical instrument during every circumambulation,
the deity was brought from the vehicle to the charming central area of the pavilion for the festival of the dialogue with Lakṣmī.

Having seated [the image] upon an auspicious throne facing the two goddesses, one should properly perform the festival named Lakṣmī-saṃvāda; one should conduct the festival including the closing of the doors and perform the dance. 41–42.
Then one should cause the Lord, the Master of the Universe, Acyuta—who is exceedingly graced by the side-glances of Lakṣmī—to enter between the two goddesses;
this is the "Beholding in the Mirror" (darpaṇadarśana). 43.
Having established the Lord, the consort of Ramā, together with the two goddesses within a single mirror at that time, people behold Him with extreme joy;
their sins are destroyed and all their riches are perfected. 44.
Having offered food consisting of rice mixed with ghee, and then milk blended with sugar (45),
along with excellent betel leaf prepared with camphor and cloves, one should then present the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) and the offering of a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali). (46)
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground with a mind imbued with devotion, one should perform the services consisting of the offerings for the bed;
this is the ritual procedure for the worship of the Lord using sprouts from earthen vessels. 47.
One should perform the rite of the sprouts (aṅkura) in the pavilion for the vessels and bowls, having offered them with affection at the feet of the God of Gods. 48.
The Procedure for the Fire Oblation (Homa).
Then, having established the fire, the preceptor should offer oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter,
and sacrificial porridge one hundred and eight times with the root mantra (mūlamantra).
Having offered the expiatory oblations, he should offer clarified butter with the five Upaniṣad mantras.
Having performed the rites beginning with the invocation of the deities of the *pūrṇāhuti*,

the preceptor should then offer the *pūrṇāhuti*. Then, the preceptor should cause the fire to be extinguished, and likewise cause the arches, banners, deities, and so forth, to be withdrawn in their proper order.
Then, having worshipped Garuḍa and performed a circumambulation,
one should dissolve the noble painting according to the method of the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
One should present the flagstaff, the banner, the cloth, and so forth, to the preceptor (ācārya).
The preceptor should take hold of the flagstaff, its rope, and its water-shed (52). By the very act of the preceptor taking [the staff], Garuḍa is fully satisfied;
having offered bali to the invited gods and men, he should dismiss them (53).
Having circumambulated the Lord and having settled the devotees who had arrived from other lands for the purpose of serving Viṣṇu,
he gave them permission to return to their own countries through the mouth of the preceptor.
Having circumambulated [the deity] clockwise throughout all the stages of purification (*sarvāvaraṇabhūmi*),
one should cause the deity to enter the inner sanctum accompanied by all auspicious musical instruments; [then follows] the offering of fees (*dakṣiṇā*) to the preceptor (*ācārya*) and so forth.
At the conclusion of the great festival, the performer of the rite should worship the Pāñcarātrika preceptor with garments, celestial ornaments, perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
and should give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of one hundred niṣkas, or as much wealth as he possesses.
He should honor the officiating priests for that purpose, as well as the attendants for that purpose,
and all those who perform dance and music according to their means;
and he should also honor the learned Brāhmaṇas with sacrificial fees and other gifts.
One should gratify the poor, the blind, and the wretched with clothing, food, and other necessities.

(59) The determination of the occasion for giving the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) has been described as the "body of the ritual action" (*kriyā-śarīra*); now the "life-force of the ritual action" (*kriyā-jīva*), which is the sacrificial fee, is being explained.

If a sacrifice is performed without the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), it lives on fruitlessly. Therefore, even a small fee should be given in the performance of a sacrificial rite; for a performer who lacks the sacrificial fee does not attain the highest good, and a sacrifice devoid of a fee results in fault for the performer.
Therefore, according to one's means, one should give even a small sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*);

with devotion, the sacrificer should honor the preceptor (*ācārya*) with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Having worshipped him and placed him upon a vehicle, he should perform a circumambulation of the village.
Regarding the fruit of performing the festival, the scripture declares:
"One should cause [the image] to enter the house with devotion, preceded by all kinds of musical instruments.
He who performs the great festival in the manner thus described—
Having reached the five desired abodes of Viṣṇu, he himself leads others across and certainly attains union with Viṣṇu. Wherever the sacrifice of Viṣṇu is performed— whether in a village,
a city, a country, or even a kingdom— there no possibility of famine arises.
O Viṣṇu, best of teachers, wherever additional recitations (adhikapāṭha) take place,
one should not perform other festivals at that same time.
When a sacrifice to the gods has already commenced, that deluded soul who performs another sacrifice to human beings perishes very soon;
likewise, one who performs a festival for another deity in the midst of a festival for Viṣṇu [perishes].
If the destruction of that kingdom and its king should certainly occur through you,
then men, liberated from all suffering, shall become happy. (Additional readings)
Therefore, with every effort, one should never perform another festival out of devotion in the midst of the auspicious rites of Hari;
thus, O Lotus-seated One, is the festival known as the Flower Sacrifice (puṣpayāga). 66.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Flower Sacrifice," in the *Śrī Puruṣottama-saṃhitā*, the Great Upaniṣad of the *Śrī Pañcarātra*.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ. This is the twenty-sixth chapter of the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā within the divine scripture (Āgama) of the Illustrious Ones.
The ritual procedure for the Pavitraka festival; the inquiry of Brahmā upon hearing the injunction for the Pavitraka festival;
Brahmā.

O Lord, O Lotus-eyed One, O Sinless One, when should the festival of the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) be performed? What are the characteristics of the sacred threads? Please tell me this.
[Additional Readings]
"For what purpose was this festival proclaimed, and what is its ritual procedure, O Lord of the World?
O Bull among Men, tell me that festival in full detail. This is the Blessed One’s reply.
The Lord said: Listen to the determination of the time for the Pavitrārohaṇa festival, which is a supreme secret.
The offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) is prescribed for the month of Śrāvaṇa, or on the full moon of Kārttika, as well as in the months of Āśvayuja or Bhādrapada;
it may also be performed according to the rules on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) or on the full moon.
On the second, thirteenth, or fifth lunar day of the bright fortnight, when the moon is auspicious, under a favorable *lagna*, and in a most excellent and beautiful constellation (nakṣatra),
the installation of the *savitṛ* (the presiding deity) should be performed, preceded by the ritual of auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura*).
The sequence for the Pavitra festival consists of twelve *pālikās*, twelve *ghaṭikās*, and twelve *śarāvas*— each in three varieties— to be taken for the rite of auspicious sprouts (*maṅgalāṅkura*).
Having performed the sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa), thereafter,
one should first cause a pavitra-maṇḍapa— a maṇḍapa possessing the prescribed characteristics— to be constructed auspiciously in front of the temple.
It should be correctly thirteen cubits [in length], with an altar nine cubits [in width];
having made the center one cubit high, it should be adorned with ornaments, provided with door-arches, and beautified with banners and flags. 7–8.

It was strewn with canopies and the like, provided with mirrors and other articles, furnished with fresh branches, and endowed with fruits such as those of the *kramuka* tree along with coconuts. 9. It was likewise provided with the fruits of the *nārikela*.
Then, one should adorn the pavilion with *nāraṅga*, *liṅgu*, and *kucī* fruits.
On the ninth day itself, the preceptor (*deśika*) should collect all the sacrificial materials (*yāgadravya*) in their entirety; this is the procedure for the preparation of the *pavitra*.
First is the woolen thread, and after that the silk thread;
the varieties of thread are linen thread as the third, and lotus fiber thread as the fourth.
One should carefully avoid cotton thread, or a string made by girls, as well as a dirty thread or one that is blue; however,
a thread made by Brahmin women should be used, having been tripled with its strands.

One should prepare the purifiers (*pavitra*); by means of them, one should make the small, the large, and the medium—such is the classification of the *pavitra*. Furthermore, there is the *vanamālā-pavitra* and the *adhivānaka-pavitra*. 14.

The purificatory rites for the retinue and the purificatory rite for the initiated one— [with additional readings such as "one should cause various types of purificatory rites to be performed in this manner"]— one should perform these purificatory rites according to their various divisions.
The *pavitra* [strainer] is of three types—superior and so forth; that which reaches from the head down to the navel is the smallest (kaniṣṭha).
Starting from that, the one reaching to the thighs is known as the middling (*madhyama*) *pavitra*.
The supreme measurement for purifiers (*pavitra*) is knee-high;
as for the measurements of the *vanamālā* and other purifiers,
the *vanamālā-pavitra* is equal in length to the height of the image.

The ring finger is the purifier, and it is the purifier that performs the consecration (adhivāsana). 17. They declare that the purifier for one who has been initiated should reach as far as the navel; having strewn darbha grass upon the ground in a place smeared with cow-dung, 18.
Seated on his throne facing the east, the wise and self-possessed master, together with all his disciples, should first recite the Gāyatrī mantra and then examine the measuring pins for the thread.
He should fashion the sacred thread (pavitra) according to the prescribed proportions, making it conform to the likeness of the deities.
The method for determining the number of threads should be understood as follows: the smallest [size] is to be known as being made with twenty-eight threads;
the middlemost, however, is to be known as having fifty-four threads.
The most excellent [garland] should consist of one hundred and eight threads;
however, that which is given to Viṣṇu by the name "Forest Garland" (vanamālā) with a count of one thousand and eight threads is the bestower of liberation. 21–22.
It should be known that for the perfuming of the threads, there are twenty-seven [units];

specifically, the forest garland (vanamālā) is classified as superior, inferior, or middling according to half, a quarter, or the full count of those threads. 23. Thus is the enumeration of the threads.
The pavitraka for the retinue is to be known as having twelve threads;
the pavitraka for the Ācārya has twenty-seven threads, and the pavitraka for the bell has twenty-three threads. 24–25.
The purificatory thread (pavitraka) for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) consists of twenty-eight threads;
that for the temple (prāsāda) consists of four hundred threads;
and the purificatory thread for the incense-stick (dhūpadaṇḍa) consists of twenty-four threads.
A sacred thread (*pavitraka*) for the lamp-stand consists of thirty-five threads;
a sacred thread for the temple consists of twenty-eight threads; and a sacred thread for the gate-tower (*gopura*) consists of nineteen threads. (27–28)
The *pavitraka* for the *balapīṭha* consists of thirty-nine threads,
while the *pavitraka* for the *upapīṭha* consists of twenty-five threads.
Having tripled the thread, one should prepare the *pavitraka* for the enclosure wall (*prākāra*).

Having thus determined the number of knots for the *pavitra*, one should then bind the *pavitra* threads and their respective knots once again; the measurement of the knots should be exactly the size of a thumb. 30. As for the knots that have been tied, they should be [of that specific measure].

The sacred thread (*pavitra*) should be measured by the length of the little finger or the middle finger; it should be auspiciously consecrated one hundred and eight times. For the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the sacred threads, twelve knots are prescribed.
In the *pavitraka* for the retinue, eight knots are to be known;
twelve knots are prescribed for *kṣema*, *āyus*, and *vivarthaṇa*.
In other *pavitrakas*, one should act according to what is appropriate. 33.
One should smear [the deity] with saffron, ushira, camphor, sandalwood, and other substances.
On the first night,
having prepared the sacred threads (pavitra) according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures, one should then proceed.

When evening has arrived, the preceptor, together with the officiating priests and accompanied by the patron of the sacrifice, should enter the temple of the Blessed One to offer prayers to the Blessed One. (35)
Having thus worshipped the deity, one should indeed prostrate like a staff (36). Rising up and becoming pure with joined palms, one should recite this verse:
"Whatever omission may have occurred during the year-long observances... (37).
O Lord, for the sake of pacifying those defects and for Your pleasure, I perform the Pavitrāropaṇa; therefore, grant me Your grace. 38.
[The Invocation of the Pavitra-cloth]
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, one should worship Viṣvaksena;
having performed the rite for the invocation of merit (puṇyāha-vācana), one should sprinkle the sacred threads (pavitra).
Having tied the protective cord (pratisara) at night, one should spread out a layer of darbha grass.
On the morning of the second day, having first performed the cleaning of the teeth,
one should perform the ritual bath, the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), and so forth, and recite the mantra according to the prescribed rule.
Having worshipped the Blessed One, one should perform the ritual bathing with water-jars (kalaśa).
Then, on the great sacrificial altar, one should feed the Vaiṣṇavas.
At night, at the conclusion of the daily worship, the Guru should rotate the discus-and-lotus diagram (cakrābja). 41–42.
Following the very sequence previously described, the preeminent teacher, having fasted and while the sound of musical instruments resounds, should worship the deities in the mandala;
he should then place the purifiers contained in vessels upon two heaps of grain.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should then scatter flowers;
having covered the vessels with a cloth, one should worship them with the Astra-mantra. (Additional readings)
One should worship the god Nārāyaṇa upon the *athivāsa-pavitra*s with the Gāyatrī and Viṣṇu-mantras; thereafter,
one should worship Hetirāja upon the *pavitra*s of those who have been initiated.

Performing the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the Wheel-King (*cakrarāja*) with the *gāyatrī*, the Lord of Teachers (*deśikeṃdra*), having invoked the Lord of Birds (*khageśvara*) into the purifiers of the retinue (*parivārapavitra*), should consecrate them with that mantra and the *gāyatrī*.
Having offered the bali-oblation in the four directions of the hall, one should cause a pit to be prepared with food according to the sequence;
then, having performed the preliminary consecration of the purifiers and the worship of the four locations, one should perform the fire sacrifice according to the prescribed rule.

The preceptor himself, having taken the sacrificial oblations (homa) and the consecrated purifiers (adhivāsa-pavitra), [should perform them] in due order in the water-pot (kumbha), the small vessel (karaka), the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and the mandala. 46.
O Lotus-born One, these [articles] should be placed using the mantra "Tad Viṣṇoḥ. Then, on the third day, at dawn, one should install the Lord of Gods upon a lotus marked with a disc and worship Him.

Having offered the items beginning with *arghya* and ending with incense and lamps, as well as the fourfold food offering (*naivedya*), one should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) as previously described and complete the remainder of the sacrifice. Then, for the ritual images (*karmārcā*) such as the *dhruva* and others, [the rites should be performed] in their proper sequence.
Through devotion to Viṣvaksena and the other [deities], as well as to Chaṇḍa and the rest, and likewise to Durgā, Rudra, Indra, the gods, and Garuḍa (the Lord of Birds),
[one attains success] through the vessels for the water-offering (*arghya*) such as the jar, and through incense and lamps. 50.
Indeed, [this applies] to the pitchers, the archways, and everything up to the sacrificial pedestals (51).
Having thus offered the sacred threads while the sound of musical instruments resounds,
they have been prepared exactly as prescribed for the purpose of being worn by the devotees (52).
The offering of the *pavitra* (sacred thread) should be performed upon the temple towers (*vimāna*) and the gate-towers (*gopura*).
Having taken up the *pavitra*s and placed them at the feet of the Deity, the patron (*yajamāna*), while holding what must be given, [should do so] in the presence of the Preceptor (*deśika*). 53.
One should cause the officiating priests, the Brāhmaṇas and others, and the devotees to wear them.
(54) Regarding the specific manner of wearing the *pavitra*:
Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas should wear it like a necklace.
The Vaiśyas who bear the marks of Vaiṣṇavas should wear this sacred thread (yajñopavīta) as a constant ornament.
(55) [Additional readings: He who, endowed with faith, wears this purifier out of devotion...]
Any omission of rites performed during that year of his [the disciple's] observance is nullified; all his rituals become complete, and he attains their full great fruit.
Then, standing by the side of the deity, the Guru should offer this prayer:
O Blessed One, O lotus-eyed one, bestower of the desires of your devotees!
(56) Whether by design or even unknowingly, during the course of a year—
By me, by those authorized by me, and likewise by other attendants,
whatever deficiency in worship or similar omissions has been committed— for the pacification of that fault and for the completion of the rite, the Pavitrāropaṇa has been performed by me. (57–58)

Therefore, please favor that [work] out of a desire to show grace to your devotees— and out of a desire to show grace to me— for I am not independent, possessing little knowledge, and unable to do anything on my own. Thus, having placed the burden upon your feet, I have been impelled by you.
"O Lord of Gods, I shall do everything; protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, the preceptor should place him upon the vehicle and perform the special festival together with the devotees who carry the sacred threads.
Then, at the conclusion of the festival, one should have the ritual bathing performed for the deity in the temple.
[Additional readings include:
"The fruit of wearing the sacred thread."]
Having worshipped [the deity] with offerings up to the final food offering (naivedya), the preceptor should install [the image] in the temple for nine days,
seven days, five days, three days, one day,
or even for a watch (yāma), half a watch, or a moment (muhūrta).
Having worshipped the God of gods with special care according to the prescribed rules,
at the conclusion of the *utsava*, on the evening of that day, the preceptor should place the Lord of Gods upon the vehicle and lead him around the village in circumambulation.
Accompanied by the sounds of dancing and musical instruments, he should enter the sanctuary;
having fed the Brāhmaṇas according to his means and extent, the preceptor, having worshipped the deity, should enter the sacrificial pavilion. 62.

There, having performed the descent of the sacred thread (pavitrāvarohaṇa) according to the rules for those situated in the mandala, those in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and likewise those within the pitcher (kumbha), one should perform the daily worship after having dismissed [the deities]. 63.
The descent [of the deity] occurs on the twenty-first day, or even on the fourteenth day, or on the seventh day, or after three nights;
the preceptor should offer all the sacred purificatory materials (pavitrāṇi).
One should cause those armor-plates to be given to the preceptor after having them consecrated;
that gift will undoubtedly lead to the pleasure of Hari.
Otherwise, if they are employed for any other purpose, the kingdom will perish.
At that time, the patron should satisfy the preceptor with wealth, beginning with the ritual fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Thus has been fully explained the supreme sequence of the Pavitrāropaṇa rite.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Installation of the Pavitra," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, which is a Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pañcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ. In the glorious Pāñcarātra, the divine scripture, in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, this is the twenty-seventh chapter.
The ritual for the annual festival:
the spring festival of the Blessed Lord.
[I shall now proclaim the supplementary readings and the sequence of vows for the year:
At the beginning of the year, one should worship Hari for the sake of satisfying the god Vasanta.

Having performed the ritual bath according to the rules, and having adorned the Lord with new garments and ornaments— such as beautiful flower garlands brought forth by the spring season— one should then worship Him while facing the south.
Whether in a temple, a garden, or on a riverbank, having worshipped the Lord with perfumes and other offerings according to one's preference, one should present fruits and other gifts.
This is the festival of Śrī Rāmanavamī.
On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, under the asterism Punarvasu,
on the birthday of Śrī Rāma, one should bathe the God of gods, the Lord of the universe, with nine jars of water and worship Him with offerings ending in oblations.
Having placed the Lord Śrī Rāma, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa and accompanied by Hanumān, upon a palanquin, one should perform the festival;
this is the Damanotsava.
On the full moon day of the month of Caitra, one should perform the Damanikā festival.
Having constructed a pavilion with flowers joined with damanī leaves,
one should then adorn the deity with flowers and damanī petals.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with the leaves of the *damanaka* plant.
On the occasion of Nṛsiṃha-jayantī in the month of Caitra, under the Śravaṇa asterism, at the time of evening, [one worships] the Man-lion (*nṛkesarin*).
Therefore, having especially worshipped the Lord who has appeared upon the ground,
one should particularly offer cool water and other offerings. Then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), one should gladden Hari with hymns of praise.
The Kalhāra Festival:
One should celebrate the festival of the Lord using only Kalhāra flowers on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, according to the prescribed rule.
10. On the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, in accordance with the path [of the scriptures].
Having performed the four-fold rite of the pillar (catuḥsthāṇuvratam), one should celebrate the village festival.
On the day, during the first half, or in the middle,
one should observe the Vāmana Jayantī, which is beneficial for the eyes.
On the Śravaṇa nakṣatra, during the forenoon, Trivikrama appeared; at that time, a twice-born man should perform a festival for him.
This is Hanumat-jayantī.
On the birth asterism of Hanumān, having bathed Māruti— who is united with Sītā and Rāghava— according to the prescribed rite, one should perform a special festival;
this is the Svāpotsava.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship the God for the purpose of his lying down; during all four months,
the preceptor should have a couch prepared in a secluded and approved place.
Then, having laid the Lord of Gods together with the two goddesses upon the bed, one should worship them;
[according to another reading, the best of teachers should perform the sleep-rite for the image on the bed].
The worship should be performed for as long as the period of the Bodhana-ekādaśī lasts.
The Śrī Kṛṣṇa Janmotsava occurs on the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) in the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, under the asterism Rohiṇī.
On that day, one should worship Śauri, the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa;
one should perform his ceremonial bathing according to one's ability and hold a great festival in the village for that day, or for a month, a fortnight, or nine days. 17–18.
For seven days, five days, three days, or even just one day,
one should celebrate a village festival with dramatic performances (*naṭaka*) of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s divine sports (*līlā*). Every day, one should perform special worship according to one's means.
In the month of Bhādrapada, on the day of Varāha-jayantī, when the moon has entered the Śravaṇa asterism,
Viṣṇu manifested as Bhū-varāha; one should worship him.
The ceremonial bathing and the festival itself should be performed according to the previously mentioned injunctions.
This is the procedure for the festival of Vīralakṣmī;
furthermore, one should perform the festival of Vīralakṣmī in the month of Āśvayuja.
Beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight, one should perform the nine-day festival (navarātra).
Having bathed [the deity] daily with water-pots and adorned him, the preceptor (deśika) should perform worship at four locations and complete the ritual up to the offering of oblations (havis).
Having placed the Goddess upon the vehicle, one should perform the circumambulation of the village with the Deity;
having done this every day, on the ninth day, at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should sprinkle [the Deity] with water from the jar and worship the Goddess together with the Deity.
On the tenth day of Vijayadaśamī, having mounted the deity upon a horse and led him in circumambulation of the village twenty-five times,
one should reach the Aśvattha tree and station the vehicle at its base.
Having worshipped Viṣvaksena, one should then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited.

Having sprinkled [the bow and arrow] with the water of the puṇyāha, one should worship the bow and the arrow as before; then, having performed the discharge of the arrow, one should worship the deity.
The fruit of wearing *śamī* leaves:
having gathered *śamī* leaves, one should worship the two gods; those men by whom *śamī* leaves are placed at the feet of the god [attain the fruit]. 28.

Those who bear [the image] upon their heads will certainly be freed from sin; thereafter, with great splendor, one should lead the Lord toward the temple. Having worshipped Him in the assembly pavilion, one should then perform the ceremonial bathing.
Having entered the temple, one should perform the daily festival.
Regarding the Dīpāvalī festival:
in ancient times, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, Hari [appeared].
Therefore, this fourteenth day is named after that [hell] which one would destroy;
on this day, one should bathe the God of gods with oil, and having bathed him, adorn him with new garments and ornaments. 31–32.
And one should offer four kinds of food and drinks on the new moon day of Dīpāvalī; having performed the daily worship in the evening, [one should proceed]. 33.
In the temples, on the pillars, along the walls, and at the gate-towers,
rows of lamps were arranged separately in various diverse forms.
Then, having placed the Lord upon his elephant-vehicle together with the two goddesses, [he proceeded].
Then, with umbrellas, chowries, musical instruments, and hosts of armed warriors,
one should cause a great festival to be held either at the rampart or in the village; thereafter, one should cause the deity to enter the temple with magnificent splendor.

The festival of awakening (Bodhanotsava) occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika; one should awaken Hari with the mantra beginning with "uttiṣṭha," preceded by the sounding of musical instruments. 37.
Then, having bathed the deity with twenty-five jars and performed the fire sacrifice according to the rules, and having worshipped as prescribed by the ritual injunctions (38),
one should conduct a great festival with the full extent of one's resources.
The Kṛttikā-lamp festival should be observed on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika under the constellation of Agni (Kṛttikā) or Rohiṇī on the following day;
one should perform the offering of lamps when the sun is in Taurus.

For that purpose, having tied a protective thread (kautuka) according to the prescribed rite upon a heap of grain, one should place a lamp-vessel in front of the deity; it may be made of metal or clay, and one should pour cow's ghee into that vessel. 40–41.
If one consumes sesame oil by mere word, one incurs a fault;
therefore, one should ignite a straight wick with the fire of the *homa* sacrifice.
Then, having recited the *agni-mantra* and worshipped the lamp with devotion.
With that very lamp, one should have all the other lamps lit by the twice-born (dvijas).
Accompanied by attendants and devotees, preceded by various musical instruments,
and having placed the deity upon a vehicle, one should display the garlands of lamps.
Having offered great oblations upon the altar, as well as cakes and *pṛthuka* grains,
one should then lead the deity back inside the temple. Thus concludes the festival of the month of Vaiśākha.
When the month of Dhanus arrives, one should worship the God of gods at the time of dawn and offer oblations of cooked mung beans and other foods.
Having performed this in that manner until the end of the month, during those twenty days, [one should continue].
Having installed the deity in the pavilion, one should perform the festival of the sacrificial seat (adhyayana-utsava).
One should place the Ṛgveda in the eastern quarter, the Yajurveda in the south,
the Sāmaveda in the west, and likewise the Atharvaveda in the north.

The Itihāsa is in the direction of Agni (southeast), the Stotra is said to be in the Nairṛti (southwest), the Dharmaśāstra in the Vāyu (northwest), and the Mantrapāṭhaka in the Īśāna (northeast). [These are performed] with hymns composed by devotees that flow with the essence of the regional languages.

One should cause a great festival to be celebrated with these and other such rites. (50) Regarding the sesame-lotus festival: on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha, the sesame-lotus festival shall take place.
On the ground in front of the deity, having smeared the surface with cow-dung (51),

and having fashioned decorative patterns and the like, the preceptor should then cover it with a cloth; thereafter, having placed a black antelope skin upon it, the Guru should mutter the Viṣṇu-sūkta (52).
Having spread out a cloth once more, one should place sesame seeds upon it— either two loads or one load— and having spread the sesame seeds,
one should place vessels filled with grain, two in each direction.

To the south, one should place jars containing oil, ghee, curd, and other substances; to the north, a jar filled with a *prastha* of oil, and another jar of the same measure containing clarified butter (*ājya*). 54. One should set these down.
One should place a pitcher filled with four *prasthas* of curd in front;
then, one should worship it with scents, flowers, and other offerings, [visualizing] the Lord accompanied by Śrī and Garuḍa in the center of a lotus. 55–56.
[Regarding the additional readings: Having worshipped the deity according to the rules, the preceptor, endowed with faith, should offer a thousand oblations of sesame seeds with the root mantra.

One should devoutly offer that lotus before the Deity with water, while reciting the mantra: "May the Lord Viṣṇu be pleased. He who gives the lotus in this manner, like sesame seeds, [attains merit]. 57–58.

One purifies oneself, all one's ancestors, and those both higher and lower by performing the festival of Śrī Mahālakṣmī on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna; thus, the Mahālakṣmī festival should be observed for the sake of welfare. 59
For that purpose, one should construct a pavilion provided with four doors;
there, having placed Viṣṇu— who resembles a dark blue cloud— seated comfortably upon a throne together with Śrī on an eight-petaled lotus.
One should worship Vāsudeva and the others in the cardinal directions according to the sequence of order, O Kamalāsana.

One should also worship the elephants in the intermediate directions on both sides of the golden pedestal; there, the two treasures (nidhis) are to be worshipped, and one should sacrifice to Indra and the other guardians of the quarters all around.
Having worshipped the door-arches, the water-pots, and so forth according to the prescribed rites,
the preceptor should then worship Mahālakṣmī together with Viṣṇu,
using lotuses, bilva leaves, and the like, as well as sacrificial porridge (caru) and milk-rice (pāyasa).
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for the Śrī Devī with the twelve-syllable mantra.
The officiating priests (ṛtvij) should recite the Śrīsūktas in the various directions in their proper order,
and one should recite hymns of praise to Lakṣmī there with a mind full of devotion.
Thus one should worship the God according to the prescribed rule until the end of the year;
thereby there shall be prosperity for the king and the kingdom, and famine will certainly be dispelled.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, the Great Upaniṣad, in the *Śrīpuruṣottamasaṃhitā*.
The twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Annual Festival," from the *Śrīpuruṣottamasaṃhitā* within the divine scripture (*divyāgama*) of the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*. Oṃ.
The Twenty-Seventh Chapter:
The Characteristics of the Sālagrāma; Brahmā’s Inquiry Regarding the Hearing of the Characteristics of the Sālagrāma.
O Brahmā, O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, O Lord who bestows all prosperity,
you ought to describe the characteristics of the forms of the Lord, such as the Śālagrāma and others.
The Blessed One spoke these words concerning the characteristics of the Śālagrāma:
the Blessed One said: [The Blessed One spoke:
"The characteristics of the Śālagrāma..."

Listen, O Brāhmaṇa, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the Sālagrāma, the worship of which is traditionally held to always bring about the destruction of all sins for men; it is auspicious. [I shall also describe] the installation and the avoidance of the Sālagrāma.
Sadāśauri always resides in the Śālagrāma; of this there is no doubt.
Having installed it according to the traditional rites, it should always be worshipped by those seeking liberation.
I shall now describe their characteristics; O child, listen attentively to them in brief.
The characteristics of the tortoise-shaped [horse]:
the back of the tortoise is elevated, its white parts are marked with hoof-prints, it has two circles, and this one named Bhūdhara bestows the fruits of all desires. 4.
The characteristics of Maṃdhara, Dhara, and Kūrma are marked by two dots (bindus), as well as two wheels and two conchs;
their names have long vowels, and they possess five earth-rings.
The Tortoise-form, the sustainer of Mount Sumeru, shall be the granter of all desires.
(6) The characteristics of the Primal Tortoise are as follows: his form is circular and elongated, and he is endowed with a golden luster.
Or, it may have the shape of a snuhi flower on both sides of the disc;
this is known as Ādikūrma, which bestows the fruit of all desires.
This is the characteristic of Kūrma.
O twice-born one, it is circular, shaped like a hand, and has a long opening;
it is properly provided with a navel-wheel and is tortoise-shaped on its sides.
It is a firm seat, elevated at its back, and dark blue-red in color.
Known as Kūrmamūrti, she bestows the increase of sons and grandsons upon Kṣatriyas (and likewise upon kings), and she is the destroyer of all enemies. [10] The characteristics of Lakṣmī-Varāha.
Resembling a sapphire, thick, marked with auspicious lines,
and with the discus situated on the right side at the proper alignment of the region,
this auspicious Varāha, endowed with a forest garland and possessing Lakṣmī, has been described. 11.
Then, resembling the color of an *atasī* flower and like a blue lotus,
it possessed the characteristics of the Earth-Boar (*bhūvarāha*), had long doors, was endowed with long doorways, and contained internal chambers.
With his back elevated and a long face, the discus is raised on his left side;
he is endowed with a line on his back and has the form of a boar, or else Brahmā has only a face, while the feet and tail are likewise [of the boar]. 13–14.
If a line in the shape of the Kaustubha gem is seen on the back and the sides, it is called Bhūvarāha; it bestows royal fortune upon men and grants women the form of a boar. 15.
The Varāha image is of two kinds.

Endowed with various jewels, possessing a dark complexion, having long doors, being smooth, and having two wheels in the middle of the door— such is the Boar (Varāha) who is celebrated as being adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
He bestows sons, grandsons, wealth, sovereignty, cattle, land, grain, and prosperity; he is the lord of the earth and the increaser of knowledge. 17.
[Additional readings: On the eleventh day, worship performed with special care grants the attainment of liberation.]
When the discus is situated on the left side, the dark-colored syllable with a bindu (kṣ) is known as Lakṣmīnṛsiṃha, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 18.
Vīralakṣmīnṛsiṃha has two wheels, a large face, and is tawny with a golden luster;
he is known as Vīralakṣmīnṛsiṃha and is worshipped by those practicing celibacy. 19.
The Lord has the appearance of a tearing tiger's claw;
he is tawny, with a knotted base, half the form of a spear-point, and shaped like a hoof;
he has a formidable face, possesses a discus of arrows, and has excellent fangs. 20.
And the one named Vidāraṇa, Nṛsiṃha with long manes, who is to be worshipped through celibacy; he is not to be worshipped in any other way. 21. Jvālāvidāraṇanārasiṃha.
With a wheel on his chest, possessing great heroism, with a head elevated by the *dīkṣā* initiation,
tearing [the world] with flames, the Man-Lion is adorned with fangs.
If he is worshipped by one devoid of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), he bestows destruction even when worshipped.
The characteristics of Nṛsiṃha are: the Narasiṃha [mantra], the three dots (tri-bindu), the tawny-colored one, the large cavity, 23.
the face made terrible by fangs, the large mouth, and the very rough one.
Or he may have the form of Narasimha, or the four-faced Brahma in his belly;
or he may have the shape of a fish, or likewise the appearance of the rim and fangs of a discus.
Known as Narasimha, he is said to be worthy of worship by ascetics.

The characteristics of the Kāpila-Nārasiṃha are: two large wheels in the middle, with a *guñjā* seed, a *lākṣā* mark, and a *raktakartana*; when the wheels are cracked or uneven, it is indeed the Kāpila-Nārasiṃha. 26.
By worshipping him, one attains liberation and becomes victorious in battle;
[he is] the Narasimha facing all directions, possessing seven wheels and many faces, adorned with gold on all sides. 27.

Bahuvarga is for liberation; Nṛsiṃha faces in all directions; Viliktāsya has a left wheel and is circular with a tawny luster (28). Bhītākhyānṛsiṃha is the Nārasiṃha who causes fear to householders; he is named Bhīti.
The characteristics of the Pātālanṛsiṃha [form] consist of being joined with wheels (cakras) beginning from the third and ending with the thirteenth, having a large belly,
being endowed with many colors, or even being provided with many doors. 29.

That which is known as Pātālanarasiṃha bestows the attainment of liberation upon ascetics and grants immortality to mendicants. (30) If it is devoid of the specific marks described for those respective forms, it is especially Pātālanarasiṃha, or it may be Bahurūpa, or Dhanañjaya. (31)

The Kukṣinārasiṃha [liṅga] is characterized by being very small, richly adorned with tiny wheels, possessing little weight, and having a large belly; it is known as Kukṣinārasiṃha and is worshipped by forest-dwellers. 32
The *rākṣasa-nṛsiṃha* has many apertures, split cheeks, and the luster of solid gold;
it has two wheels and is known as the *rākṣasa-nṛsiṃha*, which burns down houses. 33.
Vidyujjihvānṛsiṃha has a head as high as a blade of dūrvā grass; Vidyujjihvānṛsiṃhaka is endowed with the beauty of two wheels and is honored by the poverty of sacrifice (makhodāridrya). 34.
Now, the one called Adhomukhanṛsiṃha,
adorned with three discs on the face, the sides, and the back,
grants liberation from all misfortunes. 35.
The Bālanṛsiṃha [mantra],
enriched with two wheels, adorned with a forest garland (vanamālā), and situated in the subtle aperture (sūkṣmarandhra)—
known as Bālanarasiṃha— it liberates men from saṃsāra. 36
Vibhīṣaṇanṛsiṃha has a long body and long wheels, a face like a boar, and is exceedingly large;
known as Vibhīṣaṇanṛsiṃha, he always bestows suffering upon men. 37.
The characteristic of the one named Dadhi is that he is described as a dwarf with an extremely short and round face; he resembles the flower of the linseed plant and is adorned with spots. 38.
One that is joined with two wheels and possesses a white dot in the sacrificial mark (makha) shall be known by the name Dadhivāmana; it bestows cattle, land, grain, and wealth.
This is the description of the desired Vāmana.
It is circular, extremely smooth, endowed with clearly defined spokes,
short yet elevated, and its mouth is wide and deep;
it possesses pure, radiant lines, and its hub should be high.
O Brahmin, the Kesarāmbha is indeed seen on the side of the discus (41).
It should be known as Abhiṣṭavāmana, which bestows happiness and good fortune;
it grants an abundance of food, an increase in progeny, and the acquisition of land in great measure (42).

The characteristic of the dwarf (vāmana) type is that its middle circle is very short and exceedingly glossy like bell-metal; the dwarf type has clearly defined circles and grants all the desires of the three [classes]. 43.
The characteristics of the *bālavāmana* [type of linga] are as follows:
resembling the flower of the linseed plant (*atasīkusuma*), with a slightly elevated top and somewhat indistinct rings; such a *bālavāmana* grants all desires. 44.
Vāmana has broad shoulders, is round, resembles a dark-blue cloud, is adorned with a forest garland, has subtle apertures, a large belly, and is auspiciously endowed with a discus. 45.

The characteristic of Paraśurāma is that he is endowed with yellow, black, and reddish complexions; he is tall in stature with large cavities, and a discus is located on the wall portion, either on the left or on the right. 46.

If there is a dot on the rim of the disc, or if it has the shape of an axe, or if there is a line on the back or the side shaped like a fang, he should be known as Jāmadagnya; indeed, even among kings, one who possesses that form is to be worshipped as Jāmadagnya himself. 47.
Śānta Paraśurāma is marked solely by a line in the shape of an axe;
however, the son of Jamadagni known as Śānta bears a discus and is worshipped with peaceful weapons. 48.
Vīrarāma, accompanied by Bāṇa, Tūṇīra, Cāpa, and others, adorned with earrings and a blood-stained sword, and enriched by Sūkṣmaka, Kesara, and Cakra, remained there together with Śrī.
Sītārāma has a single face on his countenance; the Lord possesses four excellent discs,
is endowed with a bow, arrows, a blade of kusha grass, an umbrella, a banner, and chowries.
The god who wears a forest garland is celebrated as Sītārāma;
he is desired by means of the six chakras, the bow wounded by a weapon, and the anklet. 51.
Endowed with three pits and joined with six marks of vision (52),
with a dark, elevated back like a large rose-apple fruit, it is possessed of the Sītā-pit and resembles a long rose-apple stone (53).
Sītārāma is to be known as the one designated Tārakabrahman;
he alone possesses the eight wheels and is difficult to find even within the three worlds.
Rāma is the destroyer of the lineage of the Ten-Necked One (Rāvaṇa).
One with a wheel-mark [on the sole] is shaped like a cock; one who is dark-complexioned has a prominent nose and is endowed with two lines on the side of the foot, O Lotus-born One.
Furthermore, a line in the shape of a bow is clearly seen on the side.
Or, on the back, there may be the auspicious Rāma, the slayer of the ten-necked one (Rāvaṇa); on the back portion is Bālarāma,
with five lines, and a bow and arrow on the two sides.
Bālarāma, adorned with two discs, bestows sons; of this there is no doubt. Vijayarāma is endowed with a divine arrow and equipped with a bow and quiver.
Adorned with a wheel marked by drops of blood from his formidable fangs, the one known as Śrīdā-Viyarāma, who had made the discus of Keśin his crest-ornament,
was delighted Rāma.

Kodaṇḍarāma, who bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, has a garland, a bow, and arrows on his head, and likewise has a plowshare and a goad at his sides; he is adorned with two discs and is joyful.
Abounding in arrows, quivers, and bows, slightly rounded and elongated;
Kodaṇḍarāma is auspicious, resembling a dark blue cloud and rich in beauty;
[and] Kavitvarāma.
One with a single wheel on the face, dark-complexioned and very beautiful,
should be known as the Sārāmamūrti; it bestows poetic talent upon the worshiper,
O Kṛṣṇa, hero of the Yadus.
Kṛṣṇa, the exceedingly dark one, who is not coarse, whose discus is most beautiful,
renowned as the hero of the Yadus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who bestows prosperity, fame, and nourishment upon men. 62.
Black, yellow, and thin-bodied, with a disc on the side of the wall;
the navel should be equal to the door, and the back should be shaped like a tortoise.
Black, with discs on both sides, it bestows dharma and destroys sin. This black [liṅga], enriched with discs, bestows dharma and is a destroyer of sin.
The characteristics of Govākṛṣṇa:
[He is] endowed with a forest garland and a discus, marked with the Śrīvatsa; possessed of a forest garland, a discus, and the Śrīvatsa mark;
with horns joined by a staff, his face adorned on the sides by a bamboo flute. 65.
The form of Gopālakṛṣṇa bestows cattle, land, grain, and wealth. The characteristics of Madanagopāla are:
two heads, two discs, a flute-staff, and the Śrīvatsa mark. 66.
Adorned with a garland, flanked by a pair of *kalpavṛkṣa* trees,
and graced with earrings, Kṛṣṇa— the cowherd of Madana— bestows sons,
grandsons, wealth, sovereignty, and the singular vision of all the worlds. 67.
The iconographic characteristics of Saṃtānagopāla are as follows: he is long-bodied, dark-complexioned, and possesses a face like a half-moon and a discus (68).
This Kṛṣṇa, as Saṃtānagopāla, bestows the increase of sons and grandsons.

Bālakṛṣṇa has a prominent head, is dark-complexioned, and possesses three dots (bindus) on his forehead; he who bears these marks bestows long life, two wheels [of fortune], a handsome face, and the good fortune of sons.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa, dark-complexioned and most beautiful, with his discus positioned at the entrance—this is to be known as the Kṛṣṇa-mūrti; when worshipped, she bestows happiness. 70.
The form of the Buddha, endowed with the internal *gaṃ* and *hvara* [syllables] but lacking the *cakra*, is known as the "Form of the Buddha" (*buddhamūrti*); it bestows the supreme state. 71.
The characteristics of the *kalikīmūrti* are as follows:
it is intensely red, possesses minute pores, has a well-formed wheel, and is stable in its posture;
furthermore, there is a sword-shaped line upon the back of the door.
Kalkī shall be the destroyer of the Mlecchas and the eradicator of all sins; he will have my own form,
tall in stature, dark-complexioned, and adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
The secret of all complete success, the advancement of sons and grandsons,
the characteristics of the form of Keśava, the three lines, and the attainment of the back-lotus at the twelfth [house]. 74.
One who possesses good fortune is born from Keśava; he has four corners and is endowed with a discus.
Śyāmanārāyaṇa has the characteristic of a dark complexion; he is endowed with a dark color, has a face with a navel-disc, and is elevated therein. 76
Endowed with three long lines and a distinct cavity on the right side, he is called Śyāma-Nārāyaṇa; he bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 77.
[He is] Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa.
Having one face and four wheels, circular and dark-complexioned, endowed with a banner, a vajra, and a goad, joined with a garland and marked with a bindu;
neither too short nor too long—this is the form of Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa. 78.
Merely by seeing them, one shall obtain the desired fruit. (79) The characteristics of the form of the Lord are:
a complexion like molten gold, a smooth discus on the chest, and likewise holding a discus.
Mādhava should be known as the bestower of liberation upon ascetics (80). Govinda’s form is neither too stout, has five faces, and Govinda possesses ten wheels.
Endowed with a black color, it grants the fruits of all desires;
it has the characteristics of the form of Viṣṇu,
with a discus on the left, a wide opening, and a high center that is depressed.
