Viṣṇu, who possesses a color as glossy as that of Kapila, is the bestower of prosperity and strength;
Madhusūdana is his characteristic, and he is named Madhusūdana because of this. He is the one-wheeled deity of great splendor.
Endowed with all colors, bestowing great splendor, and auspicious;
Trivikrama, joined with two discs, has one face, while the single disc is on his side. 83.
Trivikrama is endowed with three angles; he is to be worshipped by Brahmins, but not by others.
Śrīdhara is the god who bears the Malaya mountain and is marked with a garland of forest flowers.
Hṛṣīkeśa has the appearance of a kadamba flower, is endowed with five lines, and has two wheels on his face; he is the bestower of the fruits of all desires. 85.
The Lord Hṛṣīkeśa is described as having the form of the moon of wealth;
the Lord Padmanābha, who bestows all desired objects, is joined with the wheel in his navel. 86.
The central wheel has filaments, while the wheels above it are without filaments;
this is to be known as Padmanābha, the bestower of the fruits of all desires, and [he is] Dāmodara. 87.
Dāmodara is likewise described as thick and having a circular middle; the auspicious Saṃkarṣaṇa form has a narrow opening like a blade of dūrvā grass and is endowed with yellow lines.
This is the definition of the Saṃkarṣaṇa image.
Having two wheels joined together and a single portion for the *puṣkara*, it is known as Saṃkarṣaṇa; red-hued and bestowing beauty, it is the form of Vāsudeva. 89.
In a place where the two door-panels are level and appear very beautiful, he should be known as Vāsudeva; he is white in luster and bestows auspiciousness. Pradyumna—90.
A line at the mouth of the *makara* mark, whether on the side or even from behind, does not indicate Pradyumna; rather, a subtle wheel that is yellow in color bestows auspiciousness. [Aniruddha...]
Dark-complexioned at the junction of the two doors, situated near the wall of the wheel, there shall be a small wheel above and on the side like a *caṇaka* flower;
this is known as Aniruddha, who brings happiness to all the worlds. (92-93)

The characteristic of the form of Puruṣottama is that it has a disc in the middle, is dark in color, and has a broad disc on the head; this one named Puruṣottama is highly auspicious for the worshiper. 94.
Adhokṣaja has red lines below the axle, a circular body, and possesses wheels;
he may be joined with a slight tawny hue, and he is either subtle or indeed gross. 95
The form of Acyuta, joined with the dissolution of Adhokṣaja, bestows auspiciousness upon the worshiper;
it is four-armed, with eight wheels on the left and right sides. 96.
He was presided over by one who had a single discus upon his face, adorned with earrings, and who bore the conch, Nandaka, Padma, Śārṅga, and Modakī;
he held a mace and a banner, possessed a white umbrella, and was surrounded by clouds and a goad. 97.
He is called Soccūta and Kadhita; his sight is difficult to obtain.
Janārdhana has a single face on the front portion, and he is endowed with lines [marks] on the back.
Janārdana, the wielder of the mace, the bestower of women, and the destroyer of enemies;
Upeṃdra, who has the luster of a jewel, whose feet are short and very tender, who is endowed with *māyā*, possesses subtle apertures, and is the bestower of all happiness. 99–100.
Śyāmalā, with her hair tied in a braid at her side and joined by a discus, together with Albadāsa, is Hari, the bestower of desired boons. 101.
Hayaśīrṣa.
Hayagrīva is also [red] mixed with yellow;
he has the form of an ankusha, a cow's face, and is endowed with two wheels.
Likewise, on his side, there is the form of a lotus and the form of an earring. 102.
O Lotus-born One, he is the giver of knowledge, the giver of liberation in this world, and also the giver of enjoyment; he is the eight-armed Nṛsiṃha,
possessing four wheels and eight wheels, with a long face and an uplifted form.
He is worthy of worship by the splendors of the eight-armed Nṛsiṃha;
he is the divine form of Vāsudeva,
possessing twelve discs [on his arms] and adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
"He is the divine Vāsudeva," thus he is determined in the scriptures. Sudarśana, Nārasiṃha,
and Aṣṭavaktra— his body is bowed, his mouth wide open, and he is the giver of fear.
Accompanied by the sixteen kings and joined with the slayers of enemies (the *Śatrumārakas*),
this Sudarśana-Nṛsiṃha should be dismissed at the end of the worship; such is the ritual procedure for the worship of the Sālagrāma.
Having thus examined all these characteristics,
one should perform worship with a mind endowed with devotion toward the *sālagrāma* stones, whether in temples or in houses, in a manner suitable to each particular form. 107–108.
One should regard the Śālagrāma stone as a sacred image for the purpose of ritual bathing;
however, the bathing of the Śālagrāma at night is never prohibited, nor is it ever enjoined—bathing the Śālagrāma at night [is forbidden]. 109
He who, having placed [the image] upon a conch shell, worships it with devotion using tulasī leaves.
The specific fruit of the merit of worshipping the Sālagrāma at a sacred ford (tīrtha) is as follows:
a person who drinks the water consecrated by the Sālagrāma certainly attains all desires. 110. A man who drinks the water sprinkled from the Sālagrāma [attains his goals].
All his sins shall surely perish; of this there is no doubt.
(111) Thus, the characteristics of the Śālagrāma have been briefly declared;
by the mere hearing of which a man becomes cleansed of sin. (112)
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Śālagrāma," in the *Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā*, a great Upaniṣad within the *Śrī Pañcarātra*.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ.
In the glorious Pāñcarātra, the divine scripture, within the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā,
this is the twenty-ninth chapter.
The ritual for bathing;
the determination of the proper time for the bathing of the Blessed Lord.
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I describe the procedure for the ritual bathing of Viṣṇu: during his northern and southern courses, during the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
on the king’s birthday asterism, and also on the Phalgunī and Śravaṇa constellations.
Especially at the commencement and the conclusion of festivals,
during regional disturbances, portents, or the neglect of daily worship;
likewise, when the divine image and other such objects have been touched by outcastes (cāṇḍālas) and the like.
When portents such as earthquakes and the like occur, or when signs such as the movement of the image arise, the Guru should cause the ritual bathing (*snapana*) to be performed. 4.
The Procedure for Constructing the Bathing Pavilion (*snapanamaṇḍapa*).
One should construct a pavilion endowed with the proper characteristics for the purpose of the libation (snāna),
provided with sixteen pillars— or twelve, eight, or four—
adorned with ornaments according to one's capacity.

Having constructed a pavilion (maṇṭapa) to the north of the door, one should cause a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to be made for the purpose of the fire-oblation (homa), and place a water vessel in the northeast; [one should perform] the rite of preparing the pit, the installation of the water vessel, and so forth, as well as the procedure for the invocation of the pitcher (kalaśa-āvāhana).
Having gathered water-pots made of metal, wood, or even clay according to his means (7), he should place them upon a bed of *darbha* grass while reciting the *kṣāma-vatī* verses;
they should be turned face down, and then he should again spread *darbha* grass over them. (8)
Having sprinkled [the area] with water for the arghya offering, he should scatter unbroken rice grains upon them; then,
having turned them face upwards,
the preceptor should strike the lines according to the dimensions of the jars.
One should divide those [spaces] into compartments and arrange the pedestals (pīṭhas) within them.

One should prepare a pedestal of rice grains above, and a pedestal of sesame seeds with half that measurement; one should place the water-jars (kalaśas) upon that pedestal with a measurement equal to half of that.
Eighty-one, forty-nine, ten, and seven; thus it is stated regarding the lowest [number], according to the distinctions of the highest and so forth. Two hundred and seventy-seven as well.
Likewise, eighty-five and twenty-one in the middle [mandala] in three ways;
then, four hundred increased by ninety-three; and thereafter, two hundred and twenty-five increased by eighty-one. (13–14)
In the supreme ablution (*uttama-snāpana*), the distinctions such as the "excellent" (*uttama*) and so forth have been explained;
having thus understood those various classifications, whatever is prescribed for a particular rite, that very ablution should be performed. In the lowest case, however, it is the most inferior.
The determination of the substances for the pitchers is now stated: O Brahmin, clarified butter is for the central pitcher during the ritual bath (snapana);
warm water is for the eastern one; and gems are prescribed for the southeast pitcher.
One should place fruit in the southeast and iron in the southwest; auspicious [substances] in the west, black agallochum in the northwest, and rice is prescribed for the north.
Grains are placed in the northeast pitcher, and outside in the eastern pitcher.
Having placed *tulasī* in the southeast, one should place curd in the south; white mustard seeds in the southwest, and milk is prescribed for the northwest.
Camphor should be placed in the west, and honey should be poured in the north-west.
In the north there should be the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and in the northeast, the skin of a black antelope;
having thus deposited these into the jars, one should also place bundles of kuśa grass (kūrca) within them. [Additional reading]
One should place mango sprouts, jewels, and other mineral seeds in their proper sequence, along with fruit-images;
having thus understood these distinctions, one should wrap them in new cloth and there begin the fire-oblation. 21.

The oblation for the invocation of the pitcher (*kalaśāvāhanahoma*) should be performed by offering fuel sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter (*ājya*), and sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the eight-syllabled mantra,
one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times. 22.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should sprinkle [the vessel] with the residual ghee (*saṃpāta-ājya*).
This is the procedure for the invocation of the presiding deities of the pitcher;
one should worship the gods within the pitchers, and likewise Vāsudeva with clarified butter. (23)

Then, one should worship Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Ananta in the eastern and subsequent directions respectively; thereafter, one should worship Keśava and the others in the four outer directions beginning with Indra, according to the prescribed order.
24. One should worship Viṣṇu and the others in sequence in the four outer directions starting from Indra.
In the remaining jars according to the prescribed rite, one should worship Śrīdhara and the others.
This is the procedure for the bath;
having worshipped the deity with arghya offerings, one should then bind the protective thread.
Then, having offered fragrant tooth-sticks, oil, and *āmalaka* fruit,
as well as flowers, incense, and lamps, one should perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*) of the deity with individual jars, as prescribed for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Then the preceptor, taking a jar filled with turmeric powder,
should bathe the deity with the Śrīsūkta according to the prescribed rite; thereafter,
he should perform the "thousand-stream" bath with the Nṛsūkta.
Having cleansed the Lord with a cloth and a garment, and having adorned the All-pervading One with clothes, ornaments,
perfumes, and garlands, one should offer milk-rice and other foods.
Then, having offered betel-leaf, one should prostrate on the ground like a staff, thinking:
"Whatever fruit there is in the essence of the Blessed One, with that in view, this bath has been performed by me."

"O Nārāyaṇa, grant us that fruit; salutations to you! (31) Having thus prayed to the Lord of Gods and seated Him as before, one should perform all the rites of worship and so forth according to the prescribed rules. (32)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Bathing Ceremony," in the *Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā*, a Great Upaniṣad within the *Śrī Pañcarātra*.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ.
In the divine scripture of the glorious Pāñcarātra, in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, this is the thirtieth chapter.
Brahmā spoke on the rules for expiation, the rules for expiation.
"O Lord, I wish to hear about Brahman and its inquiry; O ocean of divine compassion, please explain all those means of atonement in their entirety and in detail."
The Blessed One’s reply: The Blessed One spoke on the determination of the occasion for atonement.
O Lotus-seated One, listen as I shall declare the rules for expiation (prāyaścitta) regarding images of gods, yakṣas, lords of sages, and others established by ancient authorities; specifically,
concerning the fracture or decay of the limbs of such installed images of gods, sages, and so forth.
When a limb of an installed image is about to break,
one should diligently repair that limb with gold alone, and not otherwise.
This applies when a stone image fashioned by a deity, a sage, or others has broken.
Having fashioned that limb out of gold, it should be joined back as it was before.
(4) Even when an image installed by the gods or others is made of clay and possesses a deficient limb, it must never be discarded; rather, it should be repaired according to the prescribed rules. (5)

Thus, when there is a breakage or decay, one should diligently repair the limb; even if the image is broken or decayed in its major limbs, or if, through negligence, there is a breakage in the major limbs, the minor limbs, or the subsidiary limbs.
The wise man should join [the parts] according to their respective forms as before; however, he should completely avoid that image which is devoid of the head. 7. [Additional readings follow.]
Whoever worships that image out of greed, delusion, and other such motives,
it is established that the destruction of that village will occur, and the king and the kingdom shall perish.
One should therefore abandon images with deficient limbs and create them anew.
Even when merely concentrating on the limbs,
one should [perform] the procedure for the pot and invocation;
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even of the five metals.
One should have well-formed petals made according to each respective form;

one should wash them with pure water, fumigate them with fragrant powders, sprinkle them with meritorious water, and consecrate them by sprinkling with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). 9–10.
One should prepare a pedestal with three types of grain and other materials in front of that;
in its center, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
Having covered it with a new cloth, one should sprinkle it while reciting the root mantra.
One should fill [the vessels] in sequence with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, kusha grass, and sprouts.
Then, one should place the excellent pitcher near each respective image;
thereafter, the preceptor, having invoked the Śaktis with their own respective mantras, [should proceed].
Having worshipped the deity according to the prescribed rite, the wise practitioner should announce the time;
then, having displayed the Mahāmudrā and shown the Cakramudrā,
he should place the excellent pitcher in a secluded and approved location.
Once the installation of the principal image has been completed, one should maintain it according to the sequence previously established.
(15) Otherwise, even if a substitute image (*kauluka*) exists somewhere, one must never neglect the worship; of this there is no doubt. (16)
Or, having extracted the worn-out image with cow-hair ropes,
the best of preceptors should recite the *vyāhṛtis* and cast it into water free from obstacles;
he should then perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with *dūrvā* grass mixed with honey, using the respective mantras for each.
Having fashioned the image as before and installed it according to the ritual rules (18),
one should cause the Śakti residing within the pitcher to enter into the interior of the image through the path of the *brahmarandhra*, exactly according to the prescribed method (19).

Having closed the aperture of Brahma (*brahmaraṃdhra*) with the *praṇava* and having established [the deity] in its respective places by means of the *parameṣṭhin*, one should perform worship—especially the most excellent—when the limbs have become worn out. 20. This should be performed.
In the section on the knowledge of Brahman, there is a question concerning Brahman:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, the inner self of all beings. (21)
"O sinless one, I have previously heard of the restoration of a decayed image;
however, when only the body [of the image] remains decayed, what is prescribed as the procedure? (22) This was the Blessed One’s reply.
The Blessed One said:
"O child, listen; I shall proclaim the procedure for the duties of the limbs, which was previously taught as more secret than the secret."

When an image installed by gods and others has become worn out, one should perform the extraction of the power residing in that particular image; this should be done using a vessel made of metal or clay, provided with a cloth. 23–24.
Having filled the cavity with sprouts of jewels and a bundle of *droṇa* grass,
one should extract the power (*śakti*) from the worn-out image and install it; then,
having the artisan cut away the worn-out body with a sharp weapon.

If one should melt the metal and cast it as a stone image into the waters, and once that image has solidified again, one should sprinkle it with fragrant water; then one should perform all the rites exactly as they were previously performed during the consecration. 26–27.
One should perform everything else, omitting the ritual immersion in water (*jalādhivāsa*), the opening of the eyes (*netronmīlana*), and the ritual deposits such as the *tattvasaṃhāra-nyāsa*;
likewise, one should place the Power (*śakti*) within the pitcher and the image as previously described. 28.
Having installed the Lord of the Gods of gods, the Guru should worship him as before. (29) Regarding the description of the limbs:
the limb is to be known as fourfold, according to the distinctions of the great limb (*mahāṅga*) and so forth.
The major limbs are proclaimed to be the head, the neck, the chest, the belly, the forehead, the arms, the forearms, the hips, the thighs, the knees, and the feet. (30)
The eyes, the nose, the ears, the lips, and the fingers are declared to be the limbs;
these limbs have been definitively stated in all the scriptures. (31)
The minor limbs (upāṅgas) are the teeth along with the nails and body hair, as well as the hair on the head and so forth;
it is definitively stated in the tantras that these are called the "minor limbs" of the Lord. 32.
The minor limbs, the head, the discus, the conch, the discus, and other weapons; the ornaments, the umbrella, the chowries, the throne, the footstool, and likewise the radiance. 33.

These shall be known as the names of the individual limbs of the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. (34) [Having understood these limbs according to the various readings, by the very path previously described.]
The ritual procedure for the sprinkling of water,
the hearing of the Veda, and the inquiry into the Brahman.
"O Blessed One, let the procedure for sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) be told to me: in which rites should one perform it, and what is that procedure like? 35. The Blessed One’s reply:
O Brahmin, listen as I describe the determination of the proper time for the consecration ceremony (saṃprokṣaṇa) when a temple or its constituent parts have suffered damage.
When the banner, the pedestal, the gate, and the weapon [are damaged];
when the image itself, its limbs, or its joints are broken; when it has been restored; when the daily worship is neglected; and when the perpetual lamp and other offerings are extinguished—(36–37).
If a cat, a mouse, or a cow dies in the courtyard of the temple,
or if the image is touched by a Caṇḍāla, a Śabara, or others at that very moment; or if a cock, a crow, or similar creatures are born or die upon it.
If there is the occurrence of contact with feces, urine, and the like in the temple (39),
or if the sacrificial oblation (havis) is defiled by worms, insects, and so forth,
or if the deity laughs, moves, or likewise weeps (40).
When an ant-hill or similar growth has encroached upon a temple or even a pavilion;
when one has been touched by a thief whose identity is unknown; likewise, upon being touched by a firefly; and upon the burning of umbrellas, chowries, or garments by a blazing fire.
If the images of two deities, even when facing one another,
become drenched by rainwater, or likewise if the footprints or the temple are struck by honey or by a lightning bolt, the Guru [should perform the rite]. 42–43.
In the event of the image shaking, falling, or even burning,
as well as upon such other omens, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
If the sprinkling is not performed, there is transgression.
If one performs worship without first performing the sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa),
the builder, the temple, the village, the king, and the kingdom shall perish.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the sprinkling.
The procedure for the ritual sprinkling (*saṃprokṣaṇa*):
having first worshipped Viṣvaksena, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited. (46) [Additional readings follow.]
Having offered the sprouts according to the procedure prescribed in the scriptures,
one should prepare a pedestal of grain in front of the deity and place upon it a great water-pot endowed with all auspicious characteristics. 47
One should perform the worship of the pitcher (kumbhārcana) according to the prescribed ritual up to the end of the fire-oblation (homa);
one should offer oblations with the root mantra, preceded by the peace-offering (śāntihoma).
[This may be done] either with the three highest [mantras] or with the three middle ones. 48.
Then the twice-born preceptor should tie a bracelet upon the hand of the deity.
Having observed the intensity of any defects, the Guru should cause the ritual bathing to be performed,
taking up a great pitcher amidst the sounds of Vedic recitations and musical instruments.

Having circumambulated the temple three times, one should place [the vessel] on a pedestal of grain on the ground in front of the deity, and sprinkle it with the Viṣṇu-sūktas, the Vāruṇa hymns, the Aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta, and the Śānti-sūktas.

One should also feed the brāhmaṇas and give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to one's wealth; the preceptor should be given a fee in accordance with the extent of one's prosperity. He who performs this rite according to the injunction shall attain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The inquiry concerning Brahman for the purpose of hearing the ritual rules for the pacificatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*).
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace, O Puruṣottama, please tell me the ritual procedure for the peace-offering (śānti-homa);
for what purpose is this peace-offering ordained? Tell me all that in detail.
The words of the Blessed One regarding the Blessed One, concerning the festival of installation and the arrangement of the great festival. 55
Also during the annual festival, or according to the rules for the daily festival, when a bad dream occurs, or in the absence of auspicious omens (56),
and when there is an omission of mantras, an omission of ritual acts, or an absence of the required materials.
If the [offering] is past its time, if devotion is lost, or if faith is lost, one should quickly perform pacification according to the rules when there is mutual contact with substances;
this is the procedure for the pacificatory oblation (śāntihoma).
The preceptor, having established the fire either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (vāsthaṇḍila),
should [offer oblations] one thousand and eight times with the Mūrti-mantra of the deity, then with the Mūla-mantra, and further with the Śānti-mantras and Sūktas. 58–59.
Or else, for the sake of accomplishing peace, one should offer one hundred and eight sacrificial twigs, clarified butter, and cooked rice (caru) in sequence, each separately and individually;
one should likewise perform the fire-oblation with sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and śamī leaves.
Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should address the deity with this:
"O Brahmins, for him who always performs peace (*śānti*) according to this procedure,
there shall indeed be the completion of his ritual acts and the attainment of the fruit."
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Atonement, Sprinkling, and Peace-Offering," in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, a Great Upaniṣad within the illustrious Pāñcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Om.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā, within the Great Upaniṣad of the glorious Pañcarātra.
The procedure for the fire-ritual;
the venerable Lord’s determination of the time for the occasion of the fire-ritual.
Now, therefore, I shall explain the unsurpassed ritual of fire (vahnikārya),
which applies to all expiations, as well as to initiation,
sprinkling, festivals, and consecrations; listen attentively to it exactly as it is.
The procedure for the fire-ritual (agnikārya):
having approached the kitchen, one should worship the deities stationed at the door in due order.
Then, on the western side of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), one should face either eastward or northward.
Having sat down in the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana), one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
One should cast flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and other such items on one’s right side,
and having placed the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) on the left, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).

Having performed the consecration of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and other rites with the *ṛc* "eṣa hi deva," one should place [the fire] in front of the fire with hands holding water and *akṣata* grains, and then visualize it facing oneself. 5.
"May you be of gracious countenance, well-pleased, and the granter of boons at all times"—
having thus prayed, the wise one should sprinkle the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa).
6 [Additional Readings]

Having meditated upon Śrī within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed rite as one who has bathed after her menses, the best of preceptors should meditate upon Agni, Gaṇeśa, and Viṣṇu in the center;
he should then worship them with unbroken grains (akṣata) in the cardinal and intermediate directions in due order.
(He spoke of both the Āhavanīya and the other fire): "The word *āhavanīya* follows immediately after *gārhapatya*.
(8) Speaking thus, he mentioned the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Sabhya, the Avanejanīyāgni, the Ratnāgni, and the Dāvāgni as having two heads. (8)
One should perform the sprinkling with [mantras] beginning with *praṇava* and ending in *namaḥ*.

Having spread *darbha* grass around the fire, one should spread it in two layers on the northern side of the fire. Then, having arranged the vessels in due order, one should perform the ritual placement of the vessels (*pātrāsādana*).
The vessels are twelve, eight, six, or four;
one should employ one of these according to the requirements of the ritual.
Having performed the purification of the vessels, one should pour water into the *prokṣaṇī* vessel using two *darbha* blades as a strainer;
having purified it three times with the strainer, one should perform the sprinkling of the vessels.

Having performed the consecration of the *praṇītā* vessel and turned it face upwards, one should pour water into it. Having purified the water as before, one should draw up water to the level of the mouth.
Then, one should place the *praṇītā* vessel upon the *darbha* grass to the north of the fire;
having covered that vessel with *darbha* grass, one should honor the *brahmā* priest to the south. This is the consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*).

Having melted the vessel of clarified butter over the fire and poured the clarified butter into the pot (sthālī), one should take out the embers from the northern side and arrange them around [the fire]. Then, having filled the clarified butter pot according to the prescribed path with the strainer (pavitra), [one should proceed].
Having untied the knot with the thumb and the ring finger, one should wash [the vessel]; this is the consecration of the *sruk* and *sruva*.
One should cast them into the fire with their tips pointing eastward, and thereafter wash the *sruk* and *sruva*. 16.
Thereafter, one should wipe [the ladle] with warm water using five *kuśa* blades. One should wipe the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles with four *darbha* blades, excluding those from the center;
then, having washed them, the preceptor (*deśika*) should place the *darbha* blades into the fire.
[The handle of the ladle] should have a thickness equal to the tip of the thumb and measure three *prādeśas* in length.

One should place the enclosing sticks (paridhi) around [the fire] so that they extend toward the north; their thickness should be equal to the tip of the index finger, and their length slightly less than a span (prādeśa). 18.
One should place the enclosing stick (paridhi) in the south, with its tip pointing eastward;

its thickness should be equal to the middle finger and it should measure slightly less than three spans (prādeśa). One should place the enclosing stick in the north, and its tip is prescribed to be as before. 19–20.

One should place two fire-drills (*araṇi*), each twelve finger-breadths in length and with a thickness equal to the diameter of the little finger, with their tips pointing upward, in the south-east and north-west corners for the *idhmahoma*. 21.
This is the *idhmahoma*.
Having cast fuel-sticks into the fire accompanied by musical instruments, the preceptor takes clarified butter in a ladle using a human bone and fills the *sruva* spoon;
this is the *āghāra-homa*.
Beginning from the northwest corner (vāyavya) and ending at the southeast (vaiśvānara),
one should offer oblations while meditating on Pracaṇḍā during the first āghāra-homa.
Likewise, beginning from the southwest (nairṛti) and ending at the northeast (raudra), [one should proceed in the same manner].
Then, after meditating upon Indra, during the second *āghāra* oblation (24),
one should perform the *cakṣus* oblation: having taken clarified butter in four ladlings (*caturgṛhīta*), one should perform the *cakṣus* oblation.
Having offered oblations with the *vyāhṛtis* in the center, one should meditate upon Agni, the unsurpassed.
(25) This is the Saptajihva-homa. In the middle, one should offer to Viśvarūpa; and to Kālī, one should offer in the direction preceding that [north-east].
I am Karālī here, and Manojava is in the west; Sulohitā is in the north, and Dūmrākṣā is in the southeast corner;
one should offer oblations with the tongues Visphuliṅgā in the southwest and Jihvā in the northwest. 26–27.
One should indeed prepare the Vaiṣṇava fire according to the additional recitations, performing the consecration with the sixteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras),
and one should perform its oblation in the sequence of fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and sacrificial porridge (caru).

Having first offered with the Gāyatrī mantra, the second offering with the Viṣṇu mantra, and the third with the root mantra (mūlamantra), one should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru). Then, having considered them as those who drink the remnants (pāyinaḥ), one should offer to the Bhāgavatas.
The sequence of the lords of the directions (digīśānukrama) has been declared; it is prescribed for the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma).
Regarding the fire-oblation for the retinue and other deities:
during a festival, one should [offer] the retinue and the deities of the seven enclosures (saptāvaraṇadevatāḥ).
Having duly invoked the lunar days and other deities, the stars and their presiding gods, as well as the attendants of Vaikuṇṭha and the twenty-four forms [of Viṣṇu] stationed within the mandala,
one should offer oblations of sacrificial wood, clarified butter, and cooked rice (caru) unto each of those respective deities.

One should offer the *caru* with sixteen oblations while reciting the *Puruṣasūkta*. This is the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittahoma*). After performing the expiatory oblations—the pouring of the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the ritual purification (*mārjana*)—one should then perform the final full oblation. 32.
Having performed the purification by sprinkling water and having filled the ladle with water,
beginning from the northeast corner and proceeding clockwise around the exterior of the sacrificial pit,
one performs the circumambulation of the fire; this is the continuous stream-offering (dhārāhuti).
Having performed the *thārābhiṣeka*, the twice-born should sprinkle his own head;
having offered the fruit to the deity, he should pray with devotion. This is the offering (*samarpaṇa*) to the Blessed One.
Thus has been declared in brief the supreme procedure for the fire-ritual.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Fire-Ritual," in the Śrī Puruṣottama-saṃhitā, within the Mahopaniṣad of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
In the divine scripture of the venerable Pāñcarātra, in the Śrī Puruṣottama Saṃhitā.
The purification of the donor;
the procedure for the daily festival; the ritual arrangement for the daily festival.
This is the inquiry concerning Brahman, for the hearing of Brahman:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Sovereign of all, who pervades the universe!"
O Lord, what is the procedure for the perpetual festival, when should it be performed, and what is its fruit?
O Master, please reveal all of that in detail. This is the Blessed One’s reply.
The Blessed One [said]: "The etymological definition of the word 'utsava' is as follows:
'ud' is a word meaning 'excellent,' and 'sava' is remembered as 'sacrifice' (yajña). 2.
Since this festival is proclaimed as the most excellent and is performed constantly, it is called the "Eternal Festival" (nityotsava). This is the majesty of the Eternal Festival.
It is the purifier of all beings, a source of satisfaction, and the cause of peace;
it consists of various eternal festivals, and the eternal festival is indeed threefold, distinguished as superior, middling, and so forth. 4.
That which is well-performed during the three junctions of the day is declared to be the highest;
that which is middling—
That which is performed at two times is proclaimed as middling;
that which is performed at only one time, specifically at midday, is considered inferior.
The occasion for offering the sacrificial oblation (*bali*):
Without the offering of the *bali*, a festival does not bring about prosperity.

(Therefore, O twice-born one, one should cause the offering of the *bali* to be performed every day. Therefore, by means of the offering of the *bali*, one should cause the supreme festival to be celebrated.
Regarding the varieties of offering materials: one should offer the bali with rice grains alone at dawn, according to the prescribed sequence;
at midday, however, with food; and in the evening, with auspicious flowers.
Regarding the procedure for offering the bali-oblation:
for that purpose, the best of teachers, having taken a bali-vessel made of gold or other precious materials, should fill it with the bali-substances.
One should move that vessel before the deity and enter [the inner sanctum]; having placed it there, the pure practitioner should perform the invocation.
Having worshipped the deity residing in the vessel with *arghya* offerings as prescribed, one should worship Viṣṇu and the others in sequence within the petals situated in the vessel.
Placing that vessel upon the head of an attendant with auspicious items,
the Guru himself, preceded by the chanting of the Vedas, should personally place the *baliberam* upon a palanquin while reciting the mantra "Bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ."
Accompanied by the sounds of umbrellas, chowries, drums, and the like, as well as the resonance of dance and instrumental music,
one should circumambulate the temple in a clockwise direction, having offered the sacrificial oblation (bali) preceded by water and followed by water in due order.
Having circumambulated that pedestal, one should show the bitten [victim] the throat;

in this manner described, having offered the *bali* in sequence to all the enclosures (*āvaraṇas*), or having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should invoke Hari and enter the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*). 14–15.
Having offered the *arghya* with the root mantra, one should join it with the principal form (*mūlabera*).
Then, one should cast the remainder of the *bali* offering upon the head of Viṣvaksena.
At the time of giving the *bali*, there are various forms such as dance, song, and so forth.
Dance, which gratifies the retinue and others, should be known to be of many kinds;
song, however, is praised when joined with the middle [register] for Garuḍa. Likewise, the Gauḍa melody and the dance known as Viṣṇukrānta are prescribed.
The dance of even the Lotus-born (Brahmā) is called Svastika;
the musical mode (rāga) Gāndhāra is said to be Mukhārī.
The Sarvatobhadra belongs to Indra, and the Kheṭaka is said to belong to Agni. 18–19.
The pavement of Varuṇa and the back-pavement of Vāyu;
the wheel-dance of Yama and likewise the forest of Nirṛti (20);
the left knee of Kubera and the standing dance of Īśāna.
The variation of tone (svarabheda) is the Ṣaḍja note for Indra; O Agni, it shall be the Ṛṣabha for Yama; Gāndhāra for Varuṇa; and Madhyama for Nirṛti. 21. For Mṛtyu [it shall be] Pañcama.
The fifth is for Varuṇa; that of the Māruta [gods] is for Kubera; and the Tālabheda is for the Niṣāda and Īśāna.
For Indra, the *samatala* is prescribed; for Agni, the *dravivikrama*;
for Yama, the *bhṛṅgiṇī-tāla*; for Nirṛti, the *mallatāla*; for Varuṇa, the *maṅgala*; and for Vāyu, the *jayatāla*. 23–24.
*Bhadratāla* belongs to Kubera; [the *raudra* drum] beats the *tālaka* for Rudra; the *ḍhakkarī* belongs to the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva);
the *rāgabhda* is for Indra; the drum named *nāda* is for Vahni (Agni); and the *lalita* belongs to Yama. 25.
The *mālaya* rāga belongs to Yama; Bhairavī is remembered as belonging to Nirṛti; *megharāga* and *jīva* belong to Varuṇa; and *vasantaka* belongs to Vāyu.
*Śrīrāga* belongs to Kubera, and *śāṅkara* belongs to Śaṅkara.
In the manner thus described, one should perform dance, song, and so forth. (27) [Additional readings state:
For other deities, however, the *bhadratala* rhythm is recommended.
The *Gāndhāra-rāga*, the *viṣṇukrānta* meter, and the *madhyama* note— this is the definitive conclusion of the scriptures.
[This is] the fruit of offering oblations (*balipradāna*).
In this manner, the most excellent preceptor should cause the offering of the bali-oblation to be performed for the protection of the village, for the gratification of the gods,
for the destruction of the rākṣasas, and for the slaying of enemies. 28.
One should perform the offering of the *bali* for the sake of the complete fulfillment of all prosperity.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Daily Festival," in the *Śrīpuruṣottama-saṃhitā*, a great Upaniṣad within the *Śrīpañcarātra*.
Śrī Śrī Śrī Oṃ.
In the venerable Puruṣottama-saṃhitā, which is included within the venerable Pāñcarātra.
The thirty-third chapter:
The Characteristics of Madras; upon hearing the characteristics of Madras.
O Brahman, O Brahman,
O God of gods, O treasury of compassion, please tell me the characteristics of the mudrās.
"What is the purpose of performing the mudrās at what time?"; the Blessed One’s reply: the Blessed One said:

The etymological definition of the word *mudrā* is as follows: because it will cause the joy (*muda*) of all principles (*tattva*) to melt away (*drāvayiṣyati*), O Four-faced One, let this [mudrā] be known by that name and kept secret.
One should not show the mudrā that quickly propitiates the deity to those outside;
having smeared the hands with perfume, one should perform the binding of the mudrās. 3.
The Śaṅkha-mudrā.
Having formed a fist with the left hand and binding the thumb within it, the joining of the thumb and forefinger is celebrated as the Śaṅkha-mudrā (4).
[Next is] the Cakra-mudrā.
Having turned the right hand downward, one should join the wrist of the left hand by placing it palm-upward; through this very rotation like a wheel, it is celebrated as the *cakramudrā*. 5.
Forming a fist with both hands joined together, with the middle fingers [extended], and keeping the elbows level— this is declared to be the *gadā-mudrā*.
One should touch the tip of the index finger with the tip of the middle finger;
this is called the Śārṅga-mudrā, which strikes fear into all wicked beings.
For the *musala-mudrā*,
one should form a fist with the left hand and likewise a fist with the right; then,
having raised the thumb upward, one should place it [upon the other fist], and thus it becomes the *musala*.
The sword mudrā (khaḍgamudrā) is proclaimed as the fist formed by extending the index and middle fingers like a sword. 9.
The lotus mudrā (padmamudrā).
Having separated the fingers of both hands and joined the two elbows, that which results is called the *vanamālā-mudrā* (garland of forest flowers gesture). 10.
*Vanamālā-mudrā*.
Having joined the fingers of both hands together, one should let them hang down like a garland of forest flowers; this is called the Ananta-mudrā. 11. Ananta-mudrā.
If all the fingers are contracted and formed like a hood, it is the Garuḍa-mudrā;
when the two little fingers are touched and joined together at both hands. 12.
Likewise, having joined the two little fingers and made the two thumbs equal,
one should move them like wings along with the other fingers;
this is the Viṣvaksena-mudrā.
The fist with the index fingers extended is the Brahma-mudrā, which bestows joy upon Viśvaceṣṭa;
it consists of the touching together of all the fingers of both hands. 14.
The Brahma-mudrā is thus described, and the Viṣṇu-mudrā is now being told;
O Lotus-born One, the Viṣṇu-mudrā is formed by the ring finger and middle finger when they are released [from their usual position]. 15.
The joining of the two thumbs is proclaimed as the Rudra-mudrā; it is also known as the Muṣṭi-mudrā.
The fist-mudrā is said to be formed by clenching the fist and casting it toward the offering;
the fragrance-mudrā is the same fist-mudrā with the little finger and ring finger released.
The Flower Mudrā consists of the contraction of all the fingers, with the middle finger released; it is called the Flower Mudrā for the offering of flowers. 17.
Regarding the *yajñopavīta* mudrā:
one should touch the tip of the thumb's first joint with the middle finger;
this *yajñopavīta* mudrā grants pleasure to the God of gods. 19.
The ornament mudrā is known to be formed when the tip of the little finger touches the joint of the thumb; this is considered the mudrā of ornaments and is intended for the seat of adornment. 20.

The incense mudrā (dhūpamudrā) is formed by joining the tips of the fingers together with a gap between them; having likewise positioned the two thumbs pointing upward, it is proclaimed as the incense mudrā. 21.
Having contracted all the fingers, one should display the two middle fingers; this is proclaimed as the lamp mudrā (dīpamudrā) for both hands. 22
Having carefully joined the tips of the five fingers together with the right hand alone, that mudrā is known as the *grāsamudrā*. 23.
The *pratimāmudrā* is that in which the thumbs are raised while the other fingers are clenched into fists; this mudrā is known as the *pratimā*.
The *svāgatamudrā* [is formed by]... [the hands joined together].
With both hands turned upward and the fingers slightly bent,
having separated them while likewise keeping the two thumbs apart— this is to be known as the *āgata-mudrā*, the fire-seal (*dahanamudrā*).
Having meditated on a triangular fire in the left hand, one should place it over the substance;
this is the Dahanamudrā (Burning Gesture), which purifies all substances. [Next is] the Āpyāyanamudrā (Nourishing Gesture).
Likewise, in the hand of Nāvyā, one should visualize a sixteen-petaled lotus;
there, the Moon is situated within the Amṛta-mudrā, likewise dripping with nectar.
One should sprinkle the substances with the hand turned downwards;
this is the Surabhi-mudrā, the seal for nourishment that purifies the substances.
The ring fingers of the two middle fingers [are joined], and the little fingers and index fingers [are joined] in sequence;
if there is likewise contact between both hands with one another, this mudrā is to be known as *Asurabhī*, which bestows the fulfillment of all desires. 28–29.
The *avāhana-mudrā* is the formation of the *virala-añjali*; it is the mudrā known as *āvāhanā*,
while the *kirīṭa-mudrā* is [as follows].
The preceptor, having joined the two palms together with the thumbs, should contract the ring fingers and index fingers and place [the mudrā] upon the head; this is the Śrīvatsa Mudrā. 31.
The mudrā described for the crown is called Śrīvatsa; it is said to be constant. Having placed the left hand palm-upward, one should touch it with the thumb;
this is the Śāntubha mudrā.
Having joined the little finger of the right hand with the little finger of the left hand, one should lead that right index finger [to the palm];
the region of the first three fingers is proclaimed as the *kaustubha*. 34.
The *jñānamudrā* is the joining together of the index finger and the thumb; this is the *tattvamudrā*. 35. *Tattvamudrā*.
That same Śrīvatsa mudrā is proclaimed as the Tatva mudrā;
the Agniprākāra mudrā is formed by touching the middle joint of the index finger with the tip of the thumb.
The teacher should perform the *saṃhāramudrā* by placing the middle fingers upward, then successively encircling the index fingers,
the ring fingers, and the little fingers with the thumbs.
The *saṃhāramudrā* is declared to be intended for the withdrawal of reality;
the *sṛṣṭimudrā* consists of raising the index finger upward while joining the other fingers together.
The Sṛṣṭimudrā is said to be the sequence beginning with the placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa) and so forth;
the Śikhāmudrā is formed by placing the thumb in the middle of the fist and then applying it to the heart.
By joining the index finger with the thumb, there is the placement upon the head;
thereafter, touching the topknot with the fist and the upward-pointing thumb constitutes the armor mudrā (kavacamudrā).
Having contracted the thumbs of both hands along with the fingers, one should place [the hands] from the shoulders down to the feet; this is the *kavaca-mudrā*.
The *netra-mudrā* is as follows:
The Śikhā-mudrā is formed by turning [the hands] downward and placing them between the eyebrows;
this is called the Netra-mudrā. Likewise, the Astra-mudrā is formed with the index finger and the thumb.
And the *sphoṭana* (bursting) everywhere is proclaimed as the *astramudrā*.
Thus, the application of the mudrās for the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) has been demonstrated.
[Additional readings]
Having heard these words from Hari, Vasiṣṭha— the lotus-born one of old—
bowed down again and again to the Lord of the World with a heart full of joy.

O twice-born ones, I have related to you today in brief that entire account of how the creation of the world was commenced by my father Brahmā at the command of the Lord of the Universe, exactly as it was heard by me before.

Out of a desire to favor the world, [I shall explain] this great scripture named Pāñcarātra— the supreme and most excellent, dear to the Blessed One— which is hidden from one who is not a disciple, not a devotee, and not a wise Vaiṣṇava.
It must never be spoken; it should be kept secret, kept secret by the wise.
By the mere hearing of it, the destruction of sins becomes certain;
its recitation and contemplation are the cause for freedom from rebirth.
This great scripture, which is difficult for all people and even for the gods to obtain and is always dear to them, was heard by the sages from the high-souled Vasiṣṭha;
with delighted minds, those sages then began to praise him.
Thus has been declared in brief the supreme characteristic of the mudrās.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Characteristics of Mudrās," in the glorious *Pāñcarātra*, the Great Upaniṣad known as the *Śrī Puruṣottama-saṃhitā*.
Prosperity, prosperity, prosperity!
All is complete.
